title: Introduction to the dataset - sales, production and inventory
text: Professor Mil ind Gandhi: So, maybe it is a good time now to start looking, Siva, now that you have given us this broad overview, maybe a good idea to start looking at a dataset.  Professor Siva Kumar Padmanabhan: Exactly, fantastic.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi: GV, we will have Siva walk us through the data?  Professor Mil ind Gandhi: I will open the Excel.  Professor Siva Kumar Pa Danubian: Perhaps we can start, as I said, we are going to go from the customer backwards, sales backwards in the value chain of the company.  First thing we look at is the sales information. This is basically how much of the product was sold and a t what price was it sold and, during each month. All this data, most of this data is available for the entire 24 months, so from April 2019 all the way to March 2021 to show all the different impacts that happened the BS4 to BS6 transition, the imp act of COVID, the recovery from COVID, and so on, so forth.  What you see in the sales data is, as I said, the 10-year assemblies, which are the finished products that ACE is selling. And for each of those year assemblies, you will see the sales for each month. For example, what you are seeing right now is the April 2019. It shows a total sale of that gear assembly, the numbers up to 8960 units of that finished product was sold, and the price at which it was sold 420 rupees that was the price that it was sold at and so on. You will see from May 2019, June 2019, quantity, and price for all the months, the 24 months. That is the first dataset that you will see.  And when you see this dataset, I think you will see the impacts that we talked about in the sales, you will see that the products number one to the BS4 parts, you will see that there the sales of those products. One of the things that I want you to analyze is what happens to the sales of those BS4 products as the transition to BS6 hap pens on April 1, 2020. That is the first question. And then you will see that the parts number 3 to 8 they are applicable for both BS4 and BS6, so that means that gear sales are not going to stop just because of BS4 or 6. But can you see some seasonal pattern in the year? That is my second question.  Seasonal pattern means at some point in the year the sales is high and then another point in the year was sales is low because we have 2 years. We can start to see potentially some seasonal patterns. My second question is, are there any seasonal patterns you see in the sales data? And then the last set of products is the BS6 products, which initially you will see 0, because BS6 is not kick in till the April 1st, 2020, and then you will start to see their s ales. The question on that point is how, what is the pattern of sales of these BS6 products? Did they, when did they start selling, and why did they start selling at that point, when you did see their sales start? That is the third question.  The fourth question is what is the impact of COVID on the sales of these products? As production actually and sales slowed down after the pandemic struck in March 2020, what kind of impact are we seeing from the pandemic through the next several months as a first wave hit, and then we see that what kind of impact do you see in the sales of these products? That is another question I have. And I also want to find out some things like what are the products that are giving me the highest sales quantity and what are the products that are giving me the highest sales value. Value means revenue, which means not only that if you multiply the quantity and the price and that is when you get the sales value.  Which products gave me the best sales value that I should pay more attention to, because I obviously want to pay a lot of attention to products that giving me a lot of revenue. I want to make sure that there is no shortage of those products and so on. Those are other questions I have on that first table. What is the product that is giving me the maximum revenue, what are the products that are giving me the minimum revenue, which means I might rethink whether it is worth selling those products in the next coming years?  Those are some question s I have on that first table you see.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi: Next table seems to be more from a regional perspective, I see. Maybe you can help us understand this table.  Professor Siva Kumar Padmanabhan: Yes, absolutely. What we then say is because ACE gears sells in all four regions of the country, and automobile clusters are there as you know in multiple parts, so around the best like the Mumbai, Pune, especially, you have a cluster of manufacturers and in the south, of course, Chennai is the Detroit of India. There is a lot of manufacturing activity, also east and north where significant activity happens for companies such as Tata Motors and Mahindra and so on.  The regional sales distribution is given for just three months and is given on LY for the 8 products in this case, this because, of course, the products 9 and 10 were not selling in that particular three months we looked at October 2019, November 2019, and December 2019. This is called the Q3 of the financial year ‘20.  For each of the three months, you will see for the eight products that were selling at that time. You will see the overall sales, but you also see in which region how many units of that product sold. You will see north, east, west, and south. If you take gear assembly 1, for example, in October 2019, it sold 14,400 units. And most of the sales came from east and south, so 11,200 units in the east, and 3200 from south. There were no sales north and west for that unit. That could be because that assembly is used by a particular manufacturer who only has factories in east and south that could be the reason for that. And similarly, you will see for all the eight gears what is the regional sales for each o f the 4 regions. That is what is there in this table. And in terms of questions around this table, I want to understand which regions are most important to me, where is that I am getting the maximum sales quantity, but also the maximum sales revenue. N ow, you must look at both tables to figure out the revenue side of it. That is one part I want to find out.  And then I also want to find out, is there, I could, for example, I could give specific focus to some regions by appointing a regional sales agent. What these regional sales agents do, is they are stationed or located in that region in one of the cities, and they are make sure that, they will make sure that the customers in that region get regular with it, their feedback is incorporated, the schedules are clarified and so on, then the agents can help improve customer relationship and also improve the sales.  If I want to appoint a few agents, then which region should I appoint these agents in and then how many agents should I appoint in each region? If I want to appoint an agent in such a way that it is somewhat related to the amount of revenue I am making from that region. Every region in which I am making more than certain number of products are sold or revenues gathered, I want to appoint those agents and I have a fixed budget for how many agents I can appoint, then how should I appoint those agents?  Which region should I appoint more, and which region should I appoint less? That is another question that I would like to have.  And then I would also like to see are there some products that are clustered in some region, some products are only in cert ain region, some products are only in certain other region, is there a pattern like that? Those are some of the questions that I have from a regional perspective.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi: Then the next table seems to be, I have, let me unfreeze this, and now let us look at this table. Okay.  Professor Siva Kumar Padmanabhan: Now, this one is about production. So, we talked earlier in the case study how, based on how much you are selling, you want to start producing enough so that you do not miss any sales. You have enough product to sell depending on the customer demand.  If the customer is demanding 10,000 then if I have only 9000, I am going to lose the 1000 of sales. Basically, I do not want to do that. I want to make enough so that I can satisfy all the demand that is there. But I do not want to make too much because if I make too much, then that product will lie idle as inventory, either with me or in the regional distribution center or somewhere. That is also not good.  Another thing that is important from a production planning perspective is you do not want production to go up and down as much as the variation in sales. S ales may suddenly peak in one month and drop in another month, because there are many factors. Like for example, if there is a strike, a labor unrest in a car manufacturer’s factory and as you all follow the headlines, Toyota had such a major unrest in 2019, for example, that they had to shut down the factory for several months. Then what happens is, suddenly your demand from your customers going to drop in one month, or it could be a new model that is getting launched by that manufacturer, and initial months you have very high demand, because customers are just trying to get their hands on the product as quickly as they can. A recent example is Mahindra where they introduced the new Thar, the Thar SUV and the demand is so much that even if they produce for one whole year, they cannot catch up to the waiting list. Those types of things happen when the demand is fluctuating a lot.  But you cannot flex your production, you do not want to change your production so rapidly, because then you mean, then it means that number of labors will be idle for some time, and suddenly they will be overworked, and we would not have enough labor. What do you want as a production that is smoother ? It should be responsive to demand, but just not be as much jacked, going up and down rapidly, like the demand. You must have a production plan that is smoother and follows the sales plan.  What you see in this table is for all the 10 assemblies that we make, you will see the thing called beginning inventory, which means at the start of the month, how many of those products were already in my store, finished goods store or in my warehouse, and then you see how much was actually produced that month, then you will see the ending inventory, which is at the end of the month how many products do they have on hand, at the end of the month.  For every single one of those months, from April ‘19 to March ‘21, you will see the beginning inventory of the gear assembly 1, for example. You will see how much of gear assembly 1 was produced that month. And then you will see how much of the inventory still line with me at the end of the month. And I think as you can logically imagine the ending inventory, the inventory that I have at the end of the month will be equal to how much did I have at the beginning, how much did I make, and then how much did I sell.  Logically, you can put those three things together to find what is the ending inventory. And so similarly, you will have that data for all the 24 months for all the 10 products. So, that is what you see in this table. One thing you will see is that production does vary. So, if we look at gear assembly 1, we produce 7000 in April, we increased to 9000 in May, and then we kept 9000 for some months, and probably then we start decreasing or increasing depending on the customer demand. You see that 10,000 in September and so on. There is a pattern to this. But if you see the same gear assembly 1 in the previous table, if you see the sales, if I can go back to the first table on the top, you see the sales of gear assembly 1 it was 8960, then it fell to 7960, then it suddenly increased to 10,960 and then 5960 and so on. You see that there are a lot of ups and downs in the sales of the product. But production is also going up and down. But it is not going as rapidly up and down.  And this is the job of the what we call that the sales and operations planning that we saw on that chart earlier that says, how is my sales going to behave, and therefore, how is my production should look for each month. The sales and operation planning and the market production scheduling, which is the next step we saw. These two activities will make sure that we produce the right amount and that we produce it smoothly and not so up and down as much as the sales.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Siva just for my understanding, I mean, do I understand that each gear assembly is manufactured by a different machine and has different, as people associated with that manufacturing, because the reason I am asking that question is that we are trying to smooth each row, and we are not taking the total and smoothening the total right?  Professor Siva Kumar Padmanabhan: Yes. That is an excellent question. We should also be smoothing the overall production. So, that is also what NPS tries to look at, like what is the resources available. So, to your question, it is all shared. It is not dedicated lines. You will see later in the production scheduling part of the case study that the same robbing machine is used to make two gears in different ways. Yes, it is all shared. And the goal is, like you said, to smooth not only one product, but to smooth the entire system.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Okay.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi: Two observations I had Siva. First is, this table that you have shown us seems very similar to the ledger that we were seeing in the e-commerce case, because there what we saw was that opening stock plus incoming goods minus sales was equal to closing stock. And it seems to me, at least at first glance, that you are looking at something similar here. Professor G. Venkatesh: Except that I would, the only thing is that their incoming can be anything. Variation incoming is not a problem there. But here it must be smooth, because for whatever we discussed just now, production needs to be smoother. You cannot just have variability in production.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi: The second sort of thing that immediately strikes me is that if production is smooth and sales are sort of variable, and the amount that I have in my warehouse will keep changing constantly, actually. It will have big shifted, big swings and that would be another challenge perhaps for the warehouse manager to manage.  Professor Siva Kumar Padmanabhan: Yes, absolutely, Mil ind. That is very true. And that is the role the inventory plays slightly. Inventory is both bad and good or good and bad. The bad aspect of inventory is, if you have a lot of inventory, then it is idle products, it is locked up capital, it is not actually being used in the further in the value chain. But the good part of inventory is that it helps you to do the smoothing. It makes sure that your sales do, your production does not exactly match y our sales, because you can dip into the inventory when you need more and if you are producing more you can add to the inventory.  But as you said rightly the inventory is a very important thing to manage the store, the space that is required and the security that is required to manage the inventory, the warehousing, and sometimes some production, like we know in the case of vaccines, now cold storage is required, not in this room this kind of product, but those things are all part of the inventory management is do you have the right storage, do you have the right conditions, ambient conditions for storage, do we have enough security and control over the inventory. So, that is very important.  So, one of the questions that therefore I will have in this is how do you manage inventory from a warehouse manager perspective? How much is the maximum and the minimum? And therefore, what kind of percentage variation I am having in that inventory over the 24 months? So, how big a space should I take, like or should I, what is the level of variation that you see in the inventory is an important question in this exercise.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi: Siva you have given us the inventory data as well. And to me at first glance it seems very similar to the production plan. What is the difference between the two? Maybe you can explain this table and tell us what is the difference from the production? Professor Siva Kumar Padmanabhan: Yes. So, the first table we just saw was the is called the production plan for the finished product. If you think back on that slide, we saw there are two stages in this production. First, we must take the blanks and we must make the gears. And then we must assemble the gears together and test and pack and ship it. These are the two stages.  What you see in this table, here on the screen is the finished product assembly production plan. So, that means I must make 7000 assemblies in April 2019. That is what you see there. But to make 7000 assemblies, I need to have the two components available to make the assembly. So, what you see in the below table is the plan for the first stage, which is how do I make the two gears and how much do I make each month so that I can then create assembly in the second stage.  What you see here are the gears 2 -A, 2-B, 3-A, 3-B and so on, so these are the gears required to make the assemblies 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. So, we are showing the 6 just for the sake of managing the amount of data. For each of those assemblies there are two gears that are required. And what is the production plan for those two gears? So, this is how we go level by level.  We start with how much should we produce for finished product; how much should we produce at each of the sub-assemblies and how much should we produce of each of those parts and so on. What you see here is the production plan for the individual gears themselves because the robbing and broaching are the two steps required to make the individual gear. And then the assembly is the next stage where we put the gears together, test it and aligned it in packed little chip.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi: That, then my natural question is, what is, what was the term that you used the bluff material?  Professor Siva Kumar Padmanabhan: Yes, here we are seeing the bill of material in action.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi: And that should be a little bit of comfort for us with perhaps because then from a purchasing perspective I can smooth out the purchases' be cause the same blank is being used into products. Professor Siva Kumar Padmanabhan: Absolutely, absolutely. Even if you have, let us say, more demand for 3 -A bit at the same month you have less demand for 4 -A that means you do not have to change your purchasing of blank 011 because there will be more use in one place and less use at another place. So, the more we have common components, the more you can smooth your production and make the product structure less complex. And this is the areas on that automotive manufacturers go for platforms, the strategy of platforms.  If you look at many cars, they can be built on the same platform. So, for example, right now the Volkswagen Group is launching a platform called MQB A0 IN India. And on t op of this single platform which uses common components in the chassis and common engines, they can make a SUV, they can make compact sedans, they can make midsize sedans, they can make hatchbacks so all of these and the strategy behind that is exactly this, you have fewer components, you have fewer of assemblies on which you can build multiple different types of products.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi: Very, very interesting. Siva all the other Excel sheets have the same data, right? There is no other raw data.  Professor Siva Kumar Padmanabhan: Yes. That is the data you have not probably seeing it and then there is also data on purchasing.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi: Okay.

title: AB Testing Introduction
text: Business Data Management Professor G. Venkatesh Doctor Mil ind Gandhi Mister Venkat Subramanian Indian Institute of Technology, Madras A/B Testing Introduction Mil ind Gandhi: I think all the different insights we looked at were all pretty interesting. I am already excited to try out some of these ; maybe it makes sense for us to show pay later to younger consumers.  Maybe we do it more prominently on the mobile because people a already seem to be choosing a mobile. But one question I have is when we implement some of these recommendations and show Pay Later to these consumers, how can we be sure that we are getting the right results because of these new rules we are putting in? What does) possibly do ? G. Venkatesh: Some simulation s you want us to do? This is about you asking.  Mil ind Gandhi : I think simulation is one way to think about it. Another thing I was thinking about along the way was AB testing in the industry. If you want to test out any such concept like this, we use AB testing, where we try to see if this new method is more powerful than what we are currently doing. Maybe I can share some visual that explains the concept.  G Venkatesh : Please do that ; I think we need to understand what is A and B. I presume there are two categories of people, A and B ; you are trying to divide them into two sets, A and B. Mil ind Gandhi: The AB testing is also known as the control method. So, we will find these two words used. It is all the same. Let us say you have a whole bunch of consumers, your target population on which you want to test any particular idea. Here, we talk about marketing, but it could also be something else.  You want a whole bunch of consumers. Now you want to test whether this new idea is better or not. The right way to do it is not to implement the new idea on everyone but to split them into two groups. You can call the two groups A and B, or you can call them test and control.  G Venkatesh: I see. Mil ind Gandhi: The basic exposes only the test group to the new idea, whereas the control group continued similarly. G Venkatesh: The symbol eye you have shown there means allowing them to see it. And that cross you put on their shows that you do not let them know. They are not seeing it.  Mil ind Gandhi: Let us take o né example. Somebody tells you that your website is all very dull. Why do you not try a new pink color for your entire website? It is a very crazy idea, but maybe it will work. You do not know.  The only way to test is you do not change the website to pink color for everyone. You change it to pink for this test group of people who will see the new pink color. There is a whole group of people who are going to see the old black and white website still. Now, what you are visiting, you need to know your ultimate intent.  You want your objective. If people come to your website, you want them to sign up or maybe to want them to take membership or something like that. That is the main objective. Now, you will measure whether this test group exposed to the new pink color website is behaving differently from the control group, who did not see that website and did not see the pink color.  So, you are looking at how many of these people sign up for a membership, or how many of these people buy the product that you want them to by y, any internet action. You are mentioning the test and control groups and seeing at a per -user level whether there is a difference between the test and control populations.  So, that difference, and you measure what the difference, the lift as we call it if there is a lift is; and one more idea is essential here, that lift should not just be a lift, it should be statistically significant lift, which means that the charge should be sizable enough compared to what you are measuring.  You cannot get a small o né lift on something that h as value and say I do the lifts. There are ways in which we can probably look at that later, but there are statistical tests that will tell you whether the charge is statistically significant or not.  Once you know that, that is when you conclude that A, I see that the test group which saw the new website in pink color is statistically doing better than the control group which did not seem that, therefore I can prove that the new pink color is great. Now, I will change the website to pink for everyone. G Venkatesh: So, this test group must be carefully selected. You have to pick the test group carefully. Because it should not be that the lift is occurring for reasons other than this pink color, you have to re move all different causes.  Mil ind Gandhi: Excellent point ; I think the key criteria on for doing this is to ensure that the test group and control group, before the experiment, are exactly alike ; there is no difference between them. They must have similar people across identical age groups and preferences ; everything should be the same for them.  During the experiment, the only difference they are subjected to should be this, in this case, that website color. Then, when you observe the difference in their output, you will correlate that 100 persons that this is new only due to that particular color change and not anything else.  When we looked at this whole thing in the concept of website and all, I think this is a very, very renowned concept. Like if you think about how people test new drugs, like new medications, new vaccines, everywhere this concept is used, let us say when they come up with a new vaccine, and they want to test it on 100 people, they will not give it typically to all the 100.  They will give 90 people that vaccine and the other ten will be given a placebo, which is nothing but some empty dummy medication. Then they will see if there is a difference between these two groups. I mean, is this the treated or the tested group performing better than that control group ? So, it i s a widespread way to measure the effectiveness of any new treatment or idea in general. Venkat Subramanian: This was very interesting, G V. We should go and do this analysis and come back and show it. W e will need to look at the data from multiple periods.  How do we do this AB testing? We first looked at traditional data before we created the new method. And then we look at, or we do it in the same period but two groups. How do we do this ? Mil ind Gandhi: You have the current data of customers and their transaction behavior, all we shared with you earlier, where you draw the analysis insights. Taking that group, you need to divide your customers into two groups, the test group and the control group, making sure they look very similar.  Like let us say you compare the percentage of debit card transactions in group one to group two; it should be similar, percentage of credit cards should be similar, age and tenure everything should be similar. In that way, you can select two groups. And then, during the same period, you subject them to different treatments.  For one group, maybe you will use all the rules you gathered earlier to show them Pay Later option only for a certain combination. For example, you said Pay Later is easier to use on mobile. Maybe you say Pay Later is easier for fashion. So, for this group, you will also Pay Later using all those rules in the correct order ; for the other group, you show it randomly.  Then at the end of whatever period you are testing, if we see a difference between the behavior of these two groups, maybe one like how do we measure the difference, perhaps we can say one group becomes, does more number of transact ions than other, any metric. If we see a difference between them, then that concludes that these rules are very effective.  Venkat Subramanian: S o, you are testing within the same period; it is not an earlier period versus new. The test group versus the control group is within the same period. Mil ind Gandhi: Correct. In that earlier period, another method we call pre -post testing, where we say before doing something, there was a confidence and then after pre and post, and we measure the difference. But the problem with that method is that you can never be assured that that change between the pre and the post is only due to this factor.  Because there is) , maybe people go through different experiences in their lives. Perhaps the economy is changing.  The data typically gets) when you move from one time period to another. So, the proper testing method is to do this in a single period for two different but similar -looking populations. Venkat Subramanian: Fantastic. So, GV, shall we do this calculation, will do the analysis, and come back to Venkat.  G Venkatesh: It should be fun to do. Yes, definitely. We should do it.

title: What is credit risk analysis
text: Business Data Management Professor G. Venkatesh Doctor Milan Gandhi Mister Venkat Subramanian Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Mil ind Gandhi: The next person to talk to is Nikita Sharma. Who is Nikita?  Venkatesh Subramanian: Nikita is a global credit officer of Pay Buddy. A credit business company has a Credit Risk Officer. They ensure that the business is running the right way, the lending decisions are made with a proper rationale, and so on. Here, Nikita Sharma is in charge of the profit and loss of the credit business.  Mil ind Gandhi: I see. And what kind of problems would she typically face ? Venkatesh Subramanian: The fundamental core problem of credit is making sure that you lend to the right person with a reasonable likelihood of paying back. Typically, when you have such schemes, especially this kind of cred it, there is no collateral. For example, if you take a home loan, the home becomes underlying collateral.  You can recover the money by selling your home if you do not pay the bank. But think about credit cards and online credit ; there is no collateral. If the customer does not pay back, the company loses the entire money lent to him. But then, at the end of the day, nobody can be 100% sure that everyone will pay back. There is some level of risk that the company is taking by lending money. So, the primary role of a credit risk officer like Nikita Sharma will be to ensure that you have a reasonable estimation of how many people will pay back and how many will not. The officer also keeps s the profit and loss in the correct location.  G. Venkatesh: Nikita a Sharma would report it to the finance -CFO organization.  Venkatesh Subramanian: But in many other companies, she can likely report to the CFO because, ultimately, this is in the dollar value of the business.  Mil ind Gandhi: Some things are not clear to me, Venkat, and maybe you can help me understand. First, you spoke about credit in terms of the loan. Secondly, you also mentioned EMI and collateral. We hear these terms quite a bit, but what exactly do they mean? I think it would be good if our students understood that.  Venkatesh Subramanian: Sure sir. Whenever you borrow any amount of money, let us take this example of online credit. You are buying, let us say, a mobile phone for Rs.10000 on some e-commerce platform. Usually, you would have paid for it directly through your bank account, but now you decided to take the credit option.  You have ta ken credit from a company like Pay Buddy. Now, this Rs.10000 is the actual money you borrowed from Pay Buddy. Now you need to pay it back. Typically, most schemes do not demand you to pay it in one shot. They give you monthly options, also called easy monthly installments.  Typically, whenever there is an interest charge, they try to distribute this interest over those three or four months or whatever period and create that monthly repayment amount for you. In this case, since there is no interest, let us prob ably keep it simple. So, you have borrowed Rs.10000. Let us say you get four months to pay it back.  So, the monthly installment will look like Rs.2500 every month. On a fixed date, you pay back Rs.2500. At the end of four months, you would have paid it back entirely, and your balance is clear.  Mil ind Gandhi: So, what happens if some customer delays paying back? Venkatesh Subramanian: So, I think all of this in any credit business, you put the customers into different buckets. Some customers will have paid all their dues and fall in the 'no due bucket.' There will be other customers who are slightly delayed ; we call them up to 30 days past due, like zero to 30 days past due, where they are delayed by a week or two.  Similarly, you will have 30 to 60 days past due, 60 to 90 days, and so on. The bucketing is essential because a lot of us may pay slightly delayed just for no wrong reason. Sometimes our salary gets delayed, or we have other commitments. So, the company typically does not want to do anything at this stage, up to 30 or 60 days. The company will wait for the customer to pay back automatically.  Once it crosses that threshold, let us say 60 days past due, it probably indicates a high likelihood that the customer is doing this intentionally. He has over the intention of being back, or he is just not prioritizing this. In this case, the company will typically route him to the call cent her, which will call the customer, remind them, ask him to repay the loan, and so on. The call cent her then takes over a ND does the multiple calls over a while.  There will be some customers who will pay back once they get called a couple of times. There will be other customers who do not even pay back at that stage.  After a point, if there is no likelihood of the customer paying back, the company has two choices. One to write off that particular loan and say, okay, this is a loss I am incurring. Typically, they do this for small online loans, like what we are talking about. For a bigger loan like a home loan or a considerable amount, then the company might take legal action against the borrower.  G. Venkatesh: So, it is called the moral hazard problem. If you do not take action against the person, people will have the reputation that you are very soft. Then others also will not want to pay, right because one guy does not pay, he gets off, then other people will say and see what happens.  Venkatesh Subramanian: Correct. That is an attractive answer here. If you remember, I think very early in India, like 10 -15 years back, when the credit cards were all still new, there was this whole controversy that the card companies were sending guns to the people's houses to collect the loan back. G. Venkatesh: Right.  Venkatesh Subramanian: They went into a legal controversy around this, and the courts said they are not allowed to do that. They need to use only softer means. So, today I do not think it is happening anymore. Nobody is sending guns to people's homes, but still, they are running a business.  The main reason is that there is something called credit reporting in place, which is that all these banks have a report to a central agency that maintains the track record of repayment for every unique customer. It is called your centralized credit score. In India, there is an agency called CIBIL.  It maintains the credit rating for all of us. The score might be 700 ; my score is 300 or something. It is cumulative proof of every repayment you have made. If you miss one or two payments, your score will be slightly lower. Therefore now, why is this incentivizing you to pay back?  If you do not pay back a particular loan, maybe that particular company will not take any action against you. They will be soft, but this will reflect on your credit score. Tomorrow when you have another borrowing need, let us say you need a home loan. Other companies will think twice before lending to you because your credit score will look bad and reflect that you are a person who does not pay back.  G. Venkatesh: I see. So, there is a centralized mechanism that has been created. Is this CIBIL a government -owned entity, or is it a private company ? Or how is it?  Venkatesh Subramanian: I think it is a private company, but they have to ensure it is not like any company can go and do this. There are legal regulations and government regulations and guidelines that sort of give this special license to certain companies. CIBIL is one of them.  G. Venkatesh: It is a kind of consortium model. Everybody is to the benefit of all people giving money, all lenders. It is their joint interest to create this kind of consortium and a scoring mechanism. And so, for them to share data and all that because only if they share data would they get back some score which will tell them whether this particular person is worth lending to.  So, they have to give data to get a score. So, everybody sees the interest in doing that. Venkatesh Subramanian: Correct. That is what is happening, and it helps them in multiple ways. One, because they share data, everyone knows the credit scoring of any particular individual, whether he is a person who is likely to pay back or not. So, many of them can decide not to lend if the person turns out to be the wrong person.  Another thing these companies do is also change the interest rat e based on the credit score of the person. So, if you are an n excellent customer who is always likely to pay back, you might get a reasonable interest rate, preferably an interest rate, say 7 %. Let us say, if I am a slightly irregular person, I am not like bad.  It is not like I take the money and run away, but I am irregular. The company will fix it at a slightly higher rate if I miss one or two payments. So, I think it helps them customize their offerings and products based on the customers' risk level.  Mil ind Gandhi: I see. So, does Pay Buddy also look at some score s like this when deciding to allow credit?  Venkatesh Subramanian: Absolutely, sir. Now, if you think about it, there are two ways a company like Pay Buddy can do this. It can go to a company like CIBIL and buy the score for every customer. That is probably the cleanest and most straightforward way because it has all your history for the last ten years.  So, Pay Buddy can simply look at that score and decide that if the CIB IL score of the customer is above a specific number, let us say above 700, and then I am going to give this buy now pay later option.  If it is below, that means that person is not creditworthy, and I will not give him Buy now Pay Later. That is a simple way they can do it. But the only challenge, in this case, is that they must buy this credit score from CIBIL and pay it to CIBIL. CIBIL is an agency because it has to run itself. They charge money for every credit score give n to you as a company. Now they h ave to think whether it is worth spending that money.  What is the IR alternative if they do not want to do this?  They can try to use their internal data. If a company like Pay Buddy has some past credit product or other data, they can use internal data to create their own credit model that says whether the customer is likely to pay back. Typically, such internal models will have lower power than external ones because the amount of data available to one company Pay Buddy is less than that to a major company like CIBIL. But still, if they believe that their internal data is powerful enough, they can avoid going to CIBIL and do it internally. But one way or the other, they fundamentally need that final credit score for a customer before they decide to give him that buy now pay later loan.  G. Venkatesh: But Venkat, the CIBIL, has only information about payments. I mean, they only know how many EMIs were paid, not paid, something like that. However, inside Pay Buddy, you would have much more information about the customer. You will have all the demographic profile s, including purchasing history, which is not present in the database of CIBIL.  Venkatesh Subramanian: Correct, sir. I think that is an n excellent point. Let me slightly modify the statement I made earlier.  Even if they purchase your credit score from CIBIL, a company like Pay Buddy will ultimately still leverage other internal data points it has about you. The lending decision is not only about your credit repayment but also how likely you will become a high LY engaged customer tomorrow.  Are you in a younger age group who is likely to transact more? Many dimensions can be mixed into that ultimate decision. It may not be purely from a credit score perspective. Correct.  Mil ind Gandhi: Suppose G. V and I both have a credit score of 800. My monthly salary is one lakh, whereas G. V's monthly salary is one and a half lakhs. Then obviously you can give more loans to G. V than to me.  Venkatesh Subramanian: Correct.  Mil ind Gandhi: How is this factored in, or is it already factored into your credit score?  Venkatesh Subramanian: Typically, I do not think credit score inherently takes into account your income. It is more about your outstanding loans and your repayment history. But as Professor G. V mentioned earlier, a company like Pay Buddy knows a proxy for your income.  It knows how many transactions you are making in a month. It knows how many items you are buying online over one year. Furthermore, it knows how many luxury items you purchase and how many essential grocery items. So, all these are not directly your income but strongly correlate to your income. So, typically they will also use those parameters in making the decision to lend to you, even if they do not directly access your income.  Mil ind Gandhi e: So, even if two people have the same credit score, you would have a different maximum amount of money you would lend to somebody. Is it?  Venkatesh Subramanian: That is true. I think you bring up another interesting point. The decision is not only about whether I will lend or not. The decision is also about how much I can lend. As you said, probably even if two people have the same credit score now, depending on my assessment of their income level or spending behavior, I can decide to lend more to one person and less to another.  Mil ind Gandhi: I see.  Venkatesh Subramanian: The only word of caution I will put here is that the whole credit industry is highly regulated. In many countries, the government play s an active role in making sure that companies use fair lending policies in making sure that they lend in the right way and responsibly. Main LY the U.S. is a good example.  In the U.S., when you are making a lending decision, you cannot use certain features called protected features to make your lending decision. For example, you can never use somebody's race or ethnicity in your lending decision. Somebody's gender, you cannot use it. Somebody's age, you cannot use it. So, many of these are called protected features of consumers, and the belief is that if you allow companies to do this right, maybe they will try to give credit only to, let us say, well -earning males from a particular race or ethnicity.  G. Venkatesh: This is a little tricky because we know a correlation between income and gender, for example.  For whatever reason, there is discrimination in the workplace, and men tend to get higher salaries than women.  Venkatesh Subramanian: Correct.  G. Venkatesh: I could have used the income to decide how much to lend. Somebody could come back and say that yo u have discriminated against me because I am a woman. So, how do you make sure that you are compliant with these kind s of regulations? Venkatesh Subramanian: It is a very tricky question. So, in many companies like Pay Buddy, a separate legal committee will review your credit decision model. It could be a data science model which takes a lot of variables or a manual rule -based one like is credit score above x and that kind of whatever it is. This legal committee will review every dimension of the data point you use in your lending decision.  Sometimes it will be a direct no like, okay, you cannot use age, you cannot use gender. Sometimes, as you said, it might be an internet correlation. You are using something else as a proxy for that. For example, a good example is that in the U. S., different ethnicities or ethnic groups live in certain regions.  You will find that Indians typically live in specific zip codes. You will find that black people live in certain areas. Now, you may not use race directly in your model, but you might use some variable around the customer's zip code or the customer or the pin code of the customer. Now, indirectly you are sort of understanding where they are living and who they are without directly explicitly using that age in is not allowed.  It thoroughly scrutinizes direct and indirect correlation s to ensure that no particular group is disadvantaged in access to credit. But then I am talking primarily about the U.S. If you look at many other countries, including India, the see rules do not exist, meaning companies can still play around with different variables in deciding who to lend to. G. Venkatesh: But it will come to visit even in India.  Venkatesh Subramanian: It might come, but I would not be 100% sure. There are other developed countries like Europe. Even though they have been in this business for a long time, such rules still do not exist. It is up to the company to whom he decides to lend money. As a government, I will not interfere in such cases.  G. Venkatesh: Very interesting because normally, one would have thought Europe would be more friendly and socialized. The U.S. would take the call of rating the company. But it seems to be in reverse order.  Venkatesh Subramanian: I mean, I would not say they have entirely left it off also. They will also control it to some extent. But the U.S. is the foremost in this level of how much it tries to protect its citizens. European regulations are, at least in the credit space, slightly lighter. Mil ind Gandhi: Okay, so you have described the process to us, Venkat, but we also have some data and I thought it may be interesting to look at the process through the data angle.  Venkatesh Subramanian: Definitely, yeah. We can talk about some of these dimensions we discussed now.

title: Credit risk analysis review of data
text: Business Data Management Professor G. Venkatesh Professor Dr. Mil ind Gandhi Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Credit risk analysis: review of data G. title: Explanation of the credit risk dataset
text: Business Data Management Professor G Venkatesh, Doctor. Mil ind Gandhi, Mister. Venkat Subramanian Department of Science Indian Institute of Technology, Madras W11L5 Mil ind Gandhi: Yes. I would request you to explain the data tools.  Venkat Subramanian: Sure. So this is interesting data. Essentially, over the last three months, it talks about every customer of Pay Buddy, who applied for this particular 'Buy now pay later option, and whether they got approved or declined. It is the simplest level. So column A, as we know, talks about the customer ID ; column B talks about the date on which they applied for this particular credit offering, 'Buy now pay later '.  Column C talks about their existing customer segment, where they are highly engaged, mid engaged, or low engagement with Pay Buddy. Column D is the credit score. In this case, it is an internal credit score that Pay Buddy itself has created. But as I said, it could be a score like a CIBIL score that Pay Buddy is buying from an external agency. Either way, this is the credit score, which reflects the applicant's credit risk. Typically, the higher the score, the better.  Prof. G Venkatesh: Is there a standard norm for this? Is there a kind of standard for the Benchmark Number ? Across the world, do you get the same rating, or in different countries have different ways of scoring? Venkat Subramanian: I think different countries have different ways of scoring. But you will typically feel that the score ranges between 400 and 700, or 800. 400 is on the worst side, and 700 or 800 is on the Best end of the s core. Even in this case, the score is an internal score created by a Pay Buddy and adhere d to a scaling convention. I think it is a score ranging up to 400 or three early, like late 300 to 500.  Mil ind Gandhi: So somebody with a 588 score has been approved. But somebody with a 559 score has been declined.  Prof G Venkatesh: Pretty close.  Venkat Subramanian: It is not only the credit score. Look at the 455 and 484 scores. They are both declined.  Mil ind Gandhi: Yes.  Venkat Subramanian: So it does look like there is a threshold there. Another criteria on could be Column E, which is the Application Amount, right? It is requesting the credit or loan form. You would expect, again, that normal intuition should tell us that the lower the amount, the lower the risk.  If I am getting 200 Dollars, I do not mind, even if your credit score is as low as 450. But if I am getting, let us say, 1,000 Dollars, then probably I will put stricter criteria about how much I want your credit score to be. So that could be an essential dimension in this whole decision. Then, in column F, you see whether the customer got approved or declined when they applied.  Column G is more interesting wherever there is a decline. It says a decline reason. Now declined claim reason has multiple values. So probably, Professor, if you click on the G's, one cell, and then do a drop -down, we will see the different possible values a decline reason can have.  Mil ind Gandhi: No, I think we did this thing.  Venkat Subramanian: Ye s. So it has multiple values. So maybe I will look at the second value, which is probably the most important one, a credit risk. It says that the customer was declined because his credit rating was not good enough. Probably the most relevant to what we this cussed so far. But the other values also show you that it is not only credit risk. There could be other reasons why I am declining you.  So compliance is the reason. Now, what does compliance mean? Now this customer could be a customer that would be compliance rules which say that you cannot give credit to somebody less than ten days old in your system. You might have compliance rules which say that if the customer has not verified his address or phone number, you cannot give him credit. As I say, credit is generally regulated in every country. Only the level of regulation varies between countries.  Prof G Venkatesh: There is the age limit for compliance. Venkat Subramanian: Good question. Yes, I think you need to be at least 18 years old in most regulations to be given credit. So, these are the set of compliance rules to which the customer will be a particular application would be subjected. If the rejection is happening then, i n one way or the other way, maybe because of your age, maybe because you have not verified your address, maybe you have not given your ID proof, whatever the reason, then that will be a compliance decline. Again, eligibility is another bucket language. It is very similar to eligibility, but eligibility could be a bit more internal to the company. Pay Buddy, as a company, might have specific eligibility rules. Again, it might be to do with your age, or it might be to do with the number of days you have spent in the Pay Buddy system. They might say, "I am not going to give a credit to anyone less than 30 days old in my Pay Buddy system.  Those are basic eligibility rules. Your credit score might be very high, like an 800 credit scoring guy, but if you are less than 30 days, you are not eligible for my product. So that is an eligibility decline. Fraud risk is another thing. Most of these credit lending companies have a separate fraud model, which identifies people who are intent tonal fraudsters and who try to abuse the system.  They are the people who take us loans with no intention of paying them back. They are the people who try to steal somebody else's credit card or debit card and try to create an account. So there are lots o f, an online world is very, very prone to fraudsters. So, if the particular fraud rules and fraud model identify you as a potential fraud risk, then that could be a reason for the decline, that is the fraud risk.  And finally, you also see a bucket core system issue, which I think is that the system could not evaluate and approve your application at that particular moment. Mil ind Gandhi: So some applications may get rejected, even though they should have been approved. Venkat Subramanian: That is true. I me an the overall application approval rate will be only if you pass through all these criteria.  Mil ind Gandhi: And system issue could also impact your overall transaction throughput as).  Venkat Subramanian: Correct. Very well. Absolutely. Yes. System issue. In general, without credit, if there is a system downtime, it will affect your transaction completion.  Mil ind Gandhi : Okay, the last column is even more interesting.  Venkat Subramanian: Correct. It is a truth. Finally, they took the loan, and after those n number of installments, have they paid it back or not? Now, in that case, maybe the data is slightly simple for ease of processing by the students. The real data is a bit more complex.  It will say, "Did you pay your first installment or not? What date? How many days are delayed by you for the first installment? Similarly, for the second installment, did you pay partially? " There will be so many nuances to the data. But ultimately, at the end of the day, you are saying whether somebody paid back or defaulted on their loan. We are trying to simplify it by giving that as a binary flag between paid back and default.  Mil ind Gandhi: Okay.  Prof G Venkatesh: And all the entries for which you have given them a loan, you will have an entry in edge, which says either paid back or default.  Venkat Subramanian: Yes, you will see wherever we have declined, that value does not h ave meaning, so you see a NA there, but wherever we have given then 'Approved' as an which means they have given them a loan, you will see that they are paid back or defaulter. So, it will be interesting to see how good our decision was. I mean, like whet her this credit score reflects the likelihood of somebody to pay back.  If it is a perfect credit score in column D, you will see that you should see that the higher the score, the more likely the person is to pay back, but it is possibly not a perfect credit score. So you see, you might see an inverse relation. So all these are potential analyses we could perform.  Prof G Venkatesh: I mean, you do not know. This information is insufficient to determine how well you did on the decline side. You have no idea whether they were paid back or not because you have declined it.  So there it is lost. If you took a conservative view and declined, many people may lose some business. We do not know, and there is no way to find out. Whereas, for the people you have approved, some people may have defaulted, so if you were a little bit risky, then you will know whether you are risky or not, that you will know. But if you are conservative, you have no way of figuring out whether you are on the right path or not.  Venkat Subramanian: Very true, sir, and it is a fascinating point. It is a slightly more advanced topic, but I will give an overview. When people develop credit models, there is a whole concept or reject inferencing, which essentially talks about what you are saying. What can you infer about the customers you have dismissed or declined? One way we do it. Prof G Venkatesh: It is called Reject inferencing.  Venkat Subramanian: Reject inferencing.  Prof G Venkatesh: I see, okay.  Venkat Subramanian: One way they do this within the particular company system. You will not have data because you have just declined. So you no longer know anything about the customer. But still, external agencies like CIBIL or other agencies will have data. So just for educational purposes and for the model to learn, you will collect data about the customers you have declined, and then see whether your decision was right or not. That can be used to create a better model in this region.  Mil ind Gandhi: I see. So, I declined a loan, but maybe, G.V. gave him a loan, and actually, that guy paid the loan back to GV, then I know that my decision was wrong.  Venkat Subramanian: Exactly, exactly.  Mil ind Gandhi: Some proxy way. So, I may not, of course, know that G. V gave him a loan for the same reason. But some proxy, you try and build. Prof G Venkatesh: From the CIBIL score, you try and make out.  Venkat Subramanian: You try to make out whether you should have ideally approved or not. So your declined decisions, you can infer that way. Though it is slightly more cumbersome because the approved people wait three months, you know whether they are paying back or not.  So the approved decision and judge very quickly; declined decisions, yes, you have to go to some external agency and get the data. So it is a more cumbersome process. But to answer another dimension that Professor talked about, you could DEC line everyone, and then you are all safe, but then you lose points.  So typically, the rule of credit risk officers like Nikita Sharma is a fragile balance they have to strike between - approving the maximum number of customers while still keeping their losses to the minimum possible. If you take a very conservative approach and start declining everyone, yes, your losses will all be close to zero, but that will not make your CEO happy.  Because he wants to give more to run the business, at the same time, if you approve 100 % of people, then you will run into very high losses. So the whole trick lies in where you draw the line and how you balance between a high approval rate and a low loss rate.  Mil ind Gandhi: G. V, once again, this is a case of the balance of the trade of discussion we were having in ace years.  Prof G Venkatesh: Correct.  Mil ind Gandhi: If you go too much to one side, it is a problem. I t is also a problem if you go too much to the other side. Prof G Venkatesh: The CEO has a job sort it means, Mil ind Gandhi: Okay, Venkat, thanks. So why do not G. V and I go off, and we will do some analysis ? We will return and share the data with you before we share it with Nikita.

title: AB Testing Presentation
text: Business Data Management Professor G. Venkatesh Doctor Mil ind Gandhi Mister Venkat Subramanian Lecture 3 A.B. Testing Presentation G. Venkatesh: Venkat shared some data with us for A. B. testing. Mil ind and I had a chance to work through that data, and we have some exciting insights or observations about the experiment. We w ant to get your views.  Mil ind Gandhi: Sure.  We did two things. First, we looked at the test and control classes that must be similar in their characteristics. We did not do a pervasive analysis, but we looked at the average three -month credit and three -month debit transactions. The control, and the test group seemed to be roughly similar.  G. Venkatesh: The ratio of debt t o credit is roughly similar.  Mil ind Gandhi: Yeah.  G. Venkatesh: Is that good enough, or should we have done something else, Venkat?  Venkatesh Subramanian: I think it is okay. In general, there is no set guideline. A data set will have multiple different dimensions. In an ideal world, if n dimensions exist in a data set, you will compare the test and control group s across all these n dimensions. But then, on a practical note, it is generally not that feasible. So, we also typically choose one or two representative parameters to compare the test and the control group against. In this case, I see that you have done it based on credit and debit transactions, which is a fair equivalent because, on one level, it reflects the ratio of credit versus debit. On another level, it also demonstrates the volume of transactions the customers are doing.  It tells us that the control group test more or less has similar kinds of customers who make identical numbers of transactions and have used similar funding instruments i n the past. So, I think it is good enough to prove the equivalency.  G. Venkatesh: But are there any others that you tend to use? For example, loyalty and age with Pay Buddy might be one of the criteria we could have considered. We did not participate in the part, but we could have believed it. Venkatesh Subramanian: I think in an ideal world, whatever data points you have about the customer, you can compare the test and control groups across all these points. If you have age, you compare the age, you have engagements you can compare with that, but then what you will typically observe is that many of these are correlated to each other.  So, the moment you find that they match two or three essential dimensions, I think you will realize that even if you compare them with more measurements, they will fall into similar buckets and not differ much. So, I think it is okay. But just for an experimental purpose, maybe we can ask the students to try comparing against other dimensions to see if they match or not.  G. Venkatesh: Correct. We saw earlier that there is a relationship between age and credit debit. Right. People of longer age seem to have longer duration with Pay Buddy and have a propensity to do credit transactions. People who have just recently joined Pay Buddy seem to do more debit transactions.  That is a kind of correlation we saw. Maybe if you do that, you get some additional validation. The way we have chosen the people between the control and test group is pretty okay. I think students can try it with age as one the things. They can try a few other parameters.  Venkatesh Subramanian: Yeah.  Mil ind Gandhi: The next thing we did, Venkat, was to look at how the engagement segment is changing because of the test w e performed. So, in the rows, we have the old engagement segment, the engagement segment for the person at the beginning of the three -month test period, and the columns are the engagement segment at the end of the three months. Few people were found in the low or about -to-churn segment.  G.V. and I hypothesized that because you are assigning low or about to churn over twelve months, the fact that the person has done a transaction in the last three months automatically says that he is not in a low or about to churn category. So, everybody was in the high -medium category, but the percentage mix is interesting. Let's take a look at that.  G. Venkatesh: But Venkat, do you want to respond to that ? Is that the case that it is not possible to categorize a customer as about to churn with three months of data is what we thought ? Maybe that is why we do not find that column populated during the three -month experimental period.  Venkatesh Subramanian: As long as you have chosen a data set such that each of these customers ha s at least one transaction in the last three months, I do think you will probably technically, by definition, end up with nobody in the about to churn. The purpose of churn in many cases s in most companies is that you should not even have done one transaction in the last twelve months.  That is when you are said as churning or about to churn. So, by definition, that is possible, and it is an interesting case. We do not know yet. We can an Alyce the data. It would be best if you had a test control setup to realize whether some of these changes are incidental and can happen to anyone organically or strategically. You are following specifications for the test group.  As the professor said, percentage movements will be an ideal way to do that. We should look at how these are changing between the test and control group s to see if the test group behaves differently from the control group.  Mil ind Gandhi: Broadly, Venkat, in that case, if you look a t it, about 52 % of the people who were in the about to churn category.  Of that, 52% went to high, and about 48% went to medium.  G. Venkatesh: A roughly equal number of people are about to churn.  Mil ind Gandhi: What was more interesting for me was that ab out a third of the high people at the beginning of the three months dropped to medium. And of the low people, about 30 % continued to be low.  Almost half became high, and about a quarter w as medium.  G. Venkatesh: This is for the entire population.  Mil ind Gandhi: We will look at by test and control. And for the medium set, about a third continued to be medium, and about two -thirds jumped too high. Again, is it something that makes sense?  Venkatesh Subramanian: Yes.  It is possible. As I said, all of us change since all these engagement segments are defined for a period, and no customer behaves consistently over time. Sometimes we tend to shop more. Sometimes we do not shop more. So, organically, such movements are always possible in any group, whether you subject them to any particular experiment.  Naturally, such moments are quite possible. It has a positive feeling because, as you said, we are seeing customers moving from lower to better engagement segments. There is a positive feel to it. But maybe once we look at the split between test and control, we conclusively know whether it is because of our experience.  Mil ind Gandhi: So, we did look at it by test and control. And let me show you the result. We found that 70% of the people who were about to churn moved to medium, and about 30 % moved to high.  Venkatesh Subramanian: Interesting.  Mil ind Gandhi: About half continued to be high, and a half became medium. In the control group, low people, about half continued to be low, and a quarter each were medium and high. And in the medium category, half continued to be medium, and a half became high. So, this is the behavior of the control group. The test group's behavior seems to be a little different. So, if you look at the test group of the people who were about to churn, about 60 % became high.  G. Venkatesh: As it is 33 %. Mil ind Gandhi: It is a significant difference, and only 41 % were medium as again 68 % for about to churn. At least, to my mind, it is a positive thing.  Venkatesh Subramanian: I said the difference does look very substantial. So, it has a powerful positive direction.  Mil ind Gandhi: Yes. In the case of the high group, about two -thirds continue d to be high, almost three-fourth s continued to be high, and only one -fourth became medium.  G. Venkatesh: As against half-and-half. Mil ind Gandhi: As against half-and-half. So, again fairly strong. Low about 60 % became high. 24% became medium, and 16 % were low.  G. Venkatesh: Whereas in the control group, half the people were low, remained low. Whereas in the t est group, the nudge would be 16 % was low. The remaining 84 % seem s to have migrated either to medium or high engagement. It is a massive moment.  Mil ind And he: And then in the case of the medium, originally medium was half and a half between high and medium. But now it is three -fourth s high and one -fourth medium in the test group. So again, the nudge seems to have nudged people more towards the high category.  Venkatesh Subramanian: Definitely. I think the results are pretty interesting and very significantly positive. I want to call out another fact : if you think about how we design ed this whole strategy. Furthermore, I t was more to direct them towards the rig ht funding option or instrument, whether somebody needs credit or no credit. But w e are seeing that those small nudges are ultimately affecting the overall engagement segment of customers, which is to say that people who got the right nudge are likely to transact more.  If you are presenting the wrong option, I think we would remember what we discussed in the earlier session about a lot of customers moving till the last point of the checkout stage in a transaction and then dropping off the cart and then doing some other work. Drop -off of the cart is a prevalent problem in the e-commerce world. So, it is crucial that at the checkout stage, you present those very relevant and intuitive options to the customers so that they complete the transaction without any friction.  I think that point is very well proved here. It is not just the funding instrument we are influencing. We are control ling the likelihood of the transaction. In general, if more of the test group customers have migrated to a high LY engaged segment, they have completed more transactions compared to the control group.  Mil ind Gandhi: You know, the most important thing is you want the customer to do a transaction because that is when you make money.  Venkatesh Subramanian: That is true. One way or the other, correct? G. Venkatesh: Yeah. But there could also be this thing we have to be worried about. I mean, not a bit cautious about the analysis, the result, Venkat, that this is an experimental period. There might be excitement simply because something new has been presented ; people are excited.  Something novelty when you introduce there will be some buzz around it. So, it could be well that factor, and with time, if you give it another three months, six months, maybe you do not see things may still taper off coma red to what kind of numbers you see here.  Venkatesh Subramanian: Entirely possible, professor, and I think that is a other good point to discus s statistical significance testing in such experiments. Typically, in any experiment, when you see a difference be tween the test group and the control group, in this particular case, the contrast is very stark and very big. So, we are already thinking positively, but in some cases, let us say you are saying 59 %; in another case, you're seeing 57 %.  Now, the typical question that comes to your mind is if 2 % are significant differences or not.  Can it occur randomly, or is it happen ING because I am doing something different in the experiment? In such cases, you do hypothesis statistical testing to prove that the difference occurs due to some significant factor and is not a random occurrence.  Again, since you talked about whether these variations can taper off over a while, I think significance testing can be one way to validate whether such occurrences are pretty standard in the normal course of business or whether they are due to a particular testing strategy.  Mil ind Gandhi: So, the other thing Venkat that I was wondering about when we were having this conversation is that Pay Buddy does not make any money. It lends to the 'Buy now, Pay Later scheme. G. Venkatesh: Buy now Pay Later. Mil ind Gandhi: Pay Buddy is lending money in this process, but it is not charging any interest.  Venkatesh Subramanian: That is true. Yeah.  Mil ind Gandhi: But Pay Buddy has to pay interest from wherever it gets the funds.  Venkatesh Subramanian: That is correct. I mean, like any other company, it will have its own cost of capital and borrowing costs. Mil ind Gandhi: Where does this gap, and who funds this gap? So Pay Buddy is essentially borrowing at 5 % and lending at 0 %. Who is funding this gap?  G. Venkatesh: You are paying from your pocket to do.  Venkatesh Subramanian: The leading way to think about such things is that the borrowing costs will not be as high as 5 %. I mean, we are talking about the U.S. borrowing rate. So, we are talking about 2 %. Second, the primary advantage for companies like Pay Buddy is that customers are likely to transact more because of such options.  Last, in this particular example, the test group is doing significantly better than the control group. I mean, if let us say 70 % of a test group is high in this as opposed to 50 % of the control group, which proves that there is at least a 25 % shift in the overall number of people who transact at the level of being a high LY engaged customer. Now, this mathematics will work if the incremental revenue Pay Buddy makes from these additional transactions compensates for that interest cost paid.  Mil ind Gandhi: The expectation is that you will get higher volumes, which means higher profit and higher yield will cover this cost.  Venkatesh Subramanian: That is right. It may not do so in the short run. Typically, such schemes are suitable when they start, but they are always in losses. I think it is not unique to Pay Buddy. If you think about Indian e-commerce fields like Flipkart and Amazon, they offer you heavy discounts, which you will never see in any shop.  It is understood philosophy that they typically run into losses when they sell you mobile phones at 50 % discount rate or some electronic items. A lot of stuff they sell at a heavy discount. The primary rationale here is that while you are running into losses in the short run, you are creating a customer base that is highly engaged and habituated to using your platform and product in the long run.  So then you will eventually start making money. I think that philosophy probably holds true for companies like Pay Buddy. In the short run, they may lose all the interest money they are paying, not only the interest money. If 100 people take this 'Buy now pay later' option, not all of them will return the money.  Mil ind Gandhi: Yes. Venkatesh Subramanian: Some of them are not even going to return the amount that they have borrowed. That is also an additional cost or loss that will sit in PayBuddy's pocket. Therefore, the belief is that in the long her run, let us say for two or three ye arses, the additional incremental engagement you are generating from customers and the corresponding revenue should compensate for these interest costs and the losses you make out of the wrong customers.  Mil ind Gandhi: Clearly, much analysis needs to go into computing, and customers could go wrong in forecasting. Computing is not the right word for predicting which customers could go wrong, how much interest cost we are incurring, and so on. I think that is probably the topic of the following discussion.  G. Venkatesh: But before that, Venkat, I also understood from our conversation last time that you also have a float because people keep money in their wallet, which is cash that is held with you. So, potentially you could this funding of this 'Buy now, pay lat her scheme with your float with the money that is sitting in the wallets of various customers, which is accessible to you in some sense. You could use that float, right? Could you use it? Is it sufficient to meet this, or is float too small?  Venkatesh Sub Romanian: I think that is a good point. I mean, we could potentially use that floating money. But I think the way you will analyze this kind of business proposal is that even if it is money, let us say, lying in your wallet. If you did not put it into this scheme, you probably would have put it at least into some interest -earning deposit or something. That money could have been put in some fixed deposits or government bonds or whatever. So generally, when evaluating the scheme's profitability, you should still assume some minimal primary interest that you are either an opportunity cost or an actual borrowing cost. You are losing all that money. G. Venkatesh: Okay.
