title: How businesses are managed
text: Business Data Management Professor G. Venkatesh Doctor Mil ind Gandhi Indian Institute of Technology, Madras How Business are managed Professor G. Venkatesh: We discuss how businesses are managed in this slide. And so a lot of learning in this. For example, as we said earlier, you have to look for the right things and organize these things in a specific way. In the e-commerce case, analyzing revenue in one direction and sales when trying to put both together makes more sense.  So revenue versus sales and what Omar pointed out is a product portfolio manager, I think he also brought out this idea of product portfolio management. So how do you look at your products and try to make some sense of them so you can FOC us? Because in the case of Fab mart, you had 10 lakh SKU, right, and you cannot focus on 10 lakh SKU. Do you need a few 1000 that you can focus on?  How do you pick 1000 that you want to focus on ? The key parameters are revenue in some sets and volume. The other directions and putting these two together, you have to figure it out and also that helped me surprisingly, I thought, we found a way to organize the distribution center, using that matters.  That turned out very surprisingly it came out. So product portfolio management and its use of it seems to be a fascinating thing to do. Similarly, in inventory management, there is a tradeoff. We already discussed it between working capital on one side, CFOs thing, and ensuring that there are no stock -outs. So, it would be best to have enough inventory, so you do not have stock -outs. You are locking up a lot of capital if you have too much inventory.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yeah.  Professor G. Venkatesh: So how do you do this tradeoff?  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: The exciting thing for me in inventory management G. V. was that we saw very similar techniques used in Ace Gears and in Fab mart.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Correct, correct? Absolutely.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Even though the end objective differed, Fab mart looked more towards the end consumer. At the same time, Shiv was looking at ensuring that his production line was kept busy. Nonetheless, there are techniques in terms of creating ledgers, looking for stock -ups, and how to reorder. I think all of this technique s seemed very similar.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Very similar ; you are right. Yeah, the method is quite similar. So there are a lot of commonalities. But the difference in Ace Gears is we got to see some impact of the external map. We did not see that in Fab mart because it was 50 days of data which is too short. But this was a very eventful two years because we had the BS4 to BS6 transition. We had the COVID impact as well. So, all that exciting stuff is going on.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: But even there, G.V., my suspicion is we also saw some impact of the external environment in Pay Buddy. We did see the average credit rating scores drop off.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Yes, I saw that.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: That is probably a reflection of the environment changing. Professor G. Venkatesh: Correct. Some Pay Buddy also we saw some things. Yes.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: So I think my takeaway is that the organization has to keep listening to the environment.  Professor G. Venkatesh: They have to adapt. They will adapt or die. Either adapt or die, organizations must live and breathe every day. You go in the morning, and you look at the environment. You do something. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: I think this was a trend we saw across cases. Planning and scheduling w ere very important.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Yes.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: In the Ace Gears case, when Shiv was describing what happens if there is unplanned maintenance and breakdown maintenance, we saw that the other machine does not have the materials to work.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Yeah, the next shift is wasted because the guys will come to the office or a factory and are not paid to do anything ; there is no material to work.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Also mentioned when there is seasonality of demand, even though there is low demand at certain times, they keep producing to have stock ready at high demand.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Correct.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: So they are looking at smoothing out production.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Yes, they look at smoothing out for production. You want to smoothen out because you cannot buy 10 on day one and the next day 100. It does not work like that. So some quantity is there for material purchases, and you try to maintain the amount and smoothening of the purchases.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: But the interesting thing was the same pattern we saw in Tech Enterprises.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Right. You have to plan your recruitment. It takes a long time. I realized that especially project leader position s could take six months to recruit.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes.  Professor G. Venkatesh: And you can end up with a situation where you interview many candidates, and none are suitable.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes.  Professor G. Venkatesh: You must go through the resume sourcing business repeatedly. So a phenomenal amount of planning is required for some additional staff on the bench. It will ensure that you can tie it over requirements soon. You can do this through your bench or the internal source rather than hiring every time because if you have to keep hiring every time, you are done.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Correct. Indeed.  Professor G. Venkatesh: So quite a lot of similarities, you are right. They are also scheduling the number to hire in the first place. There are two phases arrays ; you divide 12 into 6 and 6. You use the first six and recruit the other six.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Correct. There was a lot of scheduling going on there.  Professor G. Venkatesh: And joining date is another factor. You do not know when the person is going to do it. Accordingly, you have to figure it out. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes. Then the other thing we looked at G. V. was the ABC model for material management, which was again going back. I liked your word about ‘treetop view.’ We said that some items are costly. They need to be tracked almost minute by minute, and something s are relatively low cost, and we only need to look at them monthly.  Professor G. Venkatesh: And buy large quantities and keep.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Buy large quantities, and then even in between, you need to look at a different level of granularity.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Correct. You have this safety stock concept there.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Correct. The other thing from the Ace Gears case that I thought was interesting was when we looked at the ONE calculation.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Yes, we can break down efficiency into factors responsible for different people.  Dr. Milan d Gandhi: I think that also shows how different people contribute to efficiency.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Efficiency is a part of shop floor management. You want to improve the efficiency of shop floor operation, and the third one is on quality, defect and quality and some R and D and every thing. So these three things are entirely different. So you want to locate the responsibilities correctly for the three factors. Nice.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: We also want to re-emphasize these enabling functions. They need to look well in advance, which comes from two things. HR must determine what recruitment plan they need and also which skills are available.  Professor G. Venkatesh: You must have relationships with pane ls to ensure skills are coming. The source is a resume, and numbers keep on coming. It would help if you kept the resume going somehow. So, it would be best to keep your channel business going correct LY. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes. And again, channels w ere another commonality we saw, GV.  Professor G. Venkatesh: So, you could sell through a channel. We did not see too many examples of that in our case studies. Still, you could deal through a distribution channel or source through a medium. The case of HR Tech Enterprises is sourcing through the channel, and buying through the channel.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: We did see some of that. Though we never discussed it. So if you look at Fab mart, they were selling through an e-commerce channel, Business to consumer. Ace G ears, on the other hand, I think was Business to Business ; they were selling to other companies.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Yes, to other companies.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: But here model seemed to be sales agent -based.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Yes, we saw the planning of agents. Correct. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: And then in Tech Enterprises, of course, we did not look at the sales but also the supply piece. They said that instead of trying to reach potential employees directly, they had different ways of getting them. Professor G. Venkatesh: They had to hire many people, and I did not have an HR in such a big organization. You have to get so many people into your recruitment team, directly proportional to the number of people you hire.  Like sales agent planning, you are counting the number of things we have to sell and determining the number of sales agents. Accordingly, you will hire and recruitment team. So some sizing of the functions comes out nicely is a common thing now days.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: The most fantastic thing about the Pay Buddy case GV for me was their Nudge economics.  Professor G. Venkatesh: By doing this nudge thing, you can influence consumer behavior.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes, I always thought. I did a lot of research before buying some thing, but I never realized how many companies could shape your behavior.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: You are influenced by the options and how they present them. It is consumer Psychology, and it is exciting. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: The other thing I found most interesting, G. V, was that shear statistical data could predict much of this theory.  Professor G. Venkatesh: By demographic profile, transaction data, and buying history, you can do many things.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Yes, it is powerful. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: It is compelling and sensitizing to students. A debate on the privacy and confidentiality of consumer data may help them. Professor G. Venkatesh: They are very relaxed with their data and want to give it away; actually, it is very valuable. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Very, very valuable thing.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes. Then we also provided some basics of this Nudge modeling and looked at how companies can experiment.  Professor G. Venkatesh: It is a design of experiments.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: You can experiment to see what user interface options would encourage people to buy more, which would help maximize Business in some sense.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Yeah, AV testing. It is interesting.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: And then the final topic, going back to our balance. We looked at balancing risk and returns and how risk could be evaluated from demographic data.  Professor G. Venkatesh: That is an n astonishing thing. For prediction, you can look at demographic data, historical profiles, and all.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Risk is about futures, no t the past. So through this transaction, you are saying whether this guy will default or not in the future ? For this credit, he got to default in the future. You are predicting. By looking at past profiles, you can do many things to anticipate, such as what a person will do in the future. That is interesting.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: The other thing you brought me G.V. is the importance of that credit score. Professor G. Venkatesh: How important is it?  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes, why should I maintain my score ? It is also something that we learn ed. Professor G. Venkatesh: It is being used.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Okay.

title: Processing data from business processes using spreadsheets
text: Business Data Management Professor G. Venkatesh Professor Dr. Mil ind Gandhi Indian Institute of Technology, Mars Processing data from business processes using spreadsheet Introduction to CIM Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: We had looked at how data originate. Yeah, all right. Most of the time, we just saw this raw data in tables or databases.  G. Venkatesh: You pull it, and it comes out as a CSV file or something and put it in Excel.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Correct.  G. Venkatesh: A table can be too large, then you have to filter it and make sure the table is small.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes.  G. Venkatesh: For further analysis, you have to do it with software ; you cannot do it by Excel.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes. As we said, there is so much variety you may want to store it in a system that can hold a lot of data, called an ERP. G. Venkatesh: Yeah. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: But that is merely for convenience. We could not do this in this course. The other thing that became interesting for m e G. V. Was the format in which data was available. In many cases, the data was captured directly at the source.  G. Venkatesh: In Fab Mart, it is an electronic transaction. The Pay Buddy also captures in electronic formats. On the other hand, Ace G ears and Tech Enterprises do it physically. In hiring, resumes come physically in the form of document s. The Ace G ears record s manually, maybe in a book or something. And somebody enter s that data into the computer later. I s it not? Your machine information and schedule are entered into the system later on somewhere.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: It was quite a revelation that data can be very vague. The electronically captured data can come in different formats, such as numbers, codes, approved or declined status, and customer segments.  G. Venkatesh: Finally, it all becomes a table Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes.  G. Venkatesh: Correct.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: More interestingly, we saw that there w ere some ready made tools available to us to convert unstructured data into structured data.  G. Venkatesh: Yes, I find such a difficult job where there is no table ; I mean, how do you make a table from that ? It is impossible.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Correct.  G. Venkatesh: In such cases, an H.R. person seems to have taken from the job description whatever they needed. And they made a table out of it.  Let us take certifications in one column and take what as degrees, like first degree, second degree, and so on.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Degree and skills. G. Venkatesh: Apart from them, the age, years of experience, or something you would have put in. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Correct. G. Venkatesh: So they have processed the physical job description document and turned it into some reasonably structured thing in the form of a table.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes.  G. Venkatesh: Exciting.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: In the Ace Gears case study, the data was not being captured at source ; mostly, it was numbers.  G. Venkatesh: It is already in the form of numbers. There are hardly any other number s. Even in the Pay Buddy case, you had a lot of non -numbers, approved -declined status. You have already mentioned that non -number things were there in the Pay Buddy case. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes.  G. Venkatesh: Right.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: But we could make them into codes.  G. Venkatesh: We could turn them into codes. Even in the Tech enterprise case, we turned it into codes.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Eventually, we did it. There were mistakes a few mistakes in it.  G. Venkatesh: Tableau was spell led in three different ways., An additional dot appeared somewhere ; I recall all of those things. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Correct. Initially, some amount of data cleaning, I think, is worth spending time on it. G. Venkatesh: Yes.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Of course, we have been discussing enormous data processing or organization in multiple ways that can give us some insight. So should we recap some of these organize d techniques?  G. Venkatesh: Yes. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: We do not go into details, but at least at a top level. G. Venkatesh: A revisit, I think, is a good idea.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: In the Fab mart case, we looked at revenue and volume Pareto.  G. Venkatesh: You are trying to focus on a few products. So you are basically saying that 80% of the revenue comes from 20 % of SKU s. So the focus is on that 20 %.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: And we also saw that the volume Pareto did not give us any insight.  G. Venkatesh: Yeah.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: However, the revenue Pareto came out beautifully.  G. Venkatesh: He wants to reduce it even further.  20% is not good enough for him. It was 30 SKU s, and ten lack means 20% comes to 2 lack. He has to do even more work to bring it down to save 10,000 or so. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes. That was o né way. We looked at revenues versus SKU, and volume versus SKU. The other analysis we did was we plotted revenue versus volume for each SKU.  G. Venkatesh: Yes.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: And we had portfolio analysis.  G. Venkatesh: The most exciting thing we got from this was this insight on four quadrants, a two-by-two standard trick taught in management.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes. G. Venkatesh: Organize your things into a two-by-two matrix. The first two are the industry's revenue growth versus the market share. These are the two in the BCG diagram. If your revenue and the overall market are not growing, and your market share is not increasing, then it is a dog.  If both are growing, it is a star. If your market share is growing, but your market is not growing, then it is a cash cow, something I do not know what it is. So you have cash cows, your question mark s something, and then dogs and stars.  So this two -by-two organizing things in business seems to be a standard management method of decluttering. You declutt her 1000 points by reducing it to four possible buckets s and then analyze each bucket separately. It leads to some way s to make a decision. It turned out that we got an n excellent way of organizing, and Omar pointed out this has a meaning for him in terms of organizing his distribution center.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes.  G. Venkatesh: So, what is an organization? Some of them are, I have forgotten what it is.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: So, what he had told G.V. if I remember, was that some items are expensive and high volume, like some brands of mobile phones, and he had a secure area near where he was packing. G. Venkatesh: What is on the right side ? Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: High revenue, high volume.  G. Venkatesh: That top corner is high revenue and high volume. It should be secure near the packing center. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Near the tracking center. Then some were high revenue, but not very high volume. And he said those would also be in a secure area, but that safe area could be far away from the par king area.  G. Venkatesh: Not near the packing center. Yeah.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Some things were low revenue and volume. And then there were some outliers, I think, I had removed them, but there were some low revenue and high volume. And he had said that the low revenue -high volume should be near the packing center. G. Venkatesh: But it may not be in the secure area. That is a big key thing.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes.  G. Venkatesh: So there is near packing center, not packing center, secure, non -secure, and then you have to play around.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Correct.  G. Venkatesh: It is interesting.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: In some cases, both Omar and Shiv also taught us to do some of these, and we saw a little bit of this in Pay Buddy also, when people looked at it in three buckets instead of two buckets. So, Shiv looked at ABC.  G. Venkatesh: Correct.  ABC is similar to the previous ones.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: They know they had high, mid, and low customer segments. G. Venkatesh: Correct.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi : So sometimes people looked at, instead of plotting two by two, they were looking at doing a little, maybe three by three almost, the same principle, I think.  G. Venkatesh: Yep.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Besides this, I think the one mind-boggling technique was a ledger. And we saw that both in Fab mart and Ace Gears, and the basic equation, the closing stock equals open ING stock minus sales plus income. And you do this on an n every -period basis ; the period can be days, weeks, or months. But this gives you insight into how your inventory will behave over time.  G. Venkatesh: Right.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: More importantly, it indicates when you are likely to get into trouble because your inventory is falling too low.  G. Venkatesh: To o low.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: To me, the fundamental tool in inventory management seems to be the ledger. G. Venkatesh: Yeah.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: What do you think?  G. Venkatesh: Correct. It is.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: From that, you can detect stock outs. From a ledger, one can get precise information about reorder point s, sales, method of order, date, and time of order. It also says that when orders went from Chennai to Hyderabad. All of that became clear from the Leger.  G. Venkatesh: Correct.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: The other topic that we looked at was how we plot graphs against time to detect seasonality. G. Venkatesh: It enables us to compare one period with the corresponding period of the following year. It is something where you trend in a year and then next year because there seems to be some commonality between April and April. The same thing seems to happen in April every year. It is an assumption that the IPA walk comes in October every year.  You see some sales may happen there, and you have to prepare in May and all that. Therefore, you can compare the period to the corresponding period of next year like that —just an exciting concept. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Of course, we did this analysis by time in Pay Buddy.  G. Venkatesh: Yeah.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: We did not have enough data to detect this seasonality.  G. Venkatesh: Like for two years, we could have done something interest ING. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Correct, but it is the general technique of plotting against time and looking at some trend s. Okay, we do not know whether it was a seasonal trend. But we saw a trend; your credit risk seems to be increasing.  G. Venkatesh: Correct.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: However, we saw a lot of seasonality in Ace Gears.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Beside s this study, we looked at how to do unit -level profitability calculations. And definitely, we looked at that in Ace Gears. We also saw glimpse s of it in Pay Buddy. G. Venkatesh: Yeah.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi : And that is another common technique across industries. People want to know, how much money are you making on each transaction? And possibly, I think the hope is that you can find transactions or items where you are not making enough margin, and you try and sell less of those. G. Venkatesh: The critical thing is that you should know what to do if a company is making some profit and wants to increase profit. How do you know that? Unless you have this unit level of profitability measures, you will not know what to do.  He has a unit -level profitability measure. Let us focus on those units where the profitability looks lower and see if there is anything I can do. Either I can decide not to make them and sell them, or I will try and see whether I can tweak the prices or do something else. We recommend increasing costs. But then Shiv came back and said we could not increase it. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: The table I have put here is all the recommended prices. G. Venkatesh: However, it is not possible.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi e: And he said it is not possible.  G. Venkatesh: Once we have the unit level profitability, you can decide whether there is some tweaking you can do to bring the profit up or down. Of course, at the overall level, if you have some costs, you can say, "Can I cut some H. R. people and still manage or some production people and still manage or something," but there is only a limit to what you can do like that. Where these people are big, you have decided that our production is based on the number of shifts and people required to run the machines.  Similarly, H. R. recruitment, we saw that you need many recruitment guys if you recruit so many people.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes. G. Venkatesh: So you need some strategic way of reducing costs by looking at unit profitability ; that is not the way to do it. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: The other one we saw was this entire reorder point and safety stock issue.  G. Venkatesh: Correct.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: How does that correlate with production issues and order quantity ? G. Venkatesh: Yeah. We saw that there is the inventory falls, then you have a reorder, or when you have high inventory, you basically do not reorder. So it is the opposite correlation. At the same time, if you are issuing many product s, you also have to reord her them. It is a direct correlation. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yeah.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: In the Tech Enterprises case, one of the things we looked at was giving scores to different attributes.  G. Venkatesh: The rank.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi : Yes.  G. Venkatesh: But that was the only thing we could do. What else do you do ? You have a bunch of resumes, but they all look very different. If you look at resume s, you will not find anything common.  Everything will look very different.  So you have to somehow distill from these resume s enough information to rank these people. You can compare one person to another and say, 'This guy is better than this guy is better than this.'  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes.  G. Venkatesh: So you do ranking. That is what we learned in this case.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Correct.  G. Venkatesh: One, we are ranking the candidates. And the second one, we are ranking the channels in a way. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: The other thing we learned, in this case, was dealing with unstructured data and how to represent unstructured data in some structured manner. G. Venkatesh: Codifying and splitting a comma -separated string into four columns. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes.  G. Venkatesh: Ye s.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: We also learned how to make and build some rules to automate decision -making. I think both in the Pay Buddy case and in the Tech Enterprises case, we had some notion of automating decisions.  G. Venkatesh: Correct.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: It is based on certain things.  G. Venkatesh: How to define consistency in terms of this thing? Appraisal scores or something, and then in the Pay Buddy case, we had some interesting rules.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: We examined credit score and application amount as examples. Those seem to be techniques people use to decide whether to approve an application or not.  G. Venkatesh: Even the nudge thing, decide to present the nudge to place people who were not credited if they are heavy credit people, you do not want to give them any nudge, because they are already credited ed. We want to take those guys who are debit guys for making transactions of minima l value.  And who ha s some middling ? If they have been with us for a long time and are engaged, the n there is no use. If they joined yesterday, there is no use.  Somewhere middling with us for some reason, a period of time, they are mostly debit and doing small or medium value transactions, then you nudge them towards Pay Later.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes.  G. Venkatesh: Correct.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: I think, some sort of rules was, we were able to dig out.  G. Venkatesh: Correct. Yeah.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: And finally, learnings from worksheets are some essential functions such as max, min, and average. We learned about relative and absolute addressing. We learned how to put dollars to reference cells. Furthermore, we also learned how to do sorting and filtering.  Furthermore, we learned two great techniques: LOOKUP and Pivot tables. LOOKUP allowed us to merge data from two tables into a single table. Pivot Table allowed us to cut up aggregate data from a single table and look at it from different lenses and slicing.  G. Venkatesh: Slicing and dicing the data in various ways and consolidating, taking the average of things or the sum of things or count of items or something like that.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: We aggregated the data in some ways.  G. Venkatesh: Correct.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Last but not least, one of my big takeaways was that you could not draw excellent insights from numbers unless the numbers are represented visually.  G. Venkatesh: Yeah.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Correct.  G. Venkatesh: You have to tell the story. Is a picture the equivalent of 1000 million words, hundred words, or a thousand words ?  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: A Thousand word s. G. Venkatesh: Picture is worth of thousand words, something like that. So one picture tells the story much better.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yes.  G. Venkatesh: Telling the story is much better than writing on pages.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Absolutely, right.  G. Venkatesh: Yeah. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: The functionality available in most of these worksheet tools that allow you to build these graphs is impressive. Most times, you can never recommend chart s quite well at first.  G. Venkatesh: Yeah, it recommends. I was pretty surprised when it came up with good recommendations.  Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: That was very interesting. I encourage students to play with the graphs and see what makes sense.

title: Demand and supply curves
text: Business Data Management Professor M Suresh Baby Department of Humanities and Social Sciences Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Demand and Supply Curves So, before I start this discussion on market, let me have a quick recap.  What we have been trying to say is, in formal terms - consumption decision.  And we said that there are two approaches. One approach is to see consumption in terms of a cardinal sense and the other in an ordinal sense.  The difference is that there is a numeric value in the cardinal sense of the utility that one derives from consumption.  In an ordinal sense, it is basically in terms of preferences and ranking. And using this, we can actually underset and how market mechanism works then.  Now, so there is a typical consumer that we talked about. In a market, there are many consumers, millions of consumers like us. So, what is this market that I am talking about?  The market is nothing but a group of buyers and sellers for particular goods or services.  A market can be in a geographical area. It can also be a virtual market - online.  It need not have physical space.  So, there are two agents in a market : a buyer and a seller. And buyers determine the demand for the product, and sellers determine the supply.  And depending on the demand and supply conditions, markets have different kinds of mechanisms with which they equilibrate which is exactly what we want to know. Now, please remember that in all our discussions, there is a lot of data that goes in. For example, well, prices are very important in terms of allocating our decisions as to what we should consume, and we know that. And if you want to really look at indifference curves, and if you want to really move to higher indifference curves, we need a lot of information about prices.  We also need to have information about the kind of utilities that we derive from consumption.  So all of that is basically information and data-driven in terms of understanding consumer behave or. Now, when we come to market then, analyzing the market also requires a lot of data.  Because demand for a product has to be understood, supply has to be understood. We need to understand the price of a particular commodity. Then only we can understand the market mechanism.  So, what is demand?  Demand is a very straightforward thing, which we know that is quantity demanded is nothing but the amount of a good that buyers are willing and able to purchase.  Now, I am emphasizing that able.  I might be willing to purchase so many things, but I should have the ability to purchase.  It is exactly like potential and actual.  We say that there is a lot of potential, but actuality is where we are at, that is the difference here.  So, quantity demanded ultimately, is the amount of a good that buyers are willing and able to purchase.  That ability to purchase is a function of that income, which we told, and that is the budget constraint that we talked about.  So, we draw one generalization from this: when all the things are equal in a market, then when the price of a good increases, quantity demanded of that good falls.  I think that is a straightforward generalization.  Why?  Because you have limited incomes or limited resources.  Once the price of a good increase, you will have to allocate those limited resources to different commodities you want to produce, which means that the demand must be adjusted automatically.  So, the law of demand states that, when other things remain the same. I will come to what do I mean by these other things.  When the price of a good rise, the quantity demanded falls.  How do we see that? We can see it in terms of a table. At different price levels, what is the quantity demanded.  We can also plot it as a graph, and that is where the use of data comes. We can actually look at the individual level and then we can aggregate it to the market level. So, the demand then can be analyzed in terms of demand schedule, which is a table or a graph.  And then it could be individual demand or it could be aggregate demand.  So, what is the demand schedule and demand curve?  Well, this is a demand schedule for ice creams, quantity of cone ice creams demanded at various points. If you are going to give it free, I might demand twelve cones.  But when the price increases, of course, the quantity demanded comes down, and they are going to charge 3 dollars per cone.  Then, I will not buy at all because my limited resource availability is out of reach for me. I plot this, and that is a demand curve that I was talking about. And that gives us this relation. And that is really important for us, and that is all, data and how we use data.  So, lower the price, well, higher the quantity demanded, and that is why the demand curve will always slope downward.  Now, there could be exceptions to which we will come to that in a minute.  But generally, this is the shape of the demand curve.  So, then what is the market demand curve?  Market demand curve is nothing but the sum of individual demand curves.  Each individual's demand curve, sum it up, you will get a market.  So, that is why we say the size of the market is big or small and all in terms of these summations of the individual demand curve.  The total quantity demanded of any good then varies in terms of one important variable here, and that is price, provided other things remain constant.  What are the other things?  We will come to that. So, if all the other things are constant, then we know that these other things are very important.  Given that all these other things are constant, the quantity demanded varies with price.  So, this is what I was talking about market demand curve.  This is Catherine's demand.  This is Nikolas’s demand.  Catherine's demand plus Nikolas’s demand is the market demand here.  And in this market, there are only two people.  If there are twenty people, it is a summation of each individual's demand. And in this example, what we are showing is the quantity demanded of cone ice creams.  Now, so, we know that this demand curve then can have shifts.  There are locations or rather these are possibilities, that the demand curve actually could shift. Now, an increase in demand then can actually shift the demand curve in a different way. Let me put it differently : any change that increases the quantity demanded at every price will actually increase the demand. Then the demand curve will shift to the right.  A decrease in demand means any change that decreases the quantity demanded at every price, which means that the demand curve actually shifts to the left.  I explained this: an increase in the demand curve is moving to the right.  And this is a situation of decrease in demand curve.  So, any change that raises the quantity buyers wishes to purchase at given price shifts the demand curve to the right.  That is from D1, now, the new demand curve is D2. And there is another demand curve D3, which occurs when there is any change that lowers the quantity that buyers wish to purchase at a given price.  Which actually shifts the demand curve to the left.  So, then what are the variables that affect the demand curve ? From a data point of view, that is of interest to us. So broadly, we can identify there are five variables : income straight away, we know that. Because ultimately, that is a constraint within which we are operating. Two, prices of related goods can affect.  Remember our earlier example x and y. So, the price of y could affect the price of x, and hence the demand of x also.  Sometimes the price of y could directly affect the demand for x. So, prices of related goods then are important.  Taste could change over time, tastes and preferences of consumers could change. Expectations, very important.  And finally, the number of buyers.  So, if you look at how income affects, well, we know that there are two possibilities.  For a normal good, we say that an increase in income leads to an increase in demand. I would like to now because my constraint is now moved.  So, I would like to consume more because my income has increased.  For an inferior good, what happens is that an increase in income leads to a decrease in demand.  So, that is why it is called an inferior good, that is, I would like to decrease the consumption of this good, and I would like to purchase some other good which is superior to that. So, there are two kinds of goods, normal and inferior goods.  Now, when we look at the prices of related goods, there are two kinds of goods on the basis of that we can classify goods into two kinds.  Substitutes and complements.  In the case of substitutes, an increase in the price of one leads to an increase in the demand of the other.  And in the case of complements, an increase in the price of one would lead to the decrease in the demand of other, very simple kind of example.  Substitutes, an increase in the price would lead to a kind of increase in the demand of others. That is, if you are assuming that Coke and Pepsi are perfect substitutes.  So, if the price of coke increases, people might buy Pepsi, which is the case of a substitute.  I am substituting one with the other.  In the case of complements, an example, we always talk about petrol prices and automobile sales. Once when petrol and diesel prices are high, automobile sales will get affected here.  The price of one, decreases the demand for the other commodity. So, now, we have four kinds of goods for which we have to understand demand using data, normal good, inferior good, substitutes and complements.  We will come back to the discussion of this in detail, in another context but keep that in mind.  The other variables that are, that are affecting demand of course, are changes.  Changes in taste, definitely affect changes in demand.  When taste and preferences change, demand also changes. Expectations about the future are very important. If you expect an increase in demand, then we will also plan our consumption accordingly.  If I expect an increase in my income over a period of time, I might actually be anticipating more income in the future, I might buy some things now, etc. If I expect higher prices in the future, then I will buy more now.  Because in the next period, the prices will be high.  So, there is a possibility that expectations about the future affects current demand. And then, market demand also varies with the number of buyers in the market.  So, how do we summarize these variables?  Well, we can, our discussions we can summarize in this table. That is, when the price of that good itself varies, it represents a movement along the demand curve, you are moving along the demand curve. When income change s, then the demand curve shifts.  Because your constraint is now earned.  Price of related goods - your demand curve shifts.  Because you actually then, can consume some other good more etc. Taste, your demand curve shifts, I might actually decrease consumption or increase consumption. Expectation, your demand curve shifts. And number of buyers, the demand curve shifts.  So, only under one condition will there be a movement along the demand curve, which is when price varies.  Now, when we look at demand and supply together, then we need to understand equilibrium in the market.  So, far we have been talking about demand. Exactly like that, there is supply in the market, which is the other side. Demand and supply put together, we can understand how a market works, using the concept of equilibrium in the market. Now, demand and supply forces should be in balance in a market for that market to work in a proper manner.  Otherwise, there will be a problem of shortages or there could be a problem of excesses in the market.  So, a situation in which market price has reached a level, where the quantity demanded is equal to quantity supplied. That is, where the supply and demand curves intersect, that is, the equilibrium in the market.  That equilibrium in the market comes at an equilibrium price. At that particular equilibrium price, quantity demanded and quantity supplied are balanced, by price, and we call it the market -clearing price.  When I buy tomatoes in the market, there is an equilibrium price, 12 rupees per kilo. At that price, I would actually buy whatever quantity that I require and the seller is also willing to sell at that price whatever quantity that is available to the seller.  So, that is the equilibrium price. There is also an equilibrium quantity. With that 12 rupees per kilo I can buy only two kg. That is the equilibrium quantity. And the seller also will sell that two kg. So, the quantity supplied and the quantity demanded at an equilibrium price will be the same, which is two kg here. So, you have to visualize this in terms of an equilibrium point, where there is an equilibrium price and then there is an equilibrium quantity.  So, this is the famous diagram that I was talking about.  So, there is an equilibrium price here, 2. At that equilibrium price, there is an equilibrium quantity, seven units. And then, there is an equilibrium in the market.  This is a point of equilibrium, where demand and supply intersects.  Then we say that market clearing price is 2, and market clearing quantity is 7. And this market is in equilibrium.  This is, it is a stable market then.  So, what we are doing here is we see supply and demand together. Now, there could be situations of surplus and shortage. And that is called disequilibrium.  So, what is a surplus ? A surplus is a situation where quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded.  So, what happens ? There will be downward pressure on price. Once the price is brought down, then there will be a market, new market clearing price and then there will be a new equilibrium.  In the case of a shortage, what happens?  The shortage is a situation where the quantity demanded is more than quantity supplied, your demand is more than supply.  So, there is a kind of excess demand, or there is a shortage.  Then there may be an upward movement in price.  So, the demand then equilibrates, and then there will be a new equilibrium.  So, I want to emphasize that this kind of correction mechanism takes place continuously in the market. And there will be market -clearing prices and market clearing quantities.  And this is what I was talking about, in terms of the surpluses as well as the kind of a shortage. Here you have, your actual quantity demanded is 4, but quantity supplied is 10. So, there is a surplus.  Here, the quantity demanded is 10, but what is supplied is 4. So, there is a shortage. So, price mechanism, then avoids this supply and demand bottlenecks, surpluses and shortages.  So, when we put supply and demand together then, the law of supply and law of demand when we bring it together, we know that the price of goods adjusts in such a way to bring quantity supplied and quantity demanded for that good in balance.  And in most markets, supplies and shortages are temporary.  Because there will be a correction mechanism and prices then are signals that guide the allocation of resources.  So, prices have an important role in terms of a mechanism for rationing these scarce resources. And it also determines s, who produces each good and how much should be produced in the economy.  And that is the important role of price mechanism.  And that is why we always look at price data to understand how the market works.  Now, we will try and see how we can actually bring in a slightly different perspective.

text: Business Data Management Professor G Venkatesh Professor M Suresh Baby Department of Humanities and Social Sciences Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Utility: Cardinal vs. Ordinal Indifference Curves So, last session we saw how data is important in understanding the working of an economy, and we try to understand the economy in terms of production, consumption, distribution, and resource allocation.  Today, we shall try and see some formal theories in terms of consumers' behavior and analyze markets in an economy. When I say markets, what we shall do today is to see a typical market. From here we might actually extend our analysis to different types of markets later on. So, this is an interaction or a prelude to such an analysis.  Now, let us start with a basic theory building in terms of how consumers behave.  Now, the principle assumption upon which the theory of consumer behavior, as well as market demand, is built is that a consumer has very limited resources available, in terms of income, money that is available and the consumer has or would be interested to allocate this limited income among available goods and services to maximize his or her utility.  And if I put in other terms, it’s satisfaction. So, the consumer’s problem then is to utilize these resources that are available to a variety of goods and services, which he or she would like to consume.  That is a kind of resource allocation problem as far as the consumer is concerned.  Now, this is extremely important in understanding the demand side of the market and from there to understand the demand side of the economy. Let us go in a very step-by-step manner in terms of understanding what the theoretical foundation for this demand analysis is. The concept with which we begin today is the concept of utility itself because the utility is the amount of satisfaction derived from the consumption of a commodity, and consumption then is a function of this utility.  We talked about many examples in our previous session in terms of how a typical household consumption basket varies across income groups.  This variation across income groups is because consumers assign different utility or different levels of satisfaction across various consumption baskets. We also know that this whole concept of satisfaction of you or utility is very subjective. And the differences in satisfaction across consumers are vastly different.  So, we need to have a common denominator to measure that. And that is a big problem because there is no standard common denominator with which we can measure this, or there are no units with which we can measure this. Hypothetically, let us take for the sake of convenience that utility can be measured in “utils”. So, utils is a unit for measuring utility, then our task becomes slightly easier, because a consumer would measure utility in terms of “utils” across different consumption baskets and then allocate the income accordingly.  Let us push this argument a little forward.  If we are to understand the concept of utility, then within this framework of that there is some unit called “utils” then, there are two approaches to understanding : the cardinal utility theory and the ordinal utility theory. What is the difference between these two?  Well, in the cardinal utility approach, utility is measurable in a cardinal sense. What do I mean by Cardinal sense?  We can assign values for the utility that are 100 utils can be derived from eating a slice of bread, 200 utils can be derived d from having a cone ice cream.  So, that is the cardinal approach.  That is, I repeat that we can assign values for utility. In the ordinal utility approach, as the term itself denotes, it is measurable in an ordinal sense. What does that mean?  It means that we cannot, we are rather, we do not assign values ; instead, we can rank our preferences.  And once when you rank preferences, we know our preferred choices.  So, which should come first is a priority or a preference in our scheduled time. So, if I enjoy eating more ice creams, rather, if I derive more utility from the consumption of ice creams, then my preference for ice creams over a slice of bread will be stated in my commodity basket that I am consuming. So, two broad approaches : the cardinal utility approach and the ordinal utility approach.  Now, let us take a closer look at each one of these. It is a very simple concept because we can build in terms of a demand curve The Cardinal utility approach was actually put forth by economists of 19th century and assumed that utility is measurable. And there is a unit for anything to measure; we need a unit.  Which means that the difference in between the two measurement s is in terms of a very significant numerical value. What do I mean by that?  What I mean is that suppose I am consuming two commodities, X and Y. The utility, which I derive from consumption of X can be put as a function of X, how much I am consuming and the satisfaction that I am deriving.  And I have another commodity that I am consuming Y, and the utility that I am deriving from that is a function of how much I am consuming of Y, then I will decide which one is giving me maximum utility.  But that is not a unilateral decision that I can take for two reasons.  Reason number one is that I have limited income or limited resources with which I have to fulfill this consumption.  So, I have to allocate these limited resources. Reason number two, this allocation of resources is a function of prices. Some commodities have a higher price, and some commodities have a lower price.  So, I do the allocation in terms of prices as well as the income that I have. Now, the cardinal approach then argues that well, there is a concept called marginal utility. We will look at the marginal utility of consumption and then look at the prices of commodities and then allocate my resources and arrive at a decision in terms of what I should be consuming.  Let me explain this, what is this Marginal utility.  Now so, let us start with both concepts. There is a concept called Total utility, and then there is a concept called Marginal utility. Total utility is nothing but the overall satisfaction derived from consuming a good or service. Overall, I have a bundle for my satisfaction that is in our earlier example, 100 utils from the consumption of a slice of bread.  Now, marginal utility is nothing but the additional satisfaction that an individual derives from consuming an additional unit of goods or services. Why do we emphasize this?  We emphasize this because, in real-life situations, a number of our decisions are taken at the margin. Remember, we talked about a concept called opportunity cost earlier?  That is, there is a trade -off in terms of resource utilization. And that is the opportunity costs. Now, if we are thinking about opportunity costs, then a lot of our decisions are taken in the margin.  That is, I can use this resource for something else. But if I am going to use the resource for a particular consumption of a good or service, then I will value it at the margin.  So, margin all decisions are very important and in our daily lives, almost all our, decisions are taken at the margin.  So marginal utility, then, is this additional satisfaction that an individual derives from consuming an additional unit of goods or service.  So, what is that change in total utility?  In terms of changing the quantity consumed?  So, I consumed 3 slices of bread, and I have 300 utils from that. Will the 4th slice of bread increase by utility?  Or will it remain the same?  Or will it decrease my utility?  We do not know. So the consumption decision of the 4th slice of the bread is the marginal concept that I am talking about which I would equate in terms of the change in total utility because of this change in consumption that I am having.  So these deals or deltas, ITU is the change in utility, and HQ is the change in consumption. So, what are we assuming here?  We are assuming here that every additional unit of consumption would give you certain utilities ; one. Two, we do not know whether this additional unit of consumption is adding to your utility?  Or is it leading to a decline in your utility?  That is why this decision is very important.  In this approach, we have a very interesting kind of possibility which is nothing but the Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility. The Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility states that, as more and more of a good is consumed, the process of consumption will reach a particular point where it yields smaller and smaller additions to utility.  Let me take a minute to explain this.  When I consume my first unit or first a slice of bread, remember I am hungry, and I am going to consume my first slice of bread.  The utility that I get from that is very high.  The second slice of bread; well, good, I am happy.  Third, I am almost full. When I go on consuming more and more slices of bread well, the total utility reaches a maximum point beyond that it cannot increase because I am full now.  At that point, Marginal Utility is 0. So, we stop consumption.  If you are not stopping consumption at that point, then marginal utility actually becomes negative.  That is not good. And that is a problem of overconsumption. A lot of our decisions sometimes are at the margin, as I keep saying, but are taken into account of this possibility of negative marginal utility.  So, Cardinal approach then states that there is a law of diminishing marginal utility that as more and more of a good is consumed, in this process of consumption, the consumer would reach a particular point where the additional units of consumption would actually yield smaller and smaller utility.  It becomes 0, and then it becomes s negative.  Let me just put up an example for this. So, I have purchased 5 units of a commodity here.  And I have utility derived from the consumption of these 5 units. When I consume the first unit, I have 4, 4 units of utility and that is the total utility and the marginal is also that because only one unit is consumed. The Δ is not from 0 to 1 it is only 1.  When I consume the second unit, well, my total utility increases from 4 to 7, there is an increase, which means that my marginal utility is from 4, it has become 7. So, the Δ, in my earlier expression is 3 here.  That is a change in the total utility. So, remember, the definition of marginal utility is that the change in total eternal utility from an additional unit of consumption. I go on. I consume 3 units, 4 units, 5 units. When I reach 3 units, my total utility is 8. Beyond that, 3 slices of bread my example, one that I cannot really eat. But I take one more slice.  Again, there is no increase in total utility then my marginal utility becomes 0. Once when, this is the point when I should actually be stopping. Once when marginal utility becomes 0, I should stop consumption.  If I am not stopping consumption, then I reach a point where my total utility is actually declining, which means that marginal utility is becoming negative. And that is shown in this graph.  Initially, the total utility is increasing, then it reaches a point where actually it is plateauing and after that, it slightly falls, and the marginal utility curve is mapped in line with the total utility, and then after that point, it becomes negative.  Now, I think this concept then is pretty straightforward because we can relate it easily with food consumption. In my example, the first slice of bread clarifies how much we can consume, and we cannot push food consumption beyond a point.  Now so, the idea then is that well, after a point, marginal utility starts falling. And there is a principle of diminishing marginal utility, that is, as more and more goods are consumed, the process of consumption will, at some point, yield smaller and smaller additions to utility.  This is a real-life phenomenon. We do not need much of an explanation for that.  So, then we can actually find a point where the consumer is in equilibrium. So far, we have assumed that any amount of good or service is always available for consumption, but that is not correct because we have two constraints, that is, remember, we talked about, income and prices.  Prices are actually determined in the market, and income is actually fixed for the consumer.  So, there is a limitation in terms of the consumer’s income.  So, the consumer has limited income or budget and the goods obtained are at a market price.  Now, how will the consumer then allocate this income across commodities?  Remember, the consumption basket ? There is a basket of commodities that the consumer is consuming.  I am not going to stop my consumption only with one good; in real life, we consume so many things.  So, let us consider two goods X and Y. Let us also consider that prices of X and Y are fixed, time being when I go to market, I know that this is the price that is the consumption thing that we are talking about.  We also know that a consumer's income is given at a particular point in time and there is no variation.  So, there is an optimizing condition which we can derive where the consumer would be reaching a kind of equilibrium point in consumption, when marginal utility from a commodity X by the price of X is equal to the marginal utility of another commodity Y by the price of Y. Rather, the ratio between marginal utilities and prices have an equilibrium in the market and that is a condition where the consumer derives maximum kind of satisfaction or utility.  So, it is a very, very simple kind of expression, what am I trying to do here, I am trying to do here only one small thing that if you have prices that are given to you, and if incomes are also given to you, then you will allocate the resources in terms of the available prices of goods and services, and the decision is taken by taking into account the marginal utilities.  So, a consumer would then equate marginal utilities to price. Suppose I have to make a decision in terms of consuming apples and oranges. And let us also assume that the prices of apples are more than that of oranges.  But I would consume both.  I like both.  That is, that is the basic problem of a consumer.  Now, I would equate price of apple to the marginal utility from consuming an additional unit of apple to the price of orange and the marginal utility from the consumption of an additional unit of orange and then I will decide whether I should consume 2 apples and 1 orange or 2 or apples and 5 oranges.  That is the equilibrium that we are talking about. One straightforward explanation that we can draw from this is that we will spend on particular goods that give maximum marginal utility with a lesser price.  So, if the marginal utility of X in terms of its price is higher, then we will spend more money on X and less money on Y. I think that is the kind of decision, which as consumers we make every day when we go to the market, we look for the price and then we will decide whether should I buy more of a good or less of a good. I am just formalizing it in terms of some expressions here.  Now, moving to the ordinal approach, ordinal approach is another group of economists who believe d that well utility is measurable only in an ordinal sense. That is you can only rank your preferences because there are no units with which we can measure utility.  So, the utility then is derived from the consumption of a good, such as X, for example, which is a function of the quantities of X and Y consumed by a consumer because a consumer is consuming different goods.  So, there is an overall utility, which we want to maximize which is a function of each of these goods that is consumed. Now, the ordinal utility theory argues that utility is a qualitative concept; you cannot attach a quantitative value to that. So you can only list your preferences, and these preferences can be ranked, and you can actually plot a curve out of these preferences, which we would call us the indifference curves.  I will come to that in a minute.  Now, what is the basis for such a ranking of preferences?  The basis for such a ranking of preferences is that, there is this concept of rationality.  What is that? Consumers are rational and consumers would use maximum available information and then arrive at a decision. Put it in simple terms, what does it mean? Before purchasing a product?  We might ask 5 different sellers, what is the price of that?  What am I doing there?  I am actually gathering information about price there, then I will decide whether I should consume or not. That is the notion of rationality that I am talking, I am not going blindly and purchasing something, we would call such kind of consumers as little irrational consumers.  So, rational human beings will maximize their utility by selecting the highest possible utility with their available resources. That is an upper limit, given this upper limit in terms of income, they will choose what the maximum utility that I can achieve is. So, different consumers then will have different utilities.  So, different individuals will have different preferences.  And that is exactly what we saw yesterday when we were looking at the consumption basket of different income groups.  Recall our yesterday’s discussions in terms of 3 different households of 3 different levels of income 15,000, 30,00 0 and 50,000 they had different consumption baskets, because they have different utilities for consumption of goods.  So, how do we really rank this? We rank it in terms of what we call as indifference curves and what is this indifference curves?  These curves are representations of a combination of item, when the consumer is in an indifferent situation. Hence, certain combinations of goods would give me the same level of satisfaction. What do I mean by that?  Well, I prefer to have idle and Ada for breakfast.  So, there is a combination of 2 idles and one Ada, which will give me some level of satisfaction.  There is also another combination of 1 idle and 2 vadas, which could also give me the same level of satisfaction some days. So, I will then look at these preferences, which give me the same level of satisfaction and then rank my preferences.  And this is plotted into a curve and that is called the indifference curve.  So, let me put it a little more formally, indifference curves then give us the combination that produces the same level of satisfaction for the consumer. Higher indifference curves mean a higher level of satisfaction, lower indifference curves means a lower level of satisfaction.  So please remember, a rational consumer would actually try and move to a higher indifference curve with their given income that is, his or her disposal.  Now, let me show you a sample of this curve.  These are some curves IC 1, IC 2 and IC-1. IC-1 is actually lower in terms of satisfaction, whereas IC 1 is higher and IC 2 is even higher, but unfortunately, my consumer does not have the income to reach IC 2.  Now, we can have different combination s of goods. For example, there is one combination of good called A, which is a combination of in terms of X and Y where we have two different goods.  So, we find that there is one combination here called A. There is another combination of B, C, D. These are the different combinations that I was talking about.  Now, please remember, all these different combinations would give the same level of satisfaction.  So, where do I place myself?  I place myself depending on the prices of these goods. Please remember that I allocate my resource depending on the price there, should I buy more of, see both my earlier breakfast example shows that both gives me the same level of satisfaction that is 2 idles and 1 Ada or 1 idle and 2 vadas gives me the same level of satisfaction.  Now, I allocate my resources, depending upon the price of idles and Vedas.  If Ada is more costly, perhaps I will buy more idle, very simple, straightforward kind of reasoning there and that is exactly what these combinations that I am talking about A, B, C, and D are brought on these curves.  So, there are some properties, and that is just to keep in mind how this preference ranking works, it is downward sloping, we saw that. That is what does it mean?  It means that an increase in the quantity of a certain good will definitely decrease the quantity of some other good.  These are convex to the origin that is, if you want to have more of one good, you have to there is a trade -off; you have to give up some other good.  They do not intersect because each of those indifference curves represents different bund less of satisfaction.  So always, the idea is to move to the highest possible curve.  And, different curves show different levels of satisfaction.  So, the higher the curve higher the level of satisfaction, so, as a consumer with limited income, consumers would like to move to higher and higher indifference curves.  Now, we do not, we do not go to the properties of this in-depth because we want to take this to the understanding of markets.
