text: Business Data Management Professor G Venkatesh Professor M Suresh Baby Department of Humanities and Social Sciences Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Lecture 03 Changes in Demand and Elasticity So, an important aspect of understanding demand and market is to understand what factors influence demand and how that affects the working of the market. Instead, what are the factors that contribute to variations in demand?  To understand these variations in demand, we use a very simple concept called elasticities.  Now, elasticities can be used to measure the variations in demand. Now, what is elasticity?  Elasticity is the measure of responsiveness of quantity demanded for quantity supplied. To what ? To a change in one of its determinants.  So, quantity demanded or quantity supplied responds to one of its determine ants and that is elasticity.  Let us, take price elasticity of demand, which is very important in terms of understanding demand and markets.  What do we mean by price elasticity of demand?  By price elasticity of demand, we mean how much the quantity demanded of a good responds to a change in the price of that good. I repeat how much the quantity demanded of a good responds to a change in the price of a good.  Now, price elasticity is nothing but percent age change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price.  Price Elasticity = Percentage Change in Quantity Demanded Percentage Change in Price And quantity demanded responds substantially to changes in price which we know from the law of demand or theory of demand. W hen price increases, quantity demand falls and when price falls, quantity demand increases.  So, we can have two situations of elastic demand and inelastic demand. The elastic demand is a situation where quantity demanded responds substantially to changes in price and inelastic demand is a situation where quantity demanded responds only slightly to changes in prices.  Now, what are the determinants of the price elasticity of demand?  Well, one determinant is close substitutes. I f I have a close substitute, then when the price of one commodity changes, I might substitute that with that close substitute. So availability of close substitute s is very important in assessing price elasticity of demand. That is goods with close substitutes are more elastic in demand.  The second important kind of concept that we need to keep in mind is, we can classify goods on the basis of these elasticities. F or example necessities or commodities where the demand is inelastic.  For example, medicine prices, unit prices of certain medicines are very high, we might consume that because it is a necessity for us.  Whereas for luxuries, we notice elastic demand because well when the price increases we can avoid that perhaps, so the consumption on of luxuries can be postponed, we can wait. Whereas consumption of necessities we cannot postpone, which is why it is called a necessity.  So, necessities are these commodities for which demand is inelastic, and luxuries are those commodities for which demand is elastic.  So, how do we compute this? Well, straightforward computation and compute what ? Compute the price elasticity of demand.  Price elasticity of demand is computed as a percentage change in quantity demanded divided by a percentage change in price.  And we use the absolute value because when the price increases, the quantity demanded actually decreases, so you might end up with a minus sign, so we dropped the minus sign, and we use the absolute value.  So, a very simple kind of computation, percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price will give us the elasticity of demand.  Now, then you get varieties of demand curves.  When the demand is elastic what happens?  Price elasticity of demand is greater than 1. W hen the demand is inelastic, price elasticity of demand is actually less than 1, and demand is unit elastic when price elasticity of demand is 1. Let me explain these concept s a little more.  We can have situations where the demand is perfectly inelastic. We can have situations where price elasticity of demand is 0, when the demand curve is actually vertical.  So, we have situations where perfectly inelastic demand curve, we have situations where perfectly elastic demand curve comes.  So, when the price elasticity of demand is 0, when the demand curve is vertical, we say that demand is perfectly inelastic, medicines and things of that sort, whatever the price we will consume.  Demand is perfectly elastic when the price elasticity of demand is infinite, which means the demand curve is horizontal. For very small variation in price, we might not even buy it. So, the flatter the demand curve, the greater the price elasticity of demand.  But elasticity is not just the slope but also the position on the curve, which is very important.  So, I will go back for a minute.  So, we have varieties of demand curve s which we can see, earlier we saw only one kind of demand curve, they are downward sloping, but within that we can find varieties of demand curve depending on how elastic the commodity is to changes in price.  So, we have demand inelastic, unit elastic, then we have perfectly inelastic, and then we have perfectly elastic demand curve.  Now, let me put just one example for this. Here is a situation of a perfectly inelastic demand curve, in a perfectly inelastic demand curve, we find that well, the demand is perfectly elastic that is elasticity equals 0. What does that mean?  It means that, when the price of a commodity is increasing, that is an increase in the price from 4 to 5 dollars leaves the quantity demanded unchanged. I am buying only that much, I am not going to buy more because the price has varied, or I am not going to buy less because the price has varied.  So, there is a perfectly inelastic demand curve.  Now, elasticity is less than one is another example that I have put up, that is a 22 % increase in price leads to 11 % decrease in quantity demanded.  So, price elasticity of demand, determines whether demand curve is steep or demand curve is flat. Now, so here are two examples, perfectly inelastic demand, inelastic demand. Perfectly inelastic demand is when elasticity equals 0, that is when an increase in price leaves the quantity demanded unchanged.  In the other example, we find that a 22 % increase in price leads to 11 % decrease in the quantity demanded.  So, one can have various examples like this, so we can have varieties of demand curve, not the only downward sloping kind of demand curve.  Now, here is a demand curve with unit elasticity of demand, a 22 % increase in price leads to a 22 % decrease in the quantity demanded in this example.  And here is another example where elasticity is actually greater than 1, which is 22 % increase in price, leading to a 67 % decrease in the quantity demanded.  And finally, I show that there is perfectly inelastic demand, where I find that elasticity is perfectly elastic that is at any price above 4 dollars quantity demanded is 0, I will not buy that commodity at all. So, at exactly 4 dollars consumer buys any quantity, at a price below 4 dollars quantity demanded is infinite, and at any price above 4 dollars quantity demanded is 0, a perfectly elastic demand curve. So, let me just recap these kinds of demand curves once more.  Here, perfectly inelastic demand, then inelastic demand, but elasticity is less than 1.  Here, unit elastic demand, that is, elasticity equals to 1.  Here, elastic demand where elasticity is greater than 1. And finally, perfectly inelastic demand, where elasticity equals infinity.  But, so far, we have been talking about price elasticity, exactly like that we can also have an income elasticity of demand. What does it mean?  It means that how much quantity demanded of a good responds to changes in consumer s' income, not only price, by t can also change in market situations.  So, it is nothing but the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in the consumer's income.  Given the consumer's income, we can classify goods into two: normal goods and inferior goods.  Normal goods with positive income elasticity, necessities have small her income elasticities, luxuries have larger income elasticities, and inferior goods have negative income elasticities.  I will come to that in a minute what are these negative income elasticities.  Like price and income, there is a possibility of a cross price elasticity of demand. What does that mean?  That is how much the quantity demanded of one good responds to a change in the price of another good. That is percentage change in quantity demanded of the first good divided by the percentage change in the price of the second good will help you compute the cross price elasticity of demand.  So, remember, there are three variables, price elasticity of demand, income elasticity of demand, and cross -price elasticity of demand.  Now, with the cross -price elasticity of demand, we can classify goods as substitutes and complements.  How?  For substitutes, substitutes are goods typically used in place of another good, which means that there is a positive cross price elasticity.  Complements are goods that are typically used together, which means that there is a negative cross price elasticity, so what I have been trying to tell you is that by examining these elasticities, we can actually understand the nature of good, which is a very powerful insight.  You can understand whether it is a substitute, whether it is a compliment, whether it is inferior, whether it is normal, whether it is a necessity, or whether it is luxury. Fantastic, just one simple concept in terms of elasticities. We are using it in three different context variables: price, income, and price of related goods. That is all we were actually emphasizing here.  But then I have been talking only about one side of the story that is the demand side. You can also have exactly a similar situation for the supply side. You can have a price elasticity of supply where we can see how much of quantity demanded of a good responds to a change in the price of the good, because at higher prices, suppliers would like to supply more goods.  And that is nothing but the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.  And that also depends on the flexibility of sellers to change the amount of goods they produce, because all of a sudden you cannot prove certain goods more, just because there is a change in terms of the good s demand.  So, the elasticity of supply is parallel to the elasticity of demand.  Now, like how we classified goods in terms of elasticity of demand, we can actually classify goods in terms of elasticity of supply. Certain goods have very high elasticity in supply, we call it as elastic supply that is, quantity supplied responds substantially to changes in price, when there is inelastic supply, quantity supplied actually responds only slightly to changes in price and these are all determined in terms of the time period that we have in mind, because sometimes when you have a longer time horizon, you can be a little more elastic in supplying. If it is a shorter time horizon elasticity of supply is constrained by the time period or time horizon that we are talking about.  So, when we compute elasticity of supply, again like what we did in the context of elasticity of demand, it is nothing but the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price that is positive because the supply curve is an upward sloping curve. We have varieties of supply curves, unit elastic, elastic, inelastic, exactly like in the context of a demand curve.  Now, there are two effects which we need to keep in mind when we talk about elasticities, one is called the income effect and the other is a substitution effect.  What is the income effect?  The income effect is nothing but a change in consumer's real purchasing power by a change in the price of a good that is, if the price of a good falls and if that good is a part of my consumption basket, then in effect my income is actually increasing.  Because I can use that money with now is an extra because of the fall in the price of a particular good for the consumption on of something else, that is the income effect that I am talking about.  There is also a substitution effect that is basically an incentive to increase consumption of a good whose price falls at the expense of the other, but the other good now is a relatively more expensive good.  So, you tend to substitute the consumption of one good with another good depending on the price of this another good. S o two kinds of effects we notice in the market are the income effect and substitution effect. To analyze this income effect and substitution effect, we use these concepts of elasticities, which were explained in our concepts of elasticities.  So, let me summarize this whole concept of elasticities.  We are trying to understand using the concept of elasticities to understand variations in demand and supply in the market.  From our earlier discussions, we understood that the market needs to be in an equilibrium position to have a market clearing price and demand for the quantity.  Otherwise, what happens ? Otherwise, there could be shortages or there could be surpluses.  So, there are factors that affect demand and supply, to understand how these factors affect demand and supply, we use this very simple concept of elasticities.  And we saw first in terms of price elasticity, price elasticity measures a movement along the curve, it is the responsiveness of demand to price. We also saw income elasticity, income elasticity is a shift in the demand curve.  And we also use this price elasticity and income elasticity to classify goods, for example, a normal good is a good which has got positive income elasticity, whereas an inferior good is a good which has got negative income elasticity. That is, as and when my income increases the consumption of that particular good might actually decrease.  And we can also classify goods in terms of necessities and luxuries. Typically, those goods which are having an income elasticity between 0 and 1 are necessities and luxuries are goods that have elastic cities greater than 1, and we know that necessities are which irrespective of variation in price, we tend to consume either the same quantities or perhaps marginal reductions only.  So, these three concepts of elasticities then become very important in our analysis of market situations. 1) price elasticity, 2) income elastic city and 3) cross -price elasticity. P rice elasticity measures movement along the curve, income elasticity understands the shifts in the demand curve, and cross price elasticity examines the shifts in the demand curve.  Finally, we also saw that using these concepts of elasticities we can classify goods as substitutes and complements, goods are said to be substitutes, if their elasticity is greater than 0 that is, when the demand of particular good goes up in relation to the price of another good and goods are complements when the elasticity is less than 0 that is, demand goes down as the price of another good increases, we saw examples of that, and then we can actually classify goods as close substitutes or near substitutes and arrive at a classification of goods available in the market.  So, well a very simple concept, a simple concept of elasticity then provides us very important insights into the market mechanism.  The insights into the market mechanism are in terms of classifying goods, classifying goods into normal goods, inferior goods, complements, substitutes.  And in this process of classifying goods, we need data - data in terms of prices of goods, data in terms of incomes and data in terms of prices of related goods in the market.  If we have data relating to these three variables, that is prices, incomes as well as prices of related goods, then we can actually analyze market, classify goods in the market, and understand what the factors that actually determine demand in a market and what are the factors which actually causes variations in demand in the market are. So, that is why these concepts are very important in terms of understanding demand.

title: Nudge economics
text: Business Data Management Professor G. Venkatesh Doctor Mil ind GandheMister Venkat Subramanian Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Nudge Economics Mr. Venkat Subramanian: So the basic idea here is that typically in the marketing side, reuse this concept called Nudge economics, where you assume that the customers are busy, lazy and oftentimes confused, and they are likely to take whatever option you give them as default option. What that means is, so let us say you go to, maybe Flipkart or Amazon. One good example is, they do not show everything to you. They have, like you must have seen in the other case study, they have millions of products available, but they cannot show all that. I mean, there is only so much screen space available in your mobile phone, what they do behind the scenes, they sort of do an intelligent and educated guess on what is the product that is most relevant to you. And they will make sure those products are always coming at the top. Like, based, for example, based on my purchase history, since I often keep buying diapers form child, whenever I go to Amazon, there are always some diaper offers that are popping Pat the top. Like it must be something else for you. So I think the main point here is that it snot like I can purchase other things from Amazon. If I want, maybe I can even buy a shirt from Amazon, all those options are there for me when search for them. But by default, what I am going to be shown is what Amazon thinks is the most relevant item for me. And in most cases, it also makes my own life easier also. Instead of going and typing ‘I want this size diaper’ and all every time I, the moment I go there, I say,“Hey, this is the option I want, actually.” So I just click, go to the payment option, pay, and it is done for me. So this is the concept called nudge economics where people believe that instead of giving consumers too many different options, you sort of gently nudge them towards that option that you believe is Thebes for them. 70 percent, 80 percent of the cases, maybe it is actually the best option so they are directly going to click on, their life is easier, happier and done. Maybe 20 percent it is not actually the best option, in which case, they can still go and do whatever other things that they want to do. Professor G. Venkatesh: So this is somehow complicated, Venkat, sorry Mil ind, because normally one would say that for a consumer, you give him a lot of options and then the consumers evaluate these options, and then they make decisions and so, now you are saying the opposite actually, you are saying consumers actually do not like to be given so many options. They like to be told ‘you buy this, this is good for you’. Mr. Venkat Subramanian: I think this is probably, I do not know, I am not an expert on this, Think but this is the difference between the traditional economics and behavioral economics. Professor G. Venkatesh: Okay. Mr. Venkat Subramanian: It sort of assumes everyone to be a rational agent who is evaluating all the options available to him and making a utility function and sort of maximizing… Professor G. Venkatesh: So, there is a cognitive problem which means that people cannot process information, so much of information, they would like to reduce the amount of processing I guess that that is basically. Mr. Venkat Subramanian: I have seen in my own life, when I go to a restaurant, fancy restaurant with a huge elaborate menu card, I keep browsing, not able to decide what dish Want to eat, when I go to McDonald there are only 3 or 4 options of burgers available which they show in bright big things and I always choose the first one that I typically go with. Mr. Venkat Subramanian: That is true, yeah, correct. I mean, without that nudge, probably Will forget that I have to buy a diaper. Maybe in the last month I will go to the downward shop and buy it manually. So now they are avoiding me doing that and by showing it to me, they are making sure that I always end up buying from them. Professor G. Venkatesh: Yeah, in retail stores there is this business of nudging where they keep desirable things somewhere near the checkout counter. So you are… Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Chocolate near the checkout counter. Professor G. Venkatesh: Yes, chocolate exactly when you are standing there for checkout you kind of automatically be nudged, to reach out and get it. I suppose even in ecommerce they started to do that when you are rechecking out they will say a few more things before you check out where you want to look at these things, something like that they say. Mr. Venkat Subramanian: Retail example is a good one. Traditionally we see chocolates and candies put near the checkout counter. Basically I have read one another example where, apparently, a supermarket in the US wanted to promote healthy foods, like fresh fruits and vegetables. So what they did along the walking path, they put the green arrows that lead towards the fresh fruits and vegetables. So they discovered that people who are normally unlikely to buy suddenly somehow unconsciously follow those green arrows… Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: There is an enormous amount of psychology, consumer psychology Thais being used to shape buying decisions. Mr. Venkat Subramanian: Definitely sir, I think it is a lot of psychology because traditionally people do not think about, I mean, the way like professor said, the earlier mode of thinking was, these are all the options available from my company, I am going to throw all of that at you, you as a consumer, you decide what is best for you, which is putting a lot of choice forth consumer today it is the other way around, where we are saying that I will think through what is relevant for you and only present that option. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Fantastic. Mr. Venkat Subramanian: Just to tie the loop on why it is important for us. Now think about it again, a company like Pay buddy. Now you as a consumer already have multiple different credit cards, debit cards, bank accounts, and all in your Pay Buddy wallet.  Now, I am wherever, let us say you are on the verge of making a purchase of a mobile phone, usingPaybuddy. So this creates a bit of confusion in people's mind and that is where this again Nudge economics concepts we want to use, because we want to show the customers whatever inmost relevant for that particular customer for that particular transaction. So that he does not get confused between the multiple funding options available for him. Professor G. Venkatesh: Yeah, I wanted to ask you about that AI driven because AI is something that I think everybody reacts to sooner. Venkatesh: 10 Lakh, 1 million. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: 1 million, 1 million, sorry. So there are a million SKUs in their warehouse and out of that they are able to pick up those 3 things that are most likely to buy and send them to me. Professor G. Venkatesh: Correct. Mr. Venkat Subramanian: In our examples, we took like what you normally do and they are showing you that, like they said you buy many books so they show books, I buy diapers Botha show diapers, but they do not only do this. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: Yeah, and sometimes I have seen them actually saying people also bought XYZ. But sometimes they do not tell you. Mr. Venkat Subramanian: This is called in a more formal word because I see it as recommendation engine. It is very famous in the e-commerce world. Netflix is another good example. Essentially, Netflix again, has the same problem that there are millions of movies and TV shows available on Netflix. So when I log into Netflix, now, does Netflix show something random? No, it does not. It again, uses all these recommendation engines and AI driven models in the background to decide the most relevant thing for Venkat and apparently, it is fairly the main reason they say that the main reason for Netflix's success is the AI models behind what I showed to the customer. Dr. Mil ind Gandhi: So in our case, there are all these 7–8–10 payment choices and our challenge is to figure out which payment option to recommend to the customer. Is it? Professor G. text: Business Data Management Professor G. Venkatesh Doctor Mil ind Gandhi Mister Venkat Subramanian Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Presentation of Factor That Can Be Used For Nudge Mil ind Gandhi: Venkat, we looked at the data and did some analysis. We wanted to show you the results and get your feedback if we are on the right track or if some changes are needed.  Mil ind Gandhi: The first question Venue t, as we understood, was which customers are likely to pick which options. It was our understanding of what you wanted. Here is what we did.  We looked at some of the parameters you mentioned: how old is the account, the total of the last 12 months' credit card transactions, the whole of the previous 12 months' debit card transactions, et cetera.  And we try to plot it against which option the person used to pay. So, in columns, you can see the payment method, and rows are the values. So, is this analysis something that makes sense?  Venkat Subramanian: Yes, sir. I think it i s a good way of dicing the data. From the tables, we can differentiate between the customers in a single shot. We choose different options, like, is there any fundamental difference between somebody who prefers a credit card versus Pay Later; I think we can probably get those insights from this view. Mil ind Gandhi: Correct, some excellent points can be pointed out. W e tried painting it a little bit. If you take the average age in months into account, people seem to prefer a credit card for anything that is above two and a half years. That i s what it looks like. Is this correlating with your experience, or is this some accident of data?  Venkat Subramanian: Yes, I think these are probably older and more tenured customers of Pay Buddy. And typically, I mean, there is some bit of correlation as well here. But what we have seen is tenured customers usually ten d to be higher in age. And they a re typically at a live stage where they have multiple credit cards, and they find many transactions with credit.  Whereas lately, Pay Buddy has been acquiring more young millennials and people from college as their customers, who tend to use debit banking options. So, I think this probably makes sense.  Mil ind Gandhi: I see. People are spending large volumes on debit cards, their preferred method seems to be debit cards, but interestingly, their preferred method also seems to be Pay Later.  Venkat Subramanian: That is interesting. I think this is a valuable insight we can use to tailor, and we discussed this. It was also one of the h both uses that we wanted to validate.  Somebody is already using credit cards heavily ; the benefit for them by switching to Pay Later is not much because they are getting credit from somebody anyway.  So, why will they switch? Here we are talking about somebody changing from a debit card, and they will likely use Pay Later. I think that ties to our hypothesis. It makes sense. It can probably be used as a targeting rule to decide which customers to show Pay Later.  Mil ind Gandhi: Yes, we did see that as well, Venkat.  People have traditionally preferred credit cards. So, in this row, people have usually chosen credit cards. The people who use d Pay Buddy had not used credit card s too much in the past 12 months. Venkat Subramanian: T his is pretty interesting. As h e said, in the initial months, Pay Buddy did not differentiate between whom they were giving this Pay Later option. So they were showing it to everyone. But as the data tells us, the people who would choose it w ere the predominant debit card users, not the credit card users. I think k this is giving us, in terms of who we need to nudge. Mil ind Gandhi: We also looked at the percentage of debit cards in the wallet. But there does not seem to be too much of a correlation. So me correlation is there. People with a high percentage of debit cards in their wallets seem to prefer Pay Buddy. But the correlation is not as strong as this, or do you think it is strong?  Venkat Subramanian: I think we need to analyze more. But one thing is that percentage of debit cards can be misinterpreted. If somebody has only one card, then for that person, debit card, you will say 100 % for him. Here are ten cards ; out of which three are debit cards, that person will still get a 30 %.  Even though he ha d three debit s, the first person had only one debit card. This variable is 10% for the first person and 30 % for the second person. So, I think, in general, with such variables, which operate with a lower percentage on a small number, things can swing very easily one way or the other. So, I will be more cautious. So, it is not surprising that it is not giving us any direction now, we can investigate more, or we can decide to leave that particular data point out when we create our rule.  Mil ind Gandhi: Sure, and the final point, at least that st ruck me and GV, you can jump in. But it seems to me that the minimum age, people seem to be jumping into Pay Buddy Pay Later option reasonably early in their lifecycle with Pay Buddy. Does this potentially raise some risks for us?  Venkat Subramanian: Yes, sir. As we said, it is a trade -off between marketing and credit risk. From a credit risk Perspective, yes, I would much instead prefer tenured new customers about whom I know a lot of data. Still, I think the way marketing has been working. They are probably showing these advertisements a lot to the new customers of Pay Buddy.  So, maybe the payments, the new customers are much more aware of this kind of Pay Later option. Perhaps whenever they log out the Pay Buddy, they may choose an existing debit card or credit card by default. And perhaps marketing is also not targeting them a lot, which is a good insight. Maybe we need to tell them to target so that we do not get many new customers, increasing the risk of our Pay Later customer base.  G Venkatesh: We see an unique, non -overlap, or separation between the ranges available in wallet and banking a ND the credit options. So, it also looks like people who stay with Pay Buddy for some time tend to become correct users and then stop becoming targets for this Pay Later. In some sense, this Pay Later is a bridging option. You start, you become a debit card user, then Pay Later user, and then you become a credit card user.  Venkat Subramanian: That is an excellent way to look at it. As you said, the more tenured customers tend to be also in their life stage. They tend to be more mature and already have certain premium credit cards. They tend to use them repeatedly. It is probably tough to change them.  Maybe they are not our right target population because even if I do a lot of marketing for them, they may not change that. On the other hand, my risk is very high if I go to this extreme of brand-new customers. So, this Pay Later is probably good for somebody who is slightly tenured in the system but still not very old and settled down into their existing payment method.  Mil ind Gandhi: I interesting. The following reading vertical that we looked at Venkat contains travel and electronics. So which verticals did people tend to use, and what method of paying ? The first thing we did was we looked at the average price.  As we had discussed in our initial conversation, it seemed like travel was an expensive option. Maybe there are mobile phones available in a 200 Dollar range or that kind of range. Other accessories like the mouse and other electronic accessories are probably relatively cheaper. Venkat Subramanian: Exactly.  Mil ind Gandhi: 34% of the transactions were t ravel ed, and about 64% used a credit card.  Venkat Subramanian: That is pretty interesting. Mil ind Gandhi: The other exciting thing that struck me, Venkat, and you might want to sort of, I could not figure out ; there does not seem to be a dominant category in paying for electronics. So, in all the others, there appear s to be a preferred mode of payment. For travel, it seems to be a credit card; for fashion website s and pantries, it appears s to be Pay Later. We usually tend to assume that electronics people will prefer Pay Later. That w as our assumption earlier. But I think when we look at it later, it is probably spread through.  One possibility, and we need to confirm this. As w e discussed, maybe electronics as a whole range in it, we could be talking about anything from a mouse to an mo bile phone to a laptop. Depending upon the electronic product s we are discussing, there may be a preferred way, possibly aggregated electronics level.  Perhaps it looks a bit of spread through all the different funding options.  G Venkatesh: So, you have to see whether it is a high-value electronic item or not.  Mil ind Gandhi: Maybe there is a correlation between the product's price and the option being used.  Venkat Subramaniam: It works reasonably well when there are specific categories where the price of products is in a small range, like travel is always a value. Maybe we have seen a mix of options in the c lass that spread across price ranges. Mil ind Ga NDH: The other thing that we looked at, Venkat, was the effect of the engagement segment. Imagine this as a normal distribution : one end of the tail has to fall 10 to 20% on a certain minimal amount; many people will typically drop in the middle bucket. So, I think which is 44 % is mid-engage here. Mil ind Gandhi: When we looked at the E -commerce case study, we saw some exciting Pareto analysis, where we concluded that 20 % of SKUs contributed 80 % of sales. So Marsha has some interesting problems that she would like us to look at. What I thought I will do is give a very quick overview of this company and then I am going to request Marsha to tell us a little bit more about what are some of the challenges that this company is facing.  So, it is about a 15-16-year-old company, with 3,500 employees and as an IT company goes, this is not a small company but it is not a very large company either.  Some of our larger companies would have more than 100,000 employees.  Now one very important so there are many website s that when we are looking at recruitment, there are many websites which help a prospective employee get a better understanding of the company.  One such website is Glassdoor.  There are many such in fact in this particular case, this company has a Glassdoor rating of 3.515. Professor G Venkatesh : It is a good example.  What does it mean?  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : I would say it is average.  Marsha, what do you think ? Professor Marsha Gandhi : Yeah, it is average.  So, this is based on employee s’ perceptions. So, if I am working with a certain organization I will go to either a Glassdoor. It is like any of those review sites and I will give a rating for various factors. How good is the organization ? Do I get some kind of growth ? Do I get some kind of learning?  And there is also if I’m not mistaken. A rating for the CEO. So, the leader is the most important part of an organization. What is the CEO rating ? A 3.5 is an okay rating anything below 3 we would want to just check whether there is something wrong with the organization, does it meet our requirements or not, and 4 and above would be considered fairly good.  Professor G Venkatesh : Okay all right, is good.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : And then this company seems to have an attrition rate. Marsha what is the attrition rate?  Professor Marsha Gandhi : So, if you have 100 employees, for example, Mil ind, in your organization, and this is for the whole year. From April 2020 to March 2021, say 18 of those people go away. That is not an attrition rate. In IT service s, G.V. and Mil ind what we have seen for the last 20 years we have always had this kind of attrition rate, especially in IT services companies. It is around 18 percent.  In some of the other sectors, so if you look at the manufacturing sector, your attrition on percentage out there would be in the single digits, anywhere between 5 percent to 9 percent. But in IT specifically, this is what we see. The pharma sector also sees a higher level of attrition but typically not at 18 percent which is also between 12 percent and 15 percent IT in India has the highest number of people working out of the door for the organization.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : So, internally it seems s to me Marsha is that if employees have more options, more companies that they can go and work for the attrition rate will be higher, is that correct ? Professor Marsha Gandhi : No. So there are a lot of opportunities in the other sector also. Okay.  One the of the aspects that we have seen in IT services, is that people find it is easier to set their employment contracts in terms of what is it, what is the kind of project that you can get on to? What is the kind of learning that you will get and this is really what kind of incentivizes people to look for opportunities outside ? Yes, to a certain extent it is helped by the fact that more roles are available but there is also a certain push factor from the individual itself saying that I want to go onsite or I want to have exposure to Full Stack Development.  Those are the kind of things that push a person into looking for roles outside their organization.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : Interesting, so people have a view of how their career should develop, is it?  Professor Marsha Gandhi : Exactly, yes, that is right.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : I see. That is very interesting.  Professor G Venkatesh : Shall we look at the case what are the problems ?  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : Yeah.  Yeah, so Marsha you want to walk us through ? Professor Marsha Gandhi : Yeah, sure.  So, as you can see the attrition percentage we just discussed. It was 18 percent for tech enterprises very normal for the industry. When you look at that, what you must remember is that you are hiring one out of every five employees that you have every year. Now, in this kind of situation, some of the key players that we see in tech enterprises would be the person who is managing the programs.  So if I know that I have a team of 50 people and I know that I am going to have to replace 10 people in that over the next year.  As a program manager, I must know who are the kind of people that we are hiring.  So, I have a budget to match. I have to make sure that I give, my business head s the kind of profitability that is required.  So, the first person that we have in this whole drama is Madhu RI who is a program manager at Tech Enterprises.  She is responsible for delivering solutions to her clients and she has a team that work s with her. Only from a recruitment perspective and we are just looking at that particular aspect out here.  The second person who plays an equally important role would be Ritesh who looks at recruitment.  He is part of the HR team. He would end up reporting to the HR head in Tech Enterprises but functionally he will work with Madurai and report to Vida because he is hiring. Furthermore, he is making sure that all the vacancies that Madurai has in her team are hired for and fulfilled.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : So, Marsha there is one person who is full-time looking at recruitment, is it, in a company.  Professor Marsha Gandhi : So, in a company of 3,500 typically you will have a recruitment team of about anywhere between 3 and 7 people.  So larger organizations, which have got whether it is TCS, WIPO, or Infosys, will have larger teams consisting of 100 to 200 people, who are just looking at recruitment.  And when I say recruitment it is around making sure that there are positions and there are people so they might not all be on rolls, but they might have outsourced d some of the work making sure interviews are scheduled, and candidate profiles are received. So, it is fairly work intensive or effort intensive to find a role or to find a candidate who is best suited for your positions.  Last but not least we have Vida, who is responsible for taking decisions and she is head of the business in a sense, which is called Vice President Tech Enterprises, who does not play that a big a role, but he is involved in taking decisions on who needs to get hired in this particular case. So, we will start very simple, we will start very small.  And we will go to the first case or the first case as one example of the kind of problems that Madurai and Ritesh typically have to deal with. A little bit of background about Madurai is that as we saw Tech Enterprises was set up in 2005 and she has been with Tech Enterprises right off campus, she was hired as a fresher and she has grown through the lines to become a project director, program manager in an about 13 years. She has a team of 55 employees and therefore as I said she ends up having to hire at least 10 people in a year just to maintain the team at 55 employees.  So, she comes across this very usual problem that most program managers have to deal with.  She has been hiring at least 10 to 15 people right out of the campus. One of them has been with Madurai post his graduation as an engineer.  He has decided that he is going to go do further education.  He is interested in doing a Masters abroad and therefore he has resigned. Furthermore, he is serving his notice period.  His last day is going to be May 31. And Madurai realizes that she needs a replacement for ABH because he is part of one of the most important projects that are being delivered.  So, the person that she would reach out to would be the recruitment head of the organization who is Ritesh, and tell him that I need a replacement for ABH.  So, this is where we have these are the broad problems for the first case saying that Madurai desperately needs a replacement. It is pretty much life as usual but this is a problem she needs a replacement ABH who she has trained and groomed over the last five years is now quitting the organization.  Professor G Venkatesh : Presumably the replacement will come at the same salary as the existing one? Professor Marsha Gandhi : The replacement ment should typically come at the same salary or a slightly lower salary, and also with somebody with similar experience, and a similar profile. So that is what Madurai would look for because ) otherwise would run away.  Professor G Venkatesh : This profile and all are in the database so we know exactly what. We know he is provided.  Professor Marsha Gandhi : ABH’s profile would be in the HR ERP system.  It would have things like how many years of experience he has, what are competencies, what skills he has as well as what has been his performance ratings for the last 3 or 5 years, and what is the salary that he gets currently fixed as well as variable pay.

title: Introduction to HR as a function
text: Business Data Management Professor G. Venkatesh, Professor Mil ind Gandhi, Professor Marsha Gandhi Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Introduction to HR as a function Professor G Venkatesh : We are now into our next case and this case is a bit different from the cases we have seen in the – seen earlier, which is the – the Fab Mart case and the Ace Gears case. It says that we are going to now look at recruitment into an organization. How do you fill the staff in an organization?  So, we will see in this case basically that unlike the numerical values and plotting of numerical values we saw in the previous cases, data tends to be a bit more unstructured if you look at resumes and so on, you will notice basically that data in the resume is not numerical. It is anything but numerical and so we have to deal with those kinds of things and figure out how to select candidates based on information that is in the resume.  So much more subjective let us say or much more qualitative kinds of information we will see. Yeah Mil ind, I think that is the difference in this case.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : That is correct G.V. and we did see in the Ace Gears case that one of the things that came out of their production planning schedule was the manpower requirement sort of sheet and that is a logical connection I think to the conversation that we are going to have this week. Professor G Venkatesh : Yeah, yeah, correct, yes, and for this case, we are very fortunate to have with us professional s from the HR industry.  She has been in HR for decades, Professor Marsha Gandhi. Marsha maybe you can introduce yourself and maybe explain to the students what you have done.  Currently, you are with Mercer right, last few years with Mercer.  Professor Marsha Gandhi : Yes. So last year, I have been with Mercer and you are right, I do have decades of experience. I am having 20 years of experience in HR and when we say we have experience in HR, what does that mean?  It means that I have worked on processes for organizations and that could be anywhere from setting up the salary pay ranges for example, who should get paid how much to designing engagement service s, to ensuring that people have a smooth exit either when they retire or they – or they resign for example.  So, all of those processes I have been looking at. Last few years I have been with Mercer Consulting, for the last five years.  And Mercer Consulting is a consulting organization, an HR consulting organization that is a part of a global conglomerate called Marsh McLennan.  Mercer helps organizations review and redefine their processes, sometimes putting into place completely new processes on how they will handle employees.  Mercer has about 18,000 employees worldwide. In India Mercer is the largest consulting organization and has expertise across all these areas that I’ve just mentioned to you. Professor G Venkatesh : Okay.  So I think then maybe with that introduction Marsha you can take us through the specific case that we have which is - from an IT industry right, it is the IT case, and yeah, and maybe we can discuss it.  Professor Marsha Gandhi : Sure, sure.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : So G.V. as we discussed and Marsha I think the objective of this week is really to understand what are the different steps involved in the recruitment process but more importantly how can we use data to understand where recruitment is working well, where it is not working well, what challenges are there, and so on. So I am sure Marsha will be able to tell us a lot in terms of how exactly the recruitment process works and what kind of data the recruitment process throw.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : So Marsha maybe you can begin by telling us what exactly is manpower planning. Professor Marsha Gandhi : Sure Mil ind. So let us start with what happens when an organization starts planning for the next year.  So when you are planning for the next year, it is to of all organizations.  You could have large -sized organizations like your Accenture and Infosys, WIPO and you could have small -sized start-ups that we have whether it is a Dunno or Twiggy and I will just name a few companies here.  One of the things that they do is start looking at what is going to be their business plan for the next year.  Based on their business plan they decide to say that okay these are the kind of people, these many employees we need to be able to deliver results from a business perspective. So I need 50 sales people in my organization to get me a revenue of INR 100 crores and that very simply put is called manpower planning.  Manpower planning is making sure that you have the right number of people in your organization.  You have hired them at the right time, very important.  So for example, if Hawaii slippers the season that they sell most is during the monsoons.  So if you do not have your salespeople during the monsoon, you have missed out on a large part of your business cycle. So you have to make sure that your hiring is already done by the monsoon begin s and make sure that this sales team is well organized or well-trained to be able to deliver the kind of performance that in a nutshell is called manpower planning. Who will we hire? How many people will we hire? What will they do? And what they need to make sure that they are performing for the organization is manpower planning. Professor G Venkatesh : So this is very similar Mil ind to what we saw in the previous case. ) manpower plan, yeah, from the automotive case, yeah.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : Yes as we decided to manufacture 100) setup we realize d that we needed x number of people to produce y number of tires, and that is the manpower plan I think that Marsha is referring to there.  Professor Marsha Gandhi : That is right, that is right and one of the most important processes in manpower planning is recruitment.  Now even if you have a very small organization and we have seen this in start-ups also. All startups are – it is very, very important for them to make sure that there is one person who can go and hire the kind of talent or what we call employees, required for the organization.  So that becomes one of your first roles, one of the first positions that any organization requires and the recruitment process consists of this person saying okay I have these many vacancies in my organization.  This is what I need for these vacancies.  So there is a specific position.  There is a specific job and I need to find people who can do this role who can solve the problems, and who can take decisions at that particular level.  So it is the complete hiring process recruitment, starts with hiring and goes right on to when a person gets into the company.  We call it onboarding and make sure that the person has started performing in the organization.  So this entirety is the recruitment process.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : So Marsha maybe, you tell us a little bit more in detail about how this manpower planning work because this is something we saw in the last case as well and yearly seems to be a very important piece of how planning is done every year.  Professor Marsha Gandhi : Yes, Mil ind so that is right. If you do not have a human resource plan, so that it is basically like having a blueprint of what is that that your organization will deliver.  If you have a big IT services company, you need to say okay this IT services company is going to get 500 million dollars in revenue and needs so many people to be able to deliver that revenue and this is why we look at a human resource plan.  The human resource plan not only talks about how many people will you need but what is that they will be doing, what will be level ed, or what will be the grades they will. So you would typically have heard of designations like software engineer, senior software engineer, team leader, or project leader. What does that mean ?  It indicates the kind of work that a person is supposed to be doing in that organization.  So project leader can take some decisions that maybe a software engineer or a team member cannot, and this forms the complete basis of the human resource plan, how many… Professor G Venkatesh : And also basically you will decide what compensation they should get. Professor Marsha Gandhi : Exactly so how many people at what level your level also indicates what is the kind of salary that we will be giving at that level.  So obviously a software engineer will earn much lesser than a project leader.  Typically, a CEO of an organization earns 200 times what a software engineer earns right as a fresher. This is just I am just sharing the gap that is there in salaries. And that is decided through the basis of a human resource plan, saying okay these decisions are much more important to the organization. So, we will have to pay them more. With these decisions, a lot of mistakes can happen.  It is easily replaceable, so we will pay them less so that is how you help plan the labor cost too, sorry Mil ind, yeah.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : That the heart of this it seems to me Marsha and G V the core insight is that you cannot take out one person by just casually replacing with another person.  I think what I am hearing you say Marsha is that there are certain skills that each individual has that are relevant to the job that he or she is doing and so if person x leaves, you cannot simply replace person x with person y. You will have to see that there is some amount of matching that is going on between what person x used to do, what skills person x had, and what his replacement or her replacement brings to the table Professor G Venkatesh : So more increasingly the jobs are getting specialized is that how I understand.  I mean so basically there are, there is much more specialization in the jobs, especially IT is very, very specialized in that sense.  And so this replacement becomes much more complicated because you have to look at the specialized skills that they have.  Professor Marsha Gandhi : Absolutely, yes. So, you have to make sure that the person that you are getting into the organization is an absolute fit for the role, absolute fit. He can do what is required either in the project or the product development as you talk about but you have to have those skills and as you said G V in IT becomes very, very important.  There is an inventory of skills that most IT companies have and obviously, some skills always have a premium, it becomes very important for you to have the most important, a good combination of these skills and that is how people get hired especially in IT sector.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : Yeah okay, so actually and even in the production planning G V we saw that the people who could operate the robbing machine, could not operate the other machine, you do not replace them very easily.  Professor G Venkatesh : Yeah, yeah, it is not one-to-one, yeah, that is true.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : It is not one-to-one.

title: Caselet 2 introduction Job Description
text: Business Data Management Professor G. Venkatesh Professor Dr. Mil ind Gandhi Professor Marsha Gandhi B.Sc. in Programming and Data Science, Diploma Level Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Week 09, Lecture 06 Case let 2 Introduction: Job Description Professor Marsha: In this particular case and this is also a very common business problem that most program directors typically face, and you have seen the IT industry growing by leaps and bounds over the last couple of decades.  Tech Enterprises similarly has also seen a lot of growth and a lot of this growth, therefore, requires people to be hired from outside making sure that you know you have to have a very specific recruiting process. Madhuri's team currently has won a large business deal from a telecom major at the beginning of March 2021 and for making sure that she can deliver that particular project she reaches out to them once again Ritesh and tells him that she needs 12 people on board in her team as soon as possible.  So, she needs 12 people so her team of 55 will end up becoming 67, but in June 2021 she needs five team members which are basically like five software engineers and one project leader to start working on the first milestones of the project.  She will need another five team members, she will need to ramp up the team with another five software engineers and one project leader by August 2021.  Professor Mil ind: Everybody does not have to come at the same time?  Professor Marsha: Not necessarily, once she wins the deal Madurai will create a project plan saying what the deliverables of the project plan will be, they will have milestones and these milestones will indicate saying how many people she need s to put on the team and what kind of people.  So if it is a different phase, she might not need business analysts later on in the project, she might need business analysts right up front.  So those are the kind of profiles and that is the kind of planning that Madurai will have to do the moment she wins a project. So the project plan is created which is a smaller part of the manpower planning that we discussed earlier it is to a certain extent the same thing. Professor Mil ind: And to some extent that makes Ritesh's job a little easier, I am Marsha that it is easier to get 6 people in June, and 6 people in August versus getting all 12 in June.  Professor Marsha: That is true, but if you ever tell this to any recruitment person he will probably laugh you out of the room because no recruitment person's job is easy in the IT industry. Professor Mil ind: Okay.  Professor Marsha: There is always pressure and there is always a requirement to hire the best possible profiles in us in a very specific budget and we will also come to that shortly it is very, very important that Madurai not just says what her requirements are, but really what her budget is.  Professor Venkatesh: So, you are recruiting from outside now, you are not looking at an internal candidate.  Professor Marsha: We are not looking at intern all candidates, but honestly GV even if you are looking at internal candidates you need to make sure your internal candidate is not very overpriced for the vacancy that you have. So for example, in our earlier example, Ritesh could not have given her a project leader profile somebody with eight years of experience to fill in a five-year experience kind of role just you know because that person probably can do much better, has more expertise, can probably already lead a team is looking at other things so that is how we look at it.  Professor Mil ind: Who maintains control of this budget, Marsha?  Professor Marsha: Typically, at the beginning of the year Madurai and Vida would have created a plan based on how they think the business is going to grow. So currently if they say that Vidya's team is around 150 people by the end of the year it is going to grow to say 250 people, and another 100 people are going to come on board that plan is created right up front saying that my revenues are going to grow like this, month on month, this is what I see happening in the quarter, not month on month but quarter wise.  And these are the kind of positions I will need to be able to deliver this kind of revenue and that is the custodian of that or the person who is responsible for that would be Vida supported by Madurai. All decisions will be taken by Vida saying, okay I can afford to have 100 people because I know my revenue is going to go up by this much and I know my profitability is going to go up by this much. Professor Venkatesh: And the bench, maintaining the bench or the additional staff?  Professor Marsha: That would be part of the manpower plan saying that okay if I am going to increase from 150 to 250, most organizations have a certain kind of percentage, 7 percent as a bench and that gets added on saying that okay these 10 positions or these 7 positions will be my bench.  Professor Mil ind: So when Madurai wants another 12 people, basically she has to go and request Vida to give her that budget from that addition all 100 that Vida was planning to hire this year, right?  Professor Marsha: That is right.  Madurai goes to Vida and says okay I have got this new project, we have it in the plan, but now I need you to specifically approve these 12 people out of the addition all headcount that you have agreed to. Vida looks at the plan and then gives her the approval; she might change a few things saying that you do not need so many people. There will be some amount of negotiation between Vida and Madurai saying what is the best profile and based on that approval process with Vidya's approval, Ritesh can go ahead and recruit from outside.  Professor Mil ind: So, negotiating with Vida is Madurai’s responsibility, but once that negotiation is done, then Ritesh takes over.  Professor Marsha: Exactly Professor Mil ind: And then what does Ritesh do?  Professor Marsha: So, then this indent, this approval so we are talking about the approval process Vida has approved indents for these 12 people to be hired, this is the basic start of the recruitment process flow and that is what we have out here on this slide. It is a fairly simple process at the top level, the whole idea of this process is so that Ritesh can plan out the next steps, and make sure that the process runs efficiently. The first one as we said is Vida approving the indent, the second one would be to make sure that there is a specific job description for these approved indent. Professor Venkatesh: Please explain to Marsha what you mean by job description, you will explain that.  Professor Marsha: Yes, we will go through each of the processes, Professor Venkatesh: Because this, what is an indent, what is the job, okay we will discuss it all.  Professor Marsha: We will go through it and then in the subsequent parts also, the third one would be where candidates are sourced and interviews are scheduled. Once an interview is scheduled, you get a good candidate, you would want to as an organization roll out the offer and then the person is board ed. So this in a nutshell as I said is the recruitment process and there are metrics there is data at each step that is analyzed and collated and needs to get reported back to either Ritesh, Vida, or Madurai as the case may be to make sure that this process is going on smoothly.  Professor Mil ind: And that will be interesting Marsha if later on, you explain to us what kind of data gets generated and what decisions as an example Ritesh or Vida or Madurai would make based on that data, so I am going to look forward to that.  Professor Marsha: Sure, definitely we will go through that in greater detail.  Professor Mil ind: I think GV had some questions about each of the process ES so maybe you can tell us a little bit about that. Professor Marsha: So, this as we said was the first step so we call it sub-processes, the first one is HR planning and the job indent and we have touched upon this a little bit in the beginning. It would start as we can see out here with an approved HR plan and budget and this is what we mean by Vida giving her approval for these 12 positions. Ritesh then starts off this particular process and checks to make sure that it is already there in his recruitment plan.  Some abilities have been defined, skills that have been defined, and to make sure that this HR manpower plan that we had created in the beginning has been updated with these 12 positions and there are job descriptions that are there. Once these job descriptions are there these positions are then reviewed and approved, and a revised plan and job intent are created. So what we are talking about here is the negotiation that happened between Vida and Madurai before we have approval on the indent.  Now one of the things that we are talking about out here which probably would be a new, a little bit of a jargon that we are talking about is a requisition or an indent. Now, what is the requisition or an indent ? It is typically a form that is created by HR and that is used to track some of the data that will be required later on in the dashboard. So, this is where the data begins, this is an input for the data, one of the things is what are the budgetary details which mean how many people can be hired, and at what salary levels can they be hired.  So can I hire three people at 3 lakhs, or can I hire one person at 9 lakhs is what the budgetary details basically about ? What is the timeline of the position that is required, so in this particular case Madurai’s case we saw that we needed 6 people in June and 6 people in August, so there would be a broad level plan saying that in this quarter Vidya's team is going to increase by 30 people, in quarter two another 30 people, quarter three is going to be a little low, and they will only have 10 people hired.  So those are the kind of timelines that is there in the indent saying that okay I need to hire this person by March, I need to hire this person by June. And certain specific contractual aspects are also required in the index, is this position a full-time position, is this posit ion a part-time position, can this be delivered by a gig worker or is this something that we have already on our third -party provider rules ? A lot of ID companies especially the product companies work with third -party providers and it would go on to a TPP role. Professor Mil ind: Marsha this is like very broad guidance to the dish, actually identify whether to hire person x or person y?  Professor Marsha: No this is to make sure that there is one access which is the cost and the time is managed properly; the other access which is on the detail of what the position requires to deliver is in something that we call the job description.  Okay and that is where we talk about the JD, it is called JD for short and it is usually a quick summary, a very quick summary of what is the role expected to do. This means what is the kind of problem -solving that they have to do, what is the kind of knowledge that they have to bring along with them, and what are the educational qualifications required for that particular role? So, you know a business analyst will require expertise in a domain, so I need to know some, so if I need a business analyst for the financial sector, I would like to have somebody who has worked with an ICICI or an HDFC or any of the financial services organizations.  Professor Mil ind: So Marsha that day when you sent me all this data, this is a little difficult for me to understand, so I was thinking that day when you sent me the data you had sent a sample JD. Maybe what I would request you is, maybe just explain this to us. Just hold on let me open the document itself instead of this slide.  Professor Venkatesh: So, this is for one position not, one person one position.  Professor Marsha: This is for a position.  Professor Mil ind: Maybe if you can just explain what this is to us that will be useful, what do you say GV?  Professor Venkatesh: I think that will help quite a lot.  Professor Marsha: So here we are talking about the position of an Application Security Engineer in Tech Enterprises. You will out here see that there are certain primary duties what is it that this application security engineer has to do. Conduct code reviews, develop and maintain unit and integration tests, conduct application security assessments penetration tests, etc. this is what he is supposed to be doing.  This changes, so for example, instead of a security engineer we had a project leader kind of role out here the primary duty would be to make sure that the delivery y milestones are met, testing has been conducted, the customer has been managed, the customer or the client and the client has been updated of the project development or saying you know what stage the project status is on, so that would be the primary duties this is what the person is supposed to do.  The second part would be the primary skills and requirements, this is in terms of any specific things that Madurai say wants, she wants somebody who has an experience with certain development languages. This is necessary for her, and she would like somebody with secondary skills, somebody who also has some amount of experience with security penetration, testing tools, as well as any other exposure required.  Again, I will go back to the example of a business analyst, so for a business analyst the primary skill would be the need to know processes in the financial services, and secondary skills would be I know what's happening in this particular application domain, so those are the kind of things what we talk about primary skills, secondary skills and then some very specific position requirements ah which is a little more of explanation of skills requirement.  One is of course the education qualification saying that we need a bachelor's degree in engineering, this can be changed by saying we need an MSC in CA or anything else depending on what the position require s’s and a certain more of, these are the years of experience in application development and security, five years must be also from a softer skill perspective must be able to communicate well, must be able to have a have certain kind of presentation skills, has may have to deal with a certain amount of senior executives. So, both technical skills, and software skills, are then outlined, so that Ritesh knows exactly what to search for.  Professor Venkatesh: The keywords we are seeing here, Marsha, like Java development, JavaScript, Python, Ruby or Metalloid or whatever, it is all these things become search items for some databases, and they will be keywords.  Professor Marsha: Yes, yeah and they get rated based on whether they are primary skills which are must -have skills, or secondary skills.  So, each resume profile as you go through it, they will pick up saying these many times java development came up as part of the experience, and this algorithm gives a recruiter saying that okay from a database of 15000 applications, these are a thousand applications that we need to look at more closely. There are challenges with some of the algorithms that are used, sometimes when these are very standard rules it is easier to find these kinds of profiles, but when there are specific rules the margin of error of an AI algorithm hunting out the correct profile for you is often quite high.  Professor Venkatesh: ) . Professor Mil ind: So, my impression by looking at this JD Marsha correct me if I am wrong this almost looks like some of the job advertisements that you see in newspapers or on the net on this is a little bit more detailed. title: Internal sourcing
text: Business Data Management Professor G. Venkatesh Professor Mil ind Gandhi Professor Marsha Gandhi Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Introduction to HR as a function Professor Mil ind Gandhi : So, Marsha last, you earlier told u s about this situation where ABH had left Madurai’s team or wanted, had said that he is going to leave Madurai’s team and Madurai had approached Ritesh to find a replacement for ABH. So, can you just walk us through what happens then ? What does Ritesh do ? What does Madurai do? How does this whole scenario sort of payout ? Professor Marsha Gandhi : Yeah, so why is it so important for Madurai to replace ABH right away ? As I said ABH was somebody who was part of her core team delivering a very important project for a marquee client. Now she needs a replacement as soon as possible. The typical hiring times for people in the IT sector at a lower level would be anywhere around 2 months and goes right up to 4 to 5 months. The average recruitment time is actually around 3 months but she can not wait for 3 months so she tells Ritesh just check if we have anybody internally. So, how do you get to internal sourcing this is what we call internal sourcing. The idea of internal sourcing is that you look for profiles as we said, you have to have that kind of competencies, that kind of experience, and profile. So that it fix in with what ABH has been doing and somebody who can pick up quickly transition from what ABH was doing. The best person who can do this very quickly would be somebody who knows tech enterprise systems, knows how tech enterprises work, and is already within the system. So, this is called internal sourcing and people may want to move to Madurai’s team to fill ABH’s position because they see it as a promotion. So, they know ABH is a software, a senior software engineer. I have 3 years of experience if I apply for this role, maybe I will become a senior software engineer.  Currently, I am a software engineer. So that is called promotion.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : Marsha, you mentioned something people could move to Madurai’s team. So ABH’s replacement could come, could be some outside Madurai’s team also, is it?  Professor Marsha Gandhi : Absolutely and that is what internal sourcing is all a bout. So, there are people in other projects also right, but this particular project might have some competencies. I was saying, people are interested in picking up different skills. They want to know what is happening say in another part of the project and that is how they think learnability will happen. Their resumes will grow and that is how they will get a better salary package.  So, there is either a promotion or there is what we call a lateral movement. So even though I am a software engineer, senior software engineer, I might want to move to Madurai’s team because it gives me a different kind of exposure and that is something that I would like to do and that is where the lateral movement comes in. Professor G Venkatesh : There is, Marsha there are also some additional people that the company has kept in reserve, right? It is not a bench, bench in IT.  Professor Marsha Gandhi : Exactly, exactly. So just coming to that, the lateral movement can also happen through the bench. No w bench is part of the buffer that is maintained by IT services organization because one is people have to go on leave. I mean there are 15 days of leave that everybody gets and as you saw there is attrition so it makes sense for organizations to keep maybe 7 percent buffer, maybe 5 percent buffer, 8 percent buffer and this is also part of the manpower planning saying that this will be the bench.  Bench are those people who are not linked to any project or not linked to a project that gets you revenues right. That is why we call them to bench, or we call them to buffer, and these resources can be of course placed very quickly soling Madurai’s problem.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : But then you need who is at a level that is appropriate for ABH.  Professor Marsha Gandhi : Exactly, exactly, so.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : How do you decide that ? Professor Marsha Gandhi : So, then Ritesh would go back to Madurai and say what is the kind of person who require s. So, I know ABH is going. I know he has 5 years of work experience. As I said they will be there in the HR database, and he has experience in visualization tools and basic data modeling.  What Madurai will tell him is that this person also, so ABH has been managing a team of 2 to 5 people along with him because he w as going to become a lead engineer very soon, and he has got a fantastic performance appraisal rating in the last 2 years. So that is something that we would like for the internal candidate also to have and these are the criteria that Madurai will give Rite sh and there will also be some other skills apart from visualization tools, and basic data modeling.  There will be certain another language as well as platform requirements that Madurai will not have that she would provide Ritesh with to be able to see we at would be the best sourcing from the internal sources either as we're saying people applying for that or people moving from the bench or the buffer.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : So, one of the things you would have mentioned Marsha is that ABH has always had a great performance and great appraisal. So, could you tell l us a little bit about what this appraisal is just ? Professor Marsha Gandhi : Sure, sure. So we also saw right, right at the beginning, saying that an organization type at the beginning of the year will set out some goals, right but that happens at an organization level saying I have to make 500 million US dollars of revenue this year.  How does a software engineer know, what is it that I am supposed to contribute so that the organization makes 500 million dollars of revenue ? Typically, what it would translate to is that the software engineer has to deliver a certain standard of work, a certain number of hours of work saying that okay he has to make sure that every week he has delivered 35 hours of work in this particular project. So basically, a project that gets revenues. We call it a billable project and the quality of that work has minimal errors, and very little rework, which indicates what the person’s performance is. So, what is his, what is his quantum of contribution, and what is the quality of contribution this is something that is measured by all managers and that is what is called appraisal.  So, at the end of the year, I mean all of us are used to this in academics. We get CGPA. We get a rank. In organizations typically we get a rating at the end of an appraisal and this rating HR teams use to make decisions about what is the salary hike to give a certain individual or for that matter whether this person is eligible now for the promotion or a transfer. These are some of the things that are looked at from an appraisal. So appraisal is a process, the outcome is a rating and the rating is used for other purposes in the organization.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : So, even w hen the course is over we are not going to escape exams ?  Professor Marsha Gandhi : No, no. We always have a label. We always have a rating. So actually, that is a very interest ING point for some organizations as part of a performance appraisal, there is an assessment that we have to go through to get a certain, so assessment, certifications, so you are not done with exams, you are not done with ratings, and it continues.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi : Okay, so let us go back to internal sourcing.  Professor Marsha Gandhi : Yeah. Now as we said before Madurai actually or Ritesh goes out and looks for candidates outside tech enterprises, he would do a couple of things. Once this is done the existing manager, so for example in this case if it goes to Madurai, there might b e somebody else who is getting impacted and that person needs to know that okay I will have to now hire somebody for my project if that person has not been on the bench and usually organization s look at a period of 2 months for transitioning.
