title: Sourcing channels and their analysis
text: Business Data Management Professor G. Venkatesh Professor Doctor Mil ind Gandhi Professor Marsha Gandhi Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Sourcing Channels and Their Analysis Professor Dr. Mil ind Gandhi : Now that this JD is there, Marsha what happens there ?  Professor Marsha Gandhi: So, once the JD is there, and typically Madurai will have to create these JD's for each role that she has. So for example, if the project you know, the project leader, you saw, the primary skills and the secondary skills will be different from the ones that she has for her team members.  So your application security engineer, primary skill, and secondary skills will be different.  So Ritesh takes a look at these job descriptions, just to make sure he is understood, he might have some questions from Madurai saying, okay, you have asked for this kind of experience.  What if, you know, he does not have experience only in this, but also in this?  So those are kinds of questions that he will try and understand what the job description is about.  And he creates a very short recruitment plan, just for these 12 positions.  He has an annual plan, but this is very specific for these for this, just to make sure that he and Madurai are aligned on what is going to happen. Professor G. Venkatesh: This is like a project, an HR project.  I mean, HR itself has a project to recruit 12 people.  Professor Marsha Gandhi : Absolutely, yes. Professor G. Venkatesh : It has milestones.  It has everything.  It has its things.  Professor Marsha Gandhi : Exactly, exactly.  And Ritesh is a project manager in that particular sense. Professor G. Venkatesh : For that project, to recruit people. Professor Marsha Gandhi : Yeah. And he reports to Madurai as his client.  Professor Dr. Mil ind Gandhi : Wonderful.  Ok. Very clear.  Professor Marsha Gandhi : Yeah, and the job description is basically like the specs, your project specs. Professor Dr. Mil ind Gandhi : This is what I understand now Marsha.  This is like a project plan, now you are saying. Professor Marsha Gandhi : Absolutely.  So, when he creates a project plan, he starts by saying that these are the positions and he will now talk about each position. Each position will get a number, saying project leader one, project leader two, team member one, and team member two because each of these might have different primary skill, and secondary skill requirements, based on what Madurai has said.  So, what the open position is? What is the timeline which we spoke about in the indent ? So, the timeline comes from the indent.  And what could be the channels of fulfillment ? Now, what do channels of fulfillment mean?  Channels of fulfillment mean where is Ritesh going to hire these people from.  Internal maybe not happen, because this is growth, this is not attrition. So this is, there are people, we need more people to be able to deliver this revenue.  So we are going to look at people outside. When you look at people outside that could be four or five channels that we are talking about.  In terms of, where Ritesh could get candidate profiles from. The first one is, of course, publishing this particular thing on the company website and asking for applications.  The second would be second channel would be an employee referral channel; this is what we call it. And this is where employees get a certain amount of money if they refer their friends, and families, for this particular post.  Ritesh would also look at job portals, like LinkedIn, and Nauru, and publish these jobs out there.  Each of these portals, by the way, has some amount of money that they beg by publishing these positions.  So, it all depends on, whether, these positions are budgeted, Rites h has it in his budget or not. And Ritesh will also look for third -party consultants, saying okay, project leaders, I might not find profiles in my database, okay.  From LinkedIn, from Nauru, I will need specific third -party consultants to be able to deliver that. One of the things that they can also do is, organize a Walk -In. This is very similar to putting up the putting up this position on the website.  But this is a more physical form than people that, you know, the team members can get hired.  And he can also look at the fresher pool or the bench buffer that we spoke about, for the team member positions that we have for our job.  So, what does Ritesh do? He has been tracking all the profiles. At the end of the first week, he has gone only five applications. Now, if you look at the conversion rate, typically for every one position that needs to get closed, you need anywhere between 20 and 30 resumes to be sourced, before you can hire a candidate.  Professor G. Venkatesh : So, we need to clear the 60 resumes.  Professor Marsha Gandhi : Yes, you would need 360 resumes. Professor G. Venkatesh : Good god.  Professor Marsha Gandhi : Yeah.  And, and it becomes, this funnel becomes even more difficult as your positions go higher.  So your leadership is, it is very difficult to get leadership resume s in the first part. And there your conversion rate could anywhere be between, you know, eight resume s is looked at, and one person hired, but the time taken is much higher.  So if you are hiring for a CEO, a CMO or a CEO, or CTO of an organization, your hiring time is anywhere between six months to nine months.  And you might go through about 10 to 12 profiles because you have to head-hunt them as it is called. So to be able to meet Madurai’s timelines, you can see five applications is nowhere near enough.  Five candidate resumes are nowhere near enough.  So he wonders whether you should go to recruitment consultants.  Remember recruitment consultants, LinkedIn, Nauru, all of them take money.  There is no such thing as a freelance. So, he has to make sure, he has to analyze the 10 members, should I go to a recruitment agency?  Should I do a walk -in? Should I do another glass through LinkedIn?  And this is what we call channels.  And he has to figure out, how effective is this channel. He has to look at the past data, figure out trends, figure out costs associated with each channel and make sure that he has the best possible solution for Madurai’s hires.  Professor Dr. Mil ind Gandhi : So, D. V., it may be a good idea for us to sort of doing a little bit of this channel analysis and see if we can come and present something to Marsha.  Professor G. Venkatesh : Correct.  Understand. Yeah, let us do that. Yeah.  Professor Dr. Mil ind Gandhi : Yeah.  Professor G. Venkatesh : Let us do that. Professor Dr. Mil ind Gandhi : Let us do that, and come back and present to Marsha Professor G. Venkatesh : Yeah, Professor Marsha Gandhi : Sure. So there will be some historical data that will be there, which you can analyze and then figure out which one works best for Ritesh and Madurai.

title: Summary Skills availability _ role of HR
text: Business Data Management Professor G Venkatesh Professor Mil ind Gandhi Professor Marsha Gandhi Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Summary: Skills availability & role of HR Mil ind Gandhi: So, Marsha now that we have seen all of this, a few sort of questions that I have, and wanted you to give us a little bit of thinking. See many times now we see technology keeps evolving. So, today maybe everybody is talking about cloud, tomorrow everybody is talking about AI. So, how do organizations figure out what skills will be needed? And how many skills are available in the market? So, how many AI engineers or how many CCD engineers are available in the market? So, how does an organization get a picture like that? Technology keeps evolving, things keep changing. So, it is very hard to stay on top? Marsha Gandhi: Sure, I think I have put up a couple of examples for us to look at. And this typically happens, what you are talking about are competencies moving, not just in the tech industry, but also in other industries, say like pharma, or chemical industry. So, we have seen this happening in other sectors, also, it becomes extremely critical when it comes to tech because the pace of change in tech industry everybody knows is phenomenal, but it also happens in other sectors, also, it is a little more conservative. So, the traditional conservative forecast models are created by organizations taking into consideration maybe 6 to 8 factors. And some of those factors typically would be what is the availability of labor force. So, how many people will be available in this particular region, in this particular country? And how many of them will be say bachelors, graduates in pharma, in chemical or what whichever industry we are talking about. So, that would be one part of the growth. The other thing and so, the first thing that you would do is to estimate the demand, what is it that the industry will need, how many engineers in the tech industry need, the first one is how is the labor force growing? The second one is how is the industry output itself growing? So, what is so, there are certain assumptions that you would look at in terms of this industry growing over the next few years. So, you would look at industry output, and you would look at how the aggregate economy is growing, how the sector contributes. So, how much does India IT services contribute to our GDP of the economy, GDP is Gross Domestic Product for India. What is the industry employment that is associated with that? Once you put all these into a mix, you create a model saying that this is in the year 2015, 2016. These other point forecasts say that, with this kind of industry output with this sector contribution to GDP, I will need this much amount of labor force, I will need this much amount of industry employment that is called the demand side estimation. So, all you have done in this one particular slide looking at all of this is to say that okay today Asia industry we need X lakhs of technology engineers IT engineers in this particular sector. In2025, this is what we will need. Some of them, there are some studies like the workforce for the future, which talks about which are the skills that will be important, there is that we see these skills growing and those also contribute to the demand. So, once you have looked at the demand, the next thing that you do is you also look at the supply, you have started off with 2 lakhs of engineers, you have so many more in the pipeline, these many positions are going to be coming up. In this particular example, you can see that till2010 there was a surplus number of people available for the positions that were there, but after that it has become scarce. So, the gap between the supply and your demand curves when you plot them will tell you saying okay, this is where this kind of skill is, this is where this kind of competency will become very difficult to hire for. And as an, as an industry, as a sector, we would like to focus on this particular skill set, it could be AI, it could be machine learning. So, these are something that would be required for tomorrow. But what might not be required is say skills and accounts payable, accounts receivable, because those are just posting of queries, posting of ledger entries, and that can be automated. So, those are some of the assumptions that you will see behind these numbers. But it is a fairly complex process. Organizations would love to do this, but most organizations who do this are actually part of an industry association. So, you would have somebody like a NASCAR, or you would have somebody like the Indian Chambers of Commerce. Doing these studies, doing these simulations to figure out what is going to be the talent scarcity? And where is it that they need to put money into skill development and skill building? So, Know there are a lot of big words with that, but that is how it is done. Mil ind Gandhi: So, G V this is actually a little bit of the macroeconomics piece that we looked at in the first four weeks. G Venkatesh: Correct, we did it for goods, but here this looks like for labor actually, yeah. And for each category of labor, specialized labor, so looking skill wise in some sense, what is the demand and supply? So, for HR, the people are there. You can project a demand for people, even though I did not realize that is what is done, this chart used to say, but actually creating a demand and supply for people. They are looking at the labor market. Yeah. Varsha Gandhi: So, the Singapore government actually has done detailed studies on the labor market. And they have done extensive mapping of what competencies, so typically done by governments, because they are the ones who have a macro perspective, they know what kind of people will be available, they know how the industries are growing, and what they will need to promote as education. So, the Singapore government has done a fantastic job in creating these competency libraries, and figuring out where people stand as of now. Mil ind Gandhi: Now, this is very interesting. I always see all these news items, saying India will need 1 million engineering graduates in 2025, or something like that. And now I begin to understand what is some of the work that goes in beneath those headlines? So, the second sort of summarizing question, Marsha I had I think, at least as a lay person, I understand some of the challenges in getting what, what a production person does, how he makes gears, how he, I also understand how a logistics person works, he gets a get parcel from their house to my house. What really does HR do, I think, today, you gave us a little bit of a flavor. But I am still curious what keeps the HR people busy? Because it is not a very intuitive thing. So, what, what keeps HR people busy?  Marsha Gandhi: So, there are quite a few challenges that an HR person has to deal with. And what I am sharing with you on this particular slide, is what have been the top priorities for an HR person in 2018.  Last two years, the CHAO has actually been much more central to an organization delivering its business because… G Venkatesh: Yeah, Chris, chief HR officer? Varsha Gandhi: Correct, CHAO chief HR officer, human resource officer, I guess. And before COVID happened, the CHAO had to make sure that somebody who started work in 1990 is as engaged as somebody who is going to start work in 2020. And these two generations, so if I can just even look at India, are very different. One came from an extreme scarcity mindset. And the other is somebody who is hooked on information 24/7. So, managing a multi-generational workforce has been one of the biggest challenges. How do you make sure that your benefits actually talk to both? Flexible Working before the pandemic was a big challenge for the HR folks to organize. Managers are not sure whether people are really performing to their best when it is work from home. Pandemic has… Milind Gandhi: I think in the last two years, that has changed, I think Marsha. Marsha Gandhi: So, not really, if you see some of the biggest challenges that people are facing today after the second wave. The HR people are saying, how do I get people to come back to work? Why does an HR person, or why does a manager need people to come back to work? A LOOF time is not, the people think it is wasting time at the water cooler it is not that. A lot of information gets exchanged at the water cooler. A lot of learning happens at the watercoolerwhich is currently not happening. Everybody knows, and this is equally true in education. The efficacy of education or the efficacy of having teams work together, has significantly been diluted, people do not want to come back to work. You know, very rightly so because they worried about the third wave. But leaders Andhra people need to make sure that while they allow for flexible working, there is also this kind of buildup of organization, we have been doing without it because we have not had a chance. So, how do you develop leaders for succession when you are not going to meet them? How do you get them to work with teams if they have not seen their teams, which is one of the first challenges, developing leaders for succession, building skills across the workforce, making sure you are getting top talent where you need from a leadership perspective? So, all of this requires people to make sure you can balance flexible working. What the HR people are also currently dealing with is the rise of the free agent or the gig worker. In India, there are labor and legislation issues, which may not make it that easy for gig workers. But today, you do see business models, whether it is a Twiggy or Zomato or Uber. Essentially, these are all gig workers, technically, apart from that you also have white collar gig workers anyhow do you really work with them? What is your employment model for them? How will that work?  If you have talent scarcity, how do you make sure that the gig worker is equally productive as a full-time employee? Then, of course, there is talent scarcity that I have been talking about. Last but not the least, organizations in India today are not just looking at sourcing from India, it was easy culturally to look at Indians, Indian people for Indian jobs, but increasingly we have realized that there lissome amount and this happens globally. There is that learning by having people who are divorced, and you will see leaders even in some of your IT industry, in your pharma industry, leaders who have basically been parachuted from elsewhere, just to make sure that the growth is kept at a certain level. You have seen that in one of the leading IT services players in India. You have a global leader. One of the leading pharma players has recently picked up Chief Operating Officer from Europe. All of these experiences, global sourcing makes it, throws a challenge of cultural integration. Milind Gandhi: I think automotive as well, quite a few of the senior managers are from outside India. Varsha Gandhi: Yes. Mil ind Gandhi: A lot of them are from Germany, I think. Marsha Gandhi: Yes. So, you would have diggers coming from anywhere in the world. And Thais equally true of other organizations also, if you see worldwide, you will see US MNCs with CEOs from all around the world. And so is it in Europe. So, you see that happening. So, this is what keeps the HR busy.  Making sure people are engaged.  They could be from different generations. They could do different modes of employment, making sure that people are learning and making sure that people are performing. Very, very, I mean this is, there is a lot of worth on the slides, but this is what the HR would typically want as results. Staying, learning, performing. Milind Gandhi: But they do not realize that HR does all this. Marsha Gandhi: Oh, yeah. Because typically, HR has always been an enabling or a support function. It is still the manager, in a sense, who is the last point of delivery for all of these experiences to the employee. It is the manager because of whom an employee stays a little longer. Furthermore, it is often the manager or the culture he is built because of which an employee learns little more. So, you have good managers, good coaches, good counselors, as managers. title: Recruitment process and onboarding
text: Business Data Management Professor G. Venkatesh Professor Doctor Mil ind GandheProfessor Marsha GandheIndian Institute of Technology Madras Recruitment process and onboarding Professor G. Venkatesh: So, Marsha you were talking about job description and then basically looking at different channels to source these resumes. And then after that, what happens after that? Presumably there is an interview and… Professor Marsha Gandhi: Then you come to the next step of the process, which is where organizations interview profiles that have been shortlisted. So, the typical process flow lookalike this, where you have the hiring managers, or the business, what we call it out here. They review the shortlisted CV, saying that these are profiles that really need what my expectations are. And they select certain candidates for either an interview or an assessment. In some of the organizations even today, in spite of the fact that you might have been working somewhere, you are required to go through some kind of either a written test or an assessment, it is called. It could be an aptitude assessment; it could be a technical assessment. And the HR typically or the recruitment organizes the logistics around these technical rounds of interviews as well as assessments. Post which an HR interview happens, to try and understand what it is that the individual wants to do? Is the individual actually a fit with the organization? Then the HR and the hiring manager create a shortlist of candidates and from that pool of people they think, meet the technical criteria as well as the cultural fit, they make an offer saying that this is the candidate we like from this list of say 20 people that we have interviewed, and we would like to McKean offer to this person, the candidate selection is done, and job offer is rolled out. The job offer consists of what is the designation of the person, what is the role that he or she will be performing? What is the location in which he or she will be in the role, in the position? Typically, in what function or department, and how much will the person get paid? These form the parts of the job offer typically. Professor Mil ind Gandhi: So, we went back to Marsha and said it looks like at the end of week three, Madurai had gone through 102 profiles that Ritesh had shared, and he had shortlisted seven profiles for the project leader position and another 35 for team member position. So, now what do Madurai and Ritesh do, just following that process that you just described? Professor Marsha Gandhi: Correct. So, Madurai and Ritesh will say 102 profiles have been gone through, we need to organize interviews for 32 people. Obviously, Madurai and Ritesh may not have the time to sit through interviews for 32 people. Typically, every interview takes an hour, assessments might take about half an hour to one hour per candidate. So, to administer a written test, Ritesh says that I have two people in my team, they will call these 25 team member positions together, they will administer a written test. And till the time of Madurai you choose two or three people from your team who can actually do a technical interview for this particular position, so that you know that the person you are getting can actually perform these tasks. So, there are two rounds of assessment, technical and HR, they create panels for each set of interviews, and they create and Ritesh creates the logistics for ensuring that the return tests are also administered.  Professor Mil ind Gandhi: And what is the result of these tests in interviews? Professor Marsha Gandhi: So, typically, whenever a position is created, we see the job description. There was a set of skills and there was a set of skills that was absolutely required and those that could be had. When they are going to these large numbers of candidate profiles, they ask the interviewing panel and typically the interviewing panel is trained for little bit in terms of what the kinds of questions to ask and how to fill out a template. So, Ritesh’s team will create a template based on that job description, saying that these earth five skills, these are the five competencies that I want. Please rate this person on how you think this person is likely to do in terms of a certain skill. So, for example, what are those? She very proficient in Java? Is he very proficient with certain platforms, certain languages? So, those competencies are created, and the interviewers typically fill this template and send it back to Ritesh to create a repository saying that these candidates, this is how they have performed per competency or per skills. Professor Mil ind Gandhi: And based on this feedback, then we select people, is it? Professor Marsha Gandhi: Correct. So, it is basically like what, the way we get a report ardor a great card, in that sense. So, Madurai and Ritesh will look, especially Madurai will look at those great cards and say that from the people that seven people that you have looked at forth project leader position, I think only this one candidate has all the five skills to a minimum requirement that I want everybody has a pass criterion. So, there is a pass criterion, so there is a pass criterion, if the rating scale is from one to five, sometimes the pass criterion usually is a minimum of a rating of four or five, anything below that is considered, maybe that this profile may not be able to do the role that Madurai wants them to do. So, in our particular case, what Madurai has gone ahead and done is that for the project leader. She has found one candidate who is suitable, meets all the criteria. So, he got pass marks in all the competitions. He has got good feedback from both the technical panel and the interview panel. And for the team members, there are seven candidates, which seem to have made the great for… Professor G. Venkatesh: So, if this one person, the product leader position you offer and the person does not join, you are in trouble? Professor Marsha Gandhi: Absolutely. So, it is, so there are various scenarios that happen. One is you make an offer and the person does not accept the offer. Then the second you make the offer, the person accepts that offer. And then later on, since he is anyway in the hiring process, he gets a better offer from somebody else, or maybe his own organization makes him counteroffer, and then he rejects the offer. So, in all these cases, what organizations typically have to do is to also select backup candidates and especially at project leader and above positions, your hiring times are much higher. So, even though you have liked only one candidate; Madurai would have thought about whether there is any other candidate that I can use as a backup profile as somebody else that I can share this offer to. Professor G. Venkatesh: But in this case, there is only one person, is there? Professor Marsha Gandhi: There is only one person that means so in case this person rejects, then it is back to square one for both Ritesh and... Professor G. Venkatesh: Square one, so it is more resume, then start again. Professor Marsha Gandhi: Absolutely, yes. Professor Mil ind Gandhi: And that would also happen if Madurai did not like any of the candidates. Professor Marsha Gandhi: Absolutely, almost, there was no candidate saying that in the interviews, they just did not make it, then the questions would be asked of Ritesh saying how did you source these kinds of profiles or what really went wrong? So, is the criteria of shortlisting the profiles, is it correct or not? Or does the profiling shortlist have to be much more stringent? So, those would be the questions that would get asked if there is not a single candidate who makes the great. So, that again that, that data will go and get revisited, saying what was the quality of candidates, whats the quality of shortlisting? Professor Mil ind Gandhi: So, GV, looks like in the team member position, even though we needed only five people. Seven candidates have made the cutoff. So, in this case let me keep two candidates as backup, maybe. Professor G. Venkatesh: Correct. I think it looks a little bit better. Professor Marsha Gandhi: Or what, Ritesh could do, and sometimes they do that is that they roll out all the seven offers and tell people to join some people will join, five people will join this month and maybe two people can join in the next month because I think totallyMadhuri needs ten team members. Professor G. Venkatesh: Correct. Anyway then it needs to arrive, correct. Professor Mil ind Gandhi: Correct. Professor Marsha Gandhi: So, the joining can be staggered.  Organizations also do this sometimes for freshers, sometimes very rarely. So, you stagger the offering, you stagger the onboarding, based on when is it that you really needed, need this. Professor G. Venkatesh: So, the typical statistics is what, I mean, if you make seven offer show many people will typically join? Professor Marsha Gandhi: In the IT industry, the rate of rejection is almost one third. So, there is a very high probability that the offer that you have made to an individual, he will typically take that and go shopping elsewhere, it is called going shopping. So, you ask for offers from other organizations, you put pressure on them as part of negotiation, as candidate, saying I have already got this offer, can you, I would need better terms on my fixed compensation, I would mean better terms on the joining bonus. Can you extend some other benefits in terms of medical insurance, or he might go back to disown organization and ask them to make a counteroffer? And some organizations do make counter offer, in case the person is very critical to a project, but otherwise no. Professor G. Venkatesh: So seven, so if you are saying one third, so out of seven, two will mean the probability is that two will reject and so only five will join? Professor Marsha Gandhi: Yes, there is a very high probability that one will reject, one may not join. That does happen, quite frequently. Professor Mil ind Gandhi: And so actually, it makes sense to go and make all the seven offers. Professor G. Venkatesh: All the seven offers. Professor Mil ind Gandhi: That is what it looks like. Professor G. Venkatesh: Looks like that. Professor Marsha Gandhi: So then we come to the next part, which is also, so it is here toucan see that. So, this is the scenario that we're talking about where the project leader candidate where you had only one person rejects the offer and two other team members also reject the offer because the salary does not meet their requirements, joining date does not work out for them or the location of the work that they want is not what is required. Or it just might be simply that they bought a better offer from some other organization. So, this is exactly typically, what we were discussing, this is what happened in this particular case too. And then, of course, Ritesh and Madurai have to go back and make sure that their project leader sourcing and shortlisting interviewing is that much better in terms of efficiency. Professor Mil ind Gandhi: So, Marsha is there something Ritesh and Madurai can do to get an assessment of whether the person is likely to join or there is nothing, it is just luck. Professor Marsha Gandhi: No, so the likelihood of a person joining is gauged by the technical panel to a certain extent but also by the HR. So, we were talking about the HR interview. IFR interview what typically organizations look at is this person is motivated by this kind fan experience and that is what they try and collect. This also happens in the technical interview, this also happens in the HR interview; they try to meet the expectations of the candidate. Now, this could be in terms of designation, so I might be a software engineer. The only reason I want to change my organization is that Want a team leader position. I want to make a sudden jump, for example. So, am I able to meet, so is the organization able to meet my requirements? Or being able to give me that kind of designation? Or the best offer that I can get is that of a senior software engineer, what is it that works? And these are the kind of cues where an assessment can remade as to how risky an offer is. Now, if you asked me, is data gathered formerly on this risk? Typically, no, it only gets reflected in your efficiency pipeline. But if they do sense a risk, then Madurai and Ritesh know that they have to look at other things and this is something that they would discuss inhere weekly update. There is no specific indicator that says, “Oh, I do not think I will be Ableton make it.” Professor Mil ind Gandhi: So, this is a little bit of a gut feel sort of decision-making? Professor Marsha Gandhi: Yes, this is a little bit of art. Professor Mil ind Gandhi: So, this GV is not something that we can look at from a data perspective. Professor Marsha Gandhi: Not from a dashboard perspective according to me. But it does get reviewed every week. Because this is actually, in a sense, a lead indicator that tells Manchurian Ritesh how well the process is going, whether they are comfortable or not comfortable asset. Professor G. Venkatesh: So, I mean, but so, the data you gather is, so this is more like a data that tells you about how well your process of recruitment is going whereas most of the data you have gathered is in terms of resumes, it is basically raw data. Professor Marsha Gandhi: That is raw data. Professor G. Venkatesh: An evaluation of the candidates, data that is relevant to the evaluation of candidates. Professor Marsha Gandhi: Absolutely. Professor G. Venkatesh: But the process data itself is not something that you are capturing and it is, so it is nothing much to do. Professor Marsha Gandhi: So, organizations do capture one aspect of how easy the process was. Once you ask a candidate to come over for an interview, you do gather his or her perception about what were the challenges? Professor G. Venkatesh: How feedback? Professor Marsha Gandhi: So, that feedback is collected. And people do, but it is a long term process in terms of trying to change anything in the recruitment process. It might not be easily done. But what cannot or what is not gauged in a very concrete fashion is, if the offers being rolled out what is the probability that the person will pick it up and will join? That can only be analyzed by a lag indicator saying this is what our track record shows for the last six months one year or for this particular position, this is what it takes. Professor Mil ind Gandhi: Now, this is a little different GV from all other processes we look at, because there we were mostly looking at reasonably hard data. This is a little bit of probabilistic sort of … Professor G. Venkatesh: Correct. Professor Marsha Gandhi: Yes, so while your software hardware, it is very difficult to put number to the software as they call it. So, wetware always has a little bit of a margin for error, when you make a decision for that. Professor Mil ind Gandhi: So, maybe work while Marsha if you could explain to us what earth detailed steps in this offer making because this process seems to be a little fuzzy and uncertain. So, maybe if you can just walk us through the details of how the offer is made that will be good. Professor Marsha Gandhi: Sure, so once we have decided that this is the best candidate forth project manager role. From the interview template Ritesh knows that the expectation of this particular individual is to get 18 lakhs salary fixed in a year if he would be happy with being with the designation project leader. And he is looking forward to having a team of at least four or five people under him. So, Ritesh knows the basis of the HR interview that is done. He has to go back and check with HR and with Madurai, whether this will create any disparity with the employees that you already have. So, you could have really great performing individuals who have not yet made the project leader grade, is that will that be a clash? Will there be people from the same batch that Ritesh hires, but because he is hiring them from outside, he ends up paying them more giving them a higher designation, which sometimes causes a little bit of heartburn with employees that are already there in your organization. To prevent that most HR teams create a certain kind of saying that if you have position at this level, this is a basket of designations that you can offer the person. If you have a person that you are hiring at this particular level and all of this is from the indent. So, the indent has already been approved, saying that you can hire a person at this particular grade. So, at that particular grade, you can offer him a salary anywhere between 15 lakhs to 22 lakhs depending on what experience that person gets. I am giving a very broad range. Usually the ranges could be even shorter at a lower level. So, all of that is taken into consideration. HR has spoken to say that this is what we replanning to offer. It contains as I said the offer letter contains details of designation, details of what the benefits will be and of course, details of compensation. So, what is the salary the person will receive and this offer letter, the broad aspects, again you get a quick approval from maybe Madurai if there are any exceptions, then they would have to approve. And if there are as I said any exceptions we will do a case by case study saying does this make sense or not? Is there some way we can get this particular offer to fit in our existing organizational structure? They create an Excel sheet which Ritesh will create and tell the person saying this is what we are willing to offer you, are you interested. In the Excel sheet what typically Ritesh will do is offer the candidate a breakup of that 18 lakhs figure saying that 18 lakhs figure, so much of your money will go to Provident Fund.So, much of your money will go as retrials. This is what you will get in hand, this is what Weill allocate towards, say HR, medical, this is where you will be able to save taxes. So, these are the kind of benefits that Ritesh will talk to the candidate. Ritesh will also make a pitch to the candidate saying that apart from what you see on this offer letter, these are the benefits which the organization offers. So, we give you a medical insurance of five lakhs covering all your family, we allow you apparently insurance top up Asia is because of some of the things that employers do look at when they are joining an organization.  Once this is shared, once the Excel sheet is shared and the candidate says yes, I am fine with this breakup, I am fine with this take home but I want a joining bonus and all those discussions are done. The Ritesh will then actually roll out the offer letter, which will then get signed by the individuals saying that yes, I am joining, and they will take a decision as to what will be the onboarding date.  So, typically the team member will say, “Oh, I am this organization, our notice period is three months.” Then there will be a certain negotiation on the notice period. Once all of that is agreed to the onboarding date is decided, typically it takes two months for a person to hand over his existing responsibilities and join another organization. So, once that is done, then all that remains is for Ritesh to hand over this particular successful recruitment to the HR who will pick this on, make sure that the person is on boarded. And of course, the hiring manager Madurai who will keep in touch with the candidate to make sure that the candidate is not losing interest in the organization, a lot of things can happen in two months. So, that is that again is the way the probability that we had discussed earlier is managed by keeping in constant touch with the candidate making sure the person disengaged and making sure he is still, or she is still interested in joining the organization. So, that is the cell that is required at that point of time. Professor G. Venkatesh: There is a lot of work for HR. I mean, I thought it was just about interviewing, but it looks like they have to spend a lot of effort in basically making. Professor Marsha Gandhi: There are a lot of transactional activities. Professor G. Venkatesh: Transactional activities, it is only correct, getting the correct offer out to the candidate, it was a negotiation process, I did not realize that, with each candidate one by one they have to negotiate the offer letter. Professor Marsha Gandhi: Absolutely and each aspect of the offer letter. Professor G. Venkatesh: And then you have to keep in touch with the employee as the prospective person till the person comes on board. Professor Marsha Gandhi: So, then, typically, either Ritesh’s team will conduct the onboarding, there is one whole set of documents that is required by organizations to make sure that the onboarding is as smooth as possible typically, organizations to a greater degree of detail or lesser degree of detail, asked for educational qualification certificates, asked for prior experience certificates, asked for relieving, so you get a relieving letter from your existing organization. Saying that yes, Marsha worked in this organization for five years as a project leader, she washier from 1st Jan 1995 to 31st December 2000. And this is, this was her designation typical that is a relieving letter that is given by organizations. So, Ritesh would share the contract letter with the pre-boarding document checklist. So, this is called a pre-boarding document. Typically, you will also ask for an identity proof from the person as well as for a PAN card. So, these are some of the requirements that an organization is required by the government Mohave in place before they do any transaction of salaries. So, there is something called a tax-deductible source for which they will need the PAN, they will need the identity card, they might need certain bank details from you before the payroll process and all of that is taken care of in the pre-boarding documents. Since this is largely administrator, they will be a junior HR person in Ritesh’s business team, who will take care of all this and make sure that all the documents are fine. These documents are then sent in for a verification process, they will also arrange for relocation. So, there ascertain relocation benefits that are given in case somebody has to move cities, say from Bangalore to Mumbai or from Mumbai to Delhi in terms of one truck worth of goods that cane transported. So, that payment will be made, some amount of rental advance might be given. So, all of that is started that processes started, the person is then cleared for induction, there ISA signing that happens on the first date and identity card is given a whole starting kit is given which includes typically the system, laptop, an employee handbook, other branded materials the company wishes to give and then posts that the individual the candidate who is now an employee goes through a set of training sessions. Saying how things work in this particular organization? So, in tech enterprises, what is the appraisal process, when you get paid, how do you look for reimbursements and that typically happens for anywhere between fifteen days to thirty days, depending on how thorough the induction and the onboarding process. Employees also get to meet their future managers, future team leaders as well as their team members during this induction process. And they try to make it as easy as possible for the person to get integrated into the system and then start performing. So, that is the last step of the recruitment process, which is called induction and onboarding. This is where the handover happens from recruitment to HR and the recruiting manager. Professor Mil ind Gandhi: So, the GV this sounds a little bit like taking admission to college, the things. Professor G. Venkatesh: Liked that, looks that, yeah. Professor Mil ind Gandhi: Because we joined a new college also we have to submit mark lists, all this identity proof, everything, only taking in this case still bank details, etc., little more information is needed because they have to pay us a salary. Professor Marsha Gandhi: So typically, the average time taken to fill a pre-boarding documents checklist is about six to eight hours. It takes almost a whole day. Professor G. Venkatesh: A whole day. Professor Marsha Gandhi: So, a lot of organizations have tried to see how it can become more efficient by allowing people to upload all these documents online. But just verifying these documents sometimes takes that much time. Professor Mil ind Gandhi: Say a lot of paperwork. Professor Marsha Gandhi: Lots of paperwork, lots of forms to be filled. You will have to fill nominee forms for medical insurance, you will have to fill pf, pf transfer forms, you would have to fill any other benefits that you are taking over those kinds of forms. So, to be fair, it ISA very admin intensive process. Professor G. Venkatesh: You are right.

title: Production scheduling data - plan vs actual
text: Business Data Management Professor G. Venkatesh Professor Doctor Mil ind Gandhi Professor Mister Siva Kumar Padmanabhan Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Siva Kumar: Now we co me to production schedules. After having seen how much I need to make of gear, a particular gear, in this case, I am taking the gear 6a, which is the gear that goes into assembly n umber 6, and then 6a uses a particular type of blank to convert that blank into the gear called 6a. So, now I am at a very detailed level where I am talking about just 6a, this is on the factory floor.  I am saying I want to make 6a for a particular month, which is October 2019. Now, there are two steps as I said in making that gear 6a, one is robbing and the other is broaching. So, the robbing, think of it as cutting the teeth into the blank, on the outside, where broaching is cutting the things that I need inside, the circular thing and that particular join kind of thing, which i s used to join this clear tone of the gear, the shaft and so on.  So, those are the two steps and these are normally what are called workstations. So, first I have to do ho being, take the blank and robbing, I get a gear, which is called the outside) then I have to go to the workstation called broaching where actually I do the internal shaping of that gear, and then I am done with that gear. I have now got gear 6a which I can use to assemble with 6b and create gear 6, which is later down in the production.  So, I am only now talking about robbing and broaching in the two workstations, workstation 1 and workstation 2. Now, there is a concept of scrap I want to introduce. Scrap means that when you make these gears, you will not always get how much you want to make, because some parts will not have the correct shape, for some reason the machine is overheated, or because the particular blank was not of good quality.  So, when you get to inspection, which is a quality inspection, you might have rejected, so some parts of the product will get rejected. That is the concept of scrap that shows in the spreadsheet.  When it says standard scrap two and a half percent, what we are saying is that I expect that I will not get, I will only get 97.5 percent of the loading into the robbing workstation.  So, if I start robbing 100 plans, I would only get 97.5, or rather to make it easier if I start 200 I will only get 195 at the end of hobby ING, which are good parts, the rest of it is cracked. The five parts are not good to be used, so they are, scrap means they are thrown away or sold an s scrap, and so on. So, that is the concept. And then you see what is called the loading ? The loading is really important.  And I want to spend a minute on that calendar piece, right here. This is for the robbing workstation, this is the first workstation that manufacturing process, here I am saying based on my production plan for g ear 6a, which we saw earlier for October, if you see, I want to make 9000 units, so that is the actual target. So, if you go up to the top of the worksheet again you see that the target is 9000.  But I might not get 9000. So, if the target is 9000 then the detail ed scheduler says, this is what I want to make every single day of the month to reach that 9000 units a ND each day speaking, so you see the quantities there, day one I want to make 400, day 2 I want to make 800, and so on. And there is a reason why you will see that only some weeks have quantities in them.  The reason is that I want to make gear 6a on alternate weeks, so you see the week one the quantities are there, week two there are zero quantities because that machine is now being used to make another gear during that week. In week three I come back to making 6a, in week four I make some other gear, week five I again come back to making 6a, so this is typically how machines are scheduled.  They make multiple products, and they have to change over from one product to another and that will be set up to make the new product. So, this is the picture for October 2019, this is what I want to make for the robbing workstation and the next calendar shows what I want to make in the broaching workstation. Now, you see that the quantities for broaching that I have planned are already less than the quantities for bobbin g.  So, you see that while I want to do 800 in robbing, I want to do 780 in broaching and that is because of the scrap factor I told you about like, two and a half percent of that 800 will get scrapped, I know that is the average that gets scrap ed, so my goal itself is only to do the project for 780 because of the two and a half percent loss in the process. So, this is the monthly amount that I want to make for each of these products.  Mil ind Gandhi: So, this necessarily assume s that ho being is done before broaching, you cannot do it the other way round.  Siva Kumar: Yes. There is a sequence involved. You are very right there, I want to get the robbing done, then I want to get the broaching done.  G. Venkatesh: So, you have 0 on Monday. Presumably, you have e 0 because you have not got any units from the robbing workstation.  Siva Kumar: Yes. And this will become very clear in the following table right that I am showing the yellow table below, which shows what is the actual detailed production schedule for 6a in October 2019. So, you see the first day of the month there are two shifts, I am operating two shifts in my factory ; that means, a morning shift and an evening shift.  And whenever I start the week, the very first day, the Monday of the week, the first shift in the robbing workstation, I am going to do the changeover, that means those 8 hours I am preparing the particular robbing workstation to make gear 6a, several settings need to be done to make sure it is cutting a t the right frequency and all of these things. I need to instruct those settings, record those settings, make do some trials, and all that, so that takes the entire shift. So, that shift there is no production, which is expected in the robbing workstation. Now, it is ready for production. When it comes to shift ING to the plane, the labor comes in, they start doing the hobby ING, and they plan to make 400 units in that shift and then that machine keeps running on 6a for the rest of the week, so you can see that Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday if you go, look to the right you will see that the quantity 400 is being planned regularly.  But when it comes to Saturday I want to stop. I do only one shift on Saturday, the 6th of October and then I have to leave o né shift for what is called maintenance, so every time the machine is run for a week I need one shift of maintenance, which means I need to possibly clean the machine, I need to lubricate the machine, make sure that there are no heating issues.  I want to do some sort of lubrication so that shift is dedicated to maintenance. Essentially, in this case, we have only 6 days of which two shifts are used one for changeover and one for maintenance, and so I have the remaining 10 shifts in which to do the production, so that is what you see in the plan. There are only 10 shifts that are planned.  Similarly, if you see the next line you will see that the broaching machine in a very similar way first on a Monday morning I do maintenance for one shift, then I do change over which means I am setting up the broaching machine from gear 6a, that takes a whole shift and on the next day, Tuesday morning is when I start the broaching operation. And I only plan 97.5, 390 units because I know that the 400 that is made in the previous.  So, the shift 2 of the 1st of October, those 400 I plan, only 390 will be made, so that then j umps into the next machine, that is why you see 390 on the shift one of the 2nd October and so on it goes, and then you see on Saturday that app roaching all so stops and that is the goal.  Now, this is the way it works and then if you keep going to the right you will see for the next week this machine is not used, robbing and broaching up in the plan they are the ) because I am now making 6b, so you see after the changeover gear 6b is starting and Sunday is a holiday, that is what it is showing, but the next week if you see gear 6b is being made in that particular robbing and broaching line and no production of 6a is happening.  And then the following week if you keep going to the right you will see, again I will start making 6a, so maintenance and changeover, now I have started making 6a and the following week 6b and so on. So, that is the pattern you will see throughout this plan. So, this is the detailed schedule for the machine line for that month. So, that is what we are seeing here, in the plan, right this is my plan, my action may be different, which is the next table.  So, if you come to the next table it shows actual production. So, the first table says this is my plan, I want to make so much, in each shift, in each machine, but then you see the actual, you will see that the n umber that is made is very different from what we anticipate because, in reality, a worker could make a mistake or there could be a problem in the machine or there could be some defects in the incoming raw material batch that cause more scrap than anticipated and so on.  So, in the second table, you will see that the actual quantities that are being made from robbing and bro aching are very different. So, I plan to make 400, but I only made 388. Similarly, the next shift I plan to make 400, I hit 390, which is my full plan and there are some shifts where I actually make 378 and so on. So, every shift you get the actual production. Now, you also see some cells that say breakdown maintenance.  What happened there is that the robbing machine had an unplanned breakdown. So, an unplanned breakdown can happen due to many reasons, it could be an electrical fault, which meant there was no power on that line, or it could be a jam in the machine, which meant the machine had to be completely taken down and some of it had to be taken down and rebuilt, or it could be a flywheel, which got broken.  So, there are several reasons why breakdown maintenance happens, and then that maintenance happens, in a very simple way I have shown here is that the entire shift production is lost, I wanted to make 400, but I did not make anything, there is 0 production, in the third of October, first shift in the ho being machine, there was a breakdown and there was no production.  And you see the impact further down, if you see the same day on the second shift the b roaching, I plan to make 390, but I am making zero because no hobby parts are coming to my broaching area at all, because of the breakdown maintenance. S o, you see how breakdown means disrupts further in the production chain because of that sort of thing happening. You see the actual quantities.  Mil ind Gandhi: When you are doing maintenance, I understand if there are five machines in the entire, the line then each worker is doing maintenance on each of those machines and that is understood, but if there is a breakdown, let us say one machine has broken down, then the other four are also idle because just one has broken down, the other four can not continue doing their task.  Siva Kumar: Yes, if it is subsequent in the production process. So, if the output of this machine is required for other machines to work, then they will all have to be ideal, that is why you do not want to have too much dependence on just one machine in the organization, but if you have four robbing or five hobby ING machines in parallel and one of them broke down, there is no problem, because you can continue using the other four hobby ING machines. There will be a ripple effect because the product is a semifinished product or the work in progress is not available for further steps in the production operation.  Mil ind Gandhi: Understood.  Siva Kumar: I am just going to conclude by saying that the last row you see is the cumulative output, that means after broaching, that is when I am finish ed, the gear is fully available, how much I can make, so that will keep adding, every day's production, every shift production will keep adding and then yo use e at the end of the month how much I made for gear 6a.  So, the last thing will show you how much was made, and it is less than what I planned. So, if you go all the way you will see that the cumulative output at the end of the month was 8690 units, so on the last day of the month after shift two was finished I was able to make a total of 8690 gear 6a against a production schedule of 9000. So, if you go back to our previous table and see October 2019, how much do I want to make for year 6a ?  It was in the previous worksheet we saw it was 9000, but in reality, I could only make 8690 units, so that is why we are trying to say that the actual production will differ from the planned production and the closer we can get your actual production to the planned production, the more your overall efficiency is from a manufacturing perspective.  G. Venkatesh : So, is that the key question in this Siva, I mean, that you would want to see the effectiveness or efficiency or some metric, some measure of how good production planning is and executions ? Siva Kumar: Yes. There is a very commonly used metric called overall equipment efficiency and there is a very nice illustration that shows how that is calculated, so I wonder if you can drop that particular picture.  Mil ind Gandhi : You want me to bring up the picture Siva?  Siva Kumar: Yes, for the overall equipment efficiency that will show how it is calculated.  Yes, so this is the most commonly used metric to evaluate manufacturing performance, at the end of the day there are world-class factories that do well and there are factories that are not that good, that do not do well, and how do you differentiate how good is the manufacturing system. The most commonly used formula for that is overall equipment effectiveness. It is a gold standard for measuring productivity.  And that depends on, it is a compound metric, it is based on three things, the first thing is the availability. So, the availability is how much time was lost from the planned production hours.  We saw that the ho being machine had a breakdown in one of the shifts in the month, so if your plan for the whole month was 20 shifts, and one of those shifts was a breakdown, that means that time is lost.  So, out of the 20 should say 8 hours each, so 160 hours w ere the planned production hours in this case, but the lost time is 8 hours let us say. So, the availability is 160 minus 8 divided by 160, which is 152 by 160, which then translates to 95. So, your availability for that month for the hobby ING was 95. So, that is the first part of the ONE.  So, if the machine was fully available, there was no breakdown, there was no lost time, then your availability is 100 percent, which is the ideal scenario.  If you are given already a shift for maintenance at the beginning of the week, if that was done well, you should not have lost time, because your plan should be equal to your actions, and your availability would be 100 percent.  But in reality, these things happen, so your availability will be less than 100 percent. The next part is the performance of the machine, which means what is the actual machine speed divided by the design machine speed. So, this means that in some operations, in some types of manufacturing, you want the machine to be able to produce a certain n umber of units per hour, but in reality, the machine may be running slower or the people that are running the machine may not be most -efficient.  So, your actual output is slower, or the production is slower than what you have planned, which affects performance. If the design machines speed was 100 and the action was only 90, the performance becomes 90 percent, and then finally the quality, which I talked about scrap, which says if I wanted to make 100 units of good product, but five of t hose turned out to be a bad product, because they did not meet the specifications for quality or whatever, and they become scrap, and they are thrown out, then I get only 95.  So, 95 by 100 then becomes the quality percentage. So, the quality percentage will be high when your input materials are of high quality, your process is very well-defined and stable and does not create errors, then you get 100 quality, if none of these, some of these things are not there then your quality will decrease and some of the product you make you have to throw away. So, ONE Overall Equipment Efficiency is effectiveness, it is the multiplication of all these three ratios, it is availability multi plied by performance multiplied by quality. So, if your availability is very good, if your performance is very good and your quality is very good, then your ONE will be very good. In the industry even very mature manufacturing companies have not achieved anywhere near 100 percent ONE because they would have some losses.  So, for example, if your availability was only 90 percent, your performance was only 90 percent and your quality was only 90 percent, then you can imagine the ONE will quickly drop, even though you are 90 on each when you multiply all the three 90s, now you are looking at 72, 73 percent ONE, which is kind of what is the best in class. Many companies are at 40, 45, or 50 percent ONE.  G. Venkatesh: 4 5 percent ONE, that is what it is.  Siva Kumar: Yeah, in many competitive industries, average companies will be 40 to 50 percent because there will be 80 in each, but when you multiply cumulatively, it becomes hard to achieve more than 5 0 – 60 percent.  So, world-class companies are in the 70 to 80 percent range of ONE.  G. Venkatesh: A ND the reason you have decomposed the ONE into these three things, availability, performance, and quality is because the kind of control that you need for each of these is different, what you need to do to, improve availability is one thing, what you need for performance something else and quality so meshing else.  Siva Kumar: That is a perfect point. Their responsibilities within the manufacturing company are also somewhat different. So, for example, the maintenance department is mostly evaluated on the availability, so if they are doing really good preventive maintenance and so on, the availability will be very high.  The human resources training affects performance, so if the people that are running the machine are not fully trained in it, and they are not very skilled in it, it will slow down be cause somewhere somebody will not be able to meet the required speed with which they are doing some operations, so typically that affects performance and then the supply side, the procurement department, et cetera, they have a lot to do with quality.  But also the training and everything affects quality, but definitely, if you do not get good raw materials the quality will suffer, so these are all somewhat different, like who has got more influence or impact on these three things.  Mil ind Gandhi: Should we go back to the Excel sheet ?  Siva Kumar: Yes.  Mil ind Gandhi: we were done with that Excel sheet, Siva? Siva Kumar: Yes. That is an interesting Excel sheet, and some of the questions I have. For example, what is the ONE for the different machines and doe s it changes week to week ? Is robbing better or broaching better, so in terms of ONE?  So, those are some of the questions to be analyzed. Another question that arises is - Is there a difference between shifts ?  A lot of companies consider this deeply because sometimes, especially when you are running night shifts, performance, for example, may not be as high as day shift, so do you see differences in the shifts in this case ? It is also a good question to analyze. Mil ind Gandhi: Okay.

title: Unit level profitability and material re-ordering data
text: Business Data Management Professor. G. Venkatesh Professor. Doctor Mil ind Gandhi Professor. Siva Kumar Padmanabhan Indian Institute of Technology, Madras Unit Level Profitability and Material Re -ordering Data Professor Siva: This data starts to speak about the actual costs and margins of the different products. So, we have seen that the company makes 10 different gear assemblies. We have shown a couple of them here, 3, 4, 5, and 6. And we know from the very first spreadsheet, what is the sales price of these products. You looked at it for the 6 month s from October 2020 to March 2021.  So, each of these products sells at a certain price. But how do we know which products are making more money for the company ? Which products are more profitable ? Where I should put more of my focus because it is one thing to sell them a lot of products. But if the products are not getting you the profit, then that is not going to help the business. Whereas, there could be some products that may not sell that many quantities, but are more profitable than others.  So, we need to understand as a business, which products are bringing margin or the profit margin for the company. And what this table shows is how you break down the standard costs and profitability of different products. So, think of it as different cost components that a product is made of. So, if you feel here making your assembly number 3, different cost components go into it. We know that gear assembly 3 requires gears 3 A a d B, gears 3A requires a certain type of blank and 3 B requires a certain type of blank. So, the direct materials are the cost of the material that is used in producing that particular gear. So, that will be the sum of the costs of blank use d for 3A plus the cost of the blank for 3B forms of direct material costs of that gear. So that materials or the cost of the materials are directly attributable through the bill of materials to the particular finished product. The next part is the…  Professor G. Venkatesh: The reason this is left blank is I guess you are expected to find it from the cost of the blanks, it can be determined on something else s o that is why it is not in.  Professor Siva: Rather spreadsheets that will give you what is the different parts of different blanks. So, we want you to figure out what is the cost of the direct material for gear assembly 3.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Okay.  Professor Siva: By following the bill of materials, you will be able to trace and find out. Direct labor is another co st component, which is the people that are involved in actually making that particular product, those lines the robbing line, the broaching line, the assembly line that is used for that particular gear assembly, that is direct labor. So, all the salaries, the benefits, the overtime, etcetera, that are being paid to the employees or contractors o r the staff that make those products most direct labor, and the third is production overhead.  Professor G. Venkatesh: And in that direct labor, we can compute it for on something else that is available or … Professor Siva: No, I think that should be provided, I think that might have been.  Professor Siva: So, there might be, it is that in this next spreadsheet.  Professor G. Venkatesh: Okay, okay, okay.  Professor Siva: The third one is production overhead. So, if you look in the factory, you can see that some of the components you can directly cost it, it is the direct materials and some people you know on working on the lines that are specifically used for making gear assembly 3, but you will find a lot of the cost of the factory is not cannot be directly connected to one product. For example, all the maintenance crews all the lighting and electricity that is used to run the factory overall overhead lighting which eliminate s the entire factory.  The IR conditioning if it is required, the production supervisor so may supervise multiple lines, and the factory manager's salary, all of these things are not from production overhead they are also indirect materials. So, the materials that we use to lubricate all the machines that we buy, lubricants if I use, or it could also be other types of materials that we use in a common way like for example, if we buy water to run the factory, or if we buy a certain cleaning agent to clean the factory.  Though, all those things form production overheads. So, those are all the costs that have occurred in the factory, but cannot be directly connected to one product. We collect all those costs together and then a portion that. To apportion means divided in some way so that it is allocated to all the different products. So, that is called production overhead. So, here you can see the amount of production overhead that we have decided to attribute on a portion to each of the products. And there are different ways in which an apportionment is done. There is activity -based costing is one way in which you can create a better apportionment of the overhead to the different products and so on. And then there is finally, general and administrative overhead.
